As written, creating a group with a non-default alias level loses that setting.

create does not validate or reject duplicate group names explicitly, relying on model validation error rendering

create builds a Group with the given name and calls save; if the name is a duplicate the model validation fails and render_json_error group returns the errors — this is handled. However there is no test covering duplicate-name creation or invalid names (spaces, etc.), and the client's save error handler (admin-group.js.es6 line 85) does $.parseJSON(e.responseText).errors which assumes the errors key exists. Add a spec for duplicate name creation to lock in the error contract between server and client.

each over members uses itemView="group-member" but the view/template naming may not resolve, and members is set asynchronously

The template iterates `{{each member in members itemView="group-member"}}`. The view is defined as an ES6 module default export in admin/views/group-member.js.es6 with templateName "admin/templates/group_member". In this Ember version, string itemView lookup resolves against the global namespace (Discourse.GroupMemberView), not the ES6 module registry, so the custom view (and its "item" class used by the .ac-wrap .item CSS) may never be applied, falling back to a default item view. Additionally, members is populated asynchronously by findMembers() called in setupController; before the first response the each renders nothing, which is acceptable, but there is no loading/empty state. Verify the view actually resolves (e.g. register it globally or use the resolver-compatible naming) — otherwise the remove button styling/behaviour relies on a view that may not exist.

findMembers clamps offset against a stale user_count, allowing out-of-range offsets and wrong pagination state

offset is computed as Math.min(this.get("user_count"), Math.max(this.get("offset"), 0)). On the first call user_count is the default 0, so the clamped offset is always 0 regardless of the requested offset — fine initially, but after members are removed the stored user_count shrinks while this.get("offset") may still point past the end; the clamp uses the old total, so the server returns an empty page while the client believes it is showing page N. Worse, the server response then sets offset from result.meta.offset, but the request was already sent with a bogus offset. The clamp should be against the server-reported total after the first fetch, or simply trust the server to handle out-of-range offsets and let meta correct the state; as written it can permanently wedge pagination after membership changes.

findMembers is fired without awaiting, and the public members page has no pagination UI despite the endpoint now supporting limit/offset

The public group members page calls model.findMembers() which requests only the first 50 members (model default limit: 50) and the template renders all of `members` with no pagination controls. Previously the endpoint returned all members (up to 200 for automatic groups); now large groups (e.g. trust_level_0 with thousands of users) will silently show only the first 50 members on the public page with no way to see the rest. Either add pagination to the public page or keep the public route requesting a larger limit. This is a functional regression for group member browsing.

members endpoint has no upper bound on limit, enabling expensive full-table scans / large payloads

limit = (params[:limit] || 50).to_i is used directly in .limit(limit) with no maximum clamp and no validation that it is positive. A caller can pass limit=100000000 (or a negative value, which in some ActiveRecord adapters disables the LIMIT clause entirely) and force the server to serialize every member of a large automatic group (e.g. trust_level_0, everyone) in one request, a trivial denial-of-service vector. Clamp limit to a sane maximum (e.g. [limit, 100].min) and reject non-positive values.

members response shape changed from a bare array (render_serialized) to {members, meta}, a breaking change for existing API consumers

Previously the endpoint returned render_serialized(members.to_a, GroupUserSerializer) — a top-level JSON array. It now returns { members: [...], meta: {...} }. Any existing client (including older cached JS, third-party API consumers, or the previous version of the Ember model which did result.map(...)) will break because result is no longer an array. The Ember model was updated in the same PR (result.members.map), so first-party code is consistent, but this is still a public API contract break that should be called out in the PR description and ideally versioned or kept backwards compatible.

members template iterates `members` but the group-members route sets the model to the group and members are loaded onto the group object, not the controller The route (group-members.js.es6) sets controller.set("model", model) where model is the Group, then calls model.findMembers() which sets `members` on the Group model. The template `{{#each m in members}}` looks up `members` on the controller (the template's context), not on the group model. Unless the controller proxies unknown properties to the model (ObjectController proxying was removed/changed depending on Ember version — this route's controller is a plain controller, not ObjectController), `members` will be undefined and the list will always be empty. The template should iterate `model.members` (or the route should set controller.set('members', ...) after findMembers resolves). Also note the stray `` on line 19 with no matching opening tag inside the each block, which produces invalid HTML.

offset is not validated and negative offsets produce undefined SQL behaviour

offset = params[:offset].to_i is passed straight into .offset(offset). A negative offset generates invalid SQL on PostgreSQL (OFFSET must be >= 0) and raises a 500. Validate offset >= 0 (the Ember client already clamps with Math.max(offset, 0), but the endpoint is public and must not trust clients).

remove_member deletes the join row but never saves the group, so the removal is not persisted

group.users.delete(user_id) issues a DELETE against the group_users join table directly and returns the number of rows deleted; it does not modify the in-memory association in a way that group.save would persist, and more importantly the subsequent `if group.save` only saves group attribute changes — the membership deletion has already been executed (or, depending on association caching, may be lost when the association is reloaded). The spec passes only because it reloads and the DELETE already hit the DB, but the code is misleading and fragile: if the DELETE affected 0 rows (user not a member) the endpoint still returns success_json, and the save call is dead weight. The method should check the delete result and return an error when the user was not a member, and should not rely on group.save for a membership change.

save error handler assumes e.responseText is valid JSON and .errors is an array

var message = $.parseJSON(e.responseText).errors; will throw if the response body is not JSON (e.g. a 500 HTML error page or an empty body) or if errors is a string, producing an unhandled exception inside the rejection handler and leaving disableSave stuck... actually .finally resets it, but the bootbox.alert never shows and the error is swallowed into an uncaught TypeError. Guard the parse (try/catch or check e.responseJSON) and fall back to a generic message.

setupController calls findMembers on every entry but never resets offset, so returning to a group shows a stale page

The Group model persists `offset` as instance state. Navigating away from a group (e.g. after paging to page 3) and back reuses the same Group object from the adminGroups model list (model hook finds it by name in the already-loaded collection), so findMembers() is called with the old offset and the admin lands on page 3 instead of page 1. Reset group.set('offset', 0) in setupController (or in the route's model/afterModel) before calling findMembers.

update uses Group.find which raises RecordNotFound (500) instead of a 404 for unknown ids

Group.find(params[:id].to_i) raises ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound for a missing group, which Rails turns into a 500-level error page in production rather than a 404. The same pattern exists in destroy (line 50), add_members (line 66) and remove_member (line 85). Use Group.find_by(id: ...) and render a 404, or rescue RecordNotFound, so clients get a correct status code.

true_positives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New ensure_loaded! method has a race condition: check-then-act on @loaded_locales without holding LOAD_MUTEX

The added `I18n.ensure_loaded!(locale)` method does `@loaded_locales ||= []` then `load_locale locale unless @loaded_locales.include?(locale)`. The `include?` check and the subsequent `load_locale` call are not atomic. `load_locale` itself acquires `LOAD_MUTEX`, but the `unless @loaded_locales.include?(locale)` guard is evaluated outside the mutex. In a multi-threaded server (Puma/Unicorn with threads), two threads can both observe that the locale is not loaded and both call `load_locale`. Inside `load_locale`, the mutex serializes them, and the second thread will see `@loaded_locales.include?(locale)` is true after acquiring the mutex and return early — so the actual file loading is protected. However, the `@loaded_locales ||= []` initialization is itself racy: if `@loaded_locales` is nil and two threads call `ensure_loaded!` concurrently, both may assign a new array, and one thread's `<<` in `load_locale` could be lost, causing a locale to be considered unloaded and re-loaded repeatedly, or worse, the array reference seen by `translate` (line 68: `load_locale(config.locale) unless @loaded_locales.include?(config.locale)`) may be a stale array missing entries. The consequence: duplicate translation file loading (performance degradation) and potential `nil` errors if `@loaded_locales` is read as nil in `translate` before assignment completes. The fix: initialize `@loaded_locales = []` at class load time (e.g., in the module body or via `reload!`), and make `ensure_loaded!` delegate entirely to `load_locale` (which already handles the mutex and the include? check internally), i.e., just `def ensure_loaded!(locale); load_locale(locale); end`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).

false_positives.candidate:
FallbackLocaleList#[] can return nil elements and does not guard against nil locale, causing NoMethodError or broken fallback chains

`FallbackLocaleList#[]` builds `[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en].uniq.compact`. If `locale` is nil (e.g., `I18n.locale` is nil in some code path before `set_locale` runs, such as background jobs, mailers, or initializers that call `I18n.t` before any request), the array becomes `[nil, :en_default, :en].uniq.compact` — compact removes nil so it is safe there — but `SiteSetting.default_locale` may itself be nil or blank during early boot or in test environments before the settings table is seeded, and calling `.to_sym` on nil raises `NoMethodError`. Additionally, `FallbackLocaleList` subclasses `Hash` but never populates itself; `I18n.fallbacks = FallbackLocaleList.new` relies entirely on the overridden `[]`, which is fine, but `I18n::Backend::Fallbacks` internally may call other Hash methods (e.g., `key?`, `fetch`, `each`) that will behave incorrectly on an empty Hash subclass. The consequence: a `NoMethodError` on nil during boot or in edge cases, or fallbacks silently not working because the Fallbacks module iterates the hash rather than calling `[]`. The class should not subclass Hash; it should be a plain object responding to `[]`, and `SiteSetting.default_locale` should be guarded (e.g., `SiteSetting.default_locale.to_s.to_sym` with a fallback to `:en`).

FallbackLocaleList#ensure_loaded! calls I18n.ensure_loaded! which does not exist in stock i18n gem, creating hidden coupling and potential NoMethodError

`FallbackLocaleList#ensure_loaded!` calls `I18n.ensure_loaded! l`. This method is only defined by the freedom patch in `lib/freedom_patches/translate_accelerator.rb`. The initializer comment says `# order: after 02-freedom_patches.rb`, implying it relies on load order. However, initializers in Rails are loaded alphabetically, and `config/initializers/i18n.rb` will load after `02-freedom_patches.rb` only if that file exists in `config/initializers/` — but `translate_accelerator.rb` is in `lib/freedom_patches/`, not `config/initializers/`. The freedom patches are typically loaded via `config/initializers/02-freedom_patches.rb` which requires files from `lib/freedom_patches/`. If the load order is not guaranteed (e.g., if `02-freedom_patches.rb` is renamed or the require mechanism changes), `I18n.ensure_loaded!` will be undefined and `set_locale` will raise `NoMethodError` on every request. Even if load order is currently correct, this is fragile coupling. The consequence: potential `NoMethodError: undefined method 'ensure_loaded!' for I18n:Module` on every request if load order breaks. The fix: either define `ensure_loaded!` directly on `I18n` in the initializer itself (not relying on the freedom patch), or add an explicit `require 'freedom_patches/translate_accelerator'` at the top of the initializer, or guard with `I18n.respond_to?(:ensure_loaded!)`. Better: move the `ensure_loaded!` definition into the initializer or a core lib file that is guaranteed to load before initializers.

Fallbacks module included into wrong backend class, breaking I18n fallback behavior

The initializer does `I18n.backend.class.send(:include, I18n::Backend::Fallbacks)`. At initializer time, `I18n.backend` is an instance of `I18n::Backend::Simple` (the default backend), so this includes Fallbacks into `I18n::Backend::Simple` itself. However, the translate_accelerator freedom patch reopens `I18n::Backend::Simple` and the app's actual translation path goes through the patched `I18n.translate` which calls `translate_no_cache` (the original `I18n.translate`). The Fallbacks module works by overriding `translate` on the backend to walk the fallback chain; including it into the backend class does not make `I18n::Backend::Simple#translate` perform fallback lookups unless the backend's `translate` is the Fallbacks-aware one. More importantly, `I18n::Backend::Fallbacks` must be included into the backend *instance's* class and it expects `I18n.fallbacks` to respond to `[](locale)` returning an array — which `FallbackLocaleList` does — but the standard, supported way is `I18n::Backend::Simple.send(:include, I18n::Backend::Fallbacks)` combined with `config.i18n.fallbacks = true` (which the PR removes from all environment configs). Because the PR deletes `config.i18n.fallbacks = true` from production.rb, profile.rb, and cloud66 production.rb, Rails will not enable the fallbacks machinery, and the custom `ensure_loaded!` in `FallbackLocaleList` (called from `ApplicationController#set_locale` via `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!`) preloads locale files, but the actual translation lookup will not fall back — missing translations in the user's locale will return 'translation missing' strings instead of falling back to the site default locale or English. The consequence: users with partially-translated locales see raw 'translation missing: xx.key' messages in the UI. The fix is to keep `config.i18n.fallbacks = true` in the environment configs (or set `I18n::Backend::Simple.send(:include, I18n::Backend::Fallbacks)` and ensure the fallbacks config flag is set), and include Fallbacks into `I18n::Backend::Simple` (the class), not `I18n.backend.class` (which is fragile and equivalent only by accident at boot).

I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded! called on every request in set_locale before_filter, causing repeated work

`set_locale` is a `before_filter` that runs on every request. The added line `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` calls `FallbackLocaleList#ensure_loaded!`, which iterates `self[I18n.locale]` (up to 3 locales) and calls `I18n.ensure_loaded! l` for each. `I18n.ensure_loaded!` (the new method in translate_accelerator.rb) checks `@loaded_locales.include?(locale)` and calls `load_locale` if not loaded. `load_locale` acquires `LOAD_MUTEX` on every call, even when the locale is already loaded (the `return if @loaded_locales.include?(locale)` check is inside the mutex). So every request acquires a global mutex up to 3 times (once per fallback locale), serializing all requests across all threads for the duration of the check. Under high concurrency, this becomes a significant bottleneck. The consequence: unnecessary mutex contention on every request, reducing throughput. The fix: check `@loaded_locales.include?(locale)` before acquiring the mutex in `load_locale` (double-checked locking), or cache the result of `ensure_loaded!` per locale in the FallbackLocaleList, or move the `ensure_loaded!` call to only run when the locale changes (e.g., compare with a thread-local or request-local cached value).

Pluralization module included into I18n::Backend::Simple but Fallbacks included into I18n.backend.class — inconsistent and fragile backend patching

Line 5 does `I18n::Backend::Simple.send(:include, I18n::Backend::Pluralization)` — patching the class directly. Line 9 does `I18n.backend.class.send(:include, I18n::Backend::Fallbacks)` — patching whatever class the current backend instance is. These are inconsistent patterns. If the backend is not `I18n::Backend::Simple` (e.g., if a chain backend, cache backend, or custom backend is configured elsewhere), the Fallbacks module is included into the wrong class and Pluralization is included into a class that may not be used. The consequence: fallbacks or pluralization silently not working depending on backend configuration. The fix: use `I18n::Backend::Simple.send(:include, I18n::Backend::Fallbacks)` for consistency, matching the Pluralization line and the removed `pluralization.rb` initializer pattern.

translate method reads @loaded_locales without nil guard and without mutex, inconsistent with ensure_loaded!

`I18n.translate` (line 67-68) does `load_locale(config.locale) unless @loaded_locales.include?(config.locale)`. If `translate` is called before `ensure_loaded!` or `reload!` has ever run, `@loaded_locales` is nil and `nil.include?` raises `NoMethodError`. The original code had the same latent issue but it was masked because `load_locale` was only called from `translate` itself after `@loaded_locales` was initialized elsewhere; the new `ensure_loaded!` method initializes `@loaded_locales` lazily with `||=`, but `translate` does not. In a fresh process where the first I18n call is `I18n.t` (e.g., from an initializer or rake task before any request triggers `set_locale`), this will crash. The consequence: `NoMethodError: undefined method 'include?' for nil:NilClass` on first translation lookup in a fresh process. The fix: add `@loaded_locales ||= []` at the start of `translate`, or better, initialize `@loaded_locales = []` as a class-level constant default and reset it in `reload!`.

true_positives.golden_comment: With isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user) requiring user != null, authenticate(...) will not call webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context) on the initial login page where context.getUser() is still null, so conditional passkey UI will not be set up for first-time passkey login. Consider whether this should also be enabled when no user has been selected yet so ID-less passkey authentication on the initial login form continues to work.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Conditional passkeys UI is no longer offered during re-authentication because fillContextForm is gated on a non-null user

In UsernamePasswordForm.authenticate(), the call to webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context) was moved outside the else branch and is now guarded by isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser()), which returns false whenever context.getUser() is null. During a re-authentication (e.g. OIDC prompt=login) the user is not yet set in the authentication context when the login form is first rendered, so the WebAuthn conditional UI attributes (challenge, RP ID, ENABLE_WEBAUTHN_CONDITIONAL_UI) are never set on the form. The browser therefore never invokes navigator.credentials.get() with the conditional mediation, and passwordless passkey re-authentication on the username/password form is impossible. The same gating in challenge(context, error, field) (line 137) means that after a failed password attempt during re-authentication the conditional UI is also not re-armed. The guard should be based on webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled() (as before), not on the presence of a user in the context.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In UsernameForm.authenticate(), isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() is called without passing the required UserModel parameter.

false_positives.candidate:
PasskeysUsernameFormTest still asserts that the webauthn form is absent after username entry, contradicting the new behavior where conditional passkeys remain enabled

In passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey, after the user enters a valid username on the UsernameForm, the test asserts Assert.assertThrows(NoSuchElementException.class, () -> driver.findElement(By.xpath("//form[@id='webauth']"))) (line 202), i.e. that the webauthn conditional UI form is NOT present on the subsequent password page. However, the PR's stated goal (and the corresponding change in PasskeysOrganizationAuthenticationTest, which now asserts the form IS present) is that passkeys remain enabled during the username/password flow even after the username is known. The UsernameForm+PasswordForm split flow uses PasswordForm, which does not embed the WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator, so the webauthn form may legitimately be absent here; but the test does not document why this flow differs from the UsernamePasswordForm flow, and the assertion will break if PasswordForm is later changed to support conditional passkeys. At minimum the test should comment why the webauthn form is expected to be absent in this split-form flow, otherwise a future change that enables passkeys on PasswordForm will produce a confusing failure.

Refactor to shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators() changes behavior when the method is overridden to return false but a user is present

fillContextForm() previously branched on user != null to decide whether to build the WebAuthnAuthenticatorsBean (the list of allowed authenticators for a 2FA-style identified user). It now calls shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators(context), whose default implementation is context.getUser() != null, but WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator overrides it to always return false. In WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator.fillContextForm() (which calls super.fillContextForm()), this means that even when a user IS identified in the context (re-authentication with a known user), the ALLOWED_AUTHENTICATORS attribute is never set and isUserIdentified is always false. For the conditional UI this is intentional, but the base-class contract is now misleading: any other subclass overriding shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators() to false while still wanting per-user authenticator lists would silently lose them. More importantly, the new method name and javadoc ('true if the available webauthn authenticators should be shown on the screen') does not match what it actually controls (whether the per-user allowed-authenticators list is populated), which invites future misuse. The override in WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator should instead override a narrower hook or the base method should be documented/renamed to reflect that it gates the allowed-authenticators list.

Static import of USER_SET_BEFORE_USERNAME_PASSWORD_AUTH from AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator creates a package cycle and widens a constant's visibility unnecessarily

AuthenticatorUtils (in org.keycloak.authentication.authenticators.util) now statically imports AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator.USER_SET_BEFORE_USERNAME_PASSWORD_AUTH from org.keycloak.authentication.authenticators.browser. This introduces a dependency from the generic util package back into the browser authenticator package, and it required changing the constant from protected to public in AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator (line 58) solely to make it visible across packages. A public mutable-looking constant on an abstract authenticator class is a wider API surface than needed; the constant is an internal auth-note key. The cleaner approach is to move the constant (or a copy) into AuthenticatorUtils itself or into a shared constants class, and have AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator reference it from there, avoiding both the package cycle and the visibility widening.

UsernameForm skips the username step during re-authentication when conditional passkeys are enabled, breaking the username+password+passkey flow

UsernameForm.authenticate() now skips rendering the username form (context.success()) whenever context.getUser() != null && !isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(). The intent is to allow passkey re-authentication, but the condition is inverted with respect to the surrounding logic: when conditional passkeys ARE enabled the form is skipped entirely, so a user who must re-authenticate with username+password (e.g. a non-discoverable key, or a user without a passkey) is never asked for their username and the subsequent PasswordForm cannot validate anything. Conversely, when passkeys are disabled the old behavior (skip when user is set) is preserved. The check should be !isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() only for deciding whether passkeys can bypass the form; the skip should still happen when the user has no usable passkey path. As written, the separate UsernameForm + PasswordForm flow cannot complete a password re-authentication when the PASSKEYS feature and realm passkeys are enabled.

createErrorResponse() calls setupReauthenticationInUsernamePasswordFormError() unconditionally, hiding the username field even for first-time logins

WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator.createErrorResponse() now calls AuthenticatorUtils.setupReauthenticationInUsernamePasswordFormError(context) on every WebAuthn error rendered through the conditional UI. That helper sets LoginFormsProvider.USERNAME_HIDDEN=true and REGISTRATION_DISABLED=true whenever the auth note USER_SET_BEFORE_USERNAME_PASSWORD_AUTH is 'true'. The note is only set by UsernamePasswordForm when a user is already in the context, so for a normal first-time login the helper is a no-op; however, the helper is invoked before fillContextForm(context) and before errorChallenge.apply(context), and it mutates the shared form provider obtained from context.form(). Because the same LoginFormsProvider instance is reused for the error challenge, any code path that reaches createErrorResponse() with the re-authentication note set (e.g. a passkey error during re-authentication on the username/password form) will hide the username field and disable registration on the error page. That is the desired behavior for re-authentication, but the method is placed in the generic WebAuthn error path rather than in the username/password-specific error challenge, so any future caller of WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator that is not the username/password form (the class is designed to be reusable via the errorChallenge function) would incorrectly get username-hiding/registration-disabling attributes applied to an unrelated form. The call belongs in the errorChallenge lambda supplied by UsernamePasswordForm, not in the generic authenticator.

reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey asserts absence of the webauthn form with a try/catch that swallows all exceptions, making the assertion ineffective

The test reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey verifies that the webauthn button is absent by calling driver.findElement(By.xpath("//form[@id='webauth']")) inside a try block and catching Exception, with a fail() only if findElement returns normally. Selenium's findElement throws NoSuchElementException when the element is absent, so the catch block is the expected path; however, catching the broad Exception type also swallows any other failure (e.g. StaleElementReferenceException, WebDriverException, or a page not fully loaded) and treats it as success. If the page is in an unexpected state or the driver errors for an unrelated reason, the test will pass even though the webauthn form might actually be present. The assertion should use a proper negative assertion such as assertThrows(NoSuchElementException.class, () -> driver.findElement(...)) or a Hamcrest matcher on findElements(...).isEmpty(), and the same pattern is repeated at line 312 for the re-authentication page.

webauthnLoginWithExternalKey_reauthenticationWithPasswordOrPasskey submits a password without a username during re-authentication and relies on a hidden username field

In webauthnLoginWithExternalKey_reauthenticationWithPasswordOrPasskey, after triggering re-authentication with prompt=login, the test calls loginPage.login(getPassword("test-user@localhost")) (line 377) and later loginPage.login(getPassword(USERNAME)) (line 410) with only a password argument. The single-argument login() overload submits only the password field, assuming the username is pre-filled/hidden. This works only if the form correctly sets USERNAME_HIDDEN and pre-populates the username, which is exactly the behavior changed by this PR (setupReauthenticationInUsernamePasswordFormError). If the re-authentication form regression (username not hidden / not pre-filled) occurs, the test would submit an empty username and fail with a confusing 'Invalid username or password' error rather than clearly asserting the re-authentication form state. The test should explicitly assert that the username field is hidden and contains the expected user (e.g. via loginPage.getAttemptedUsername() or by checking the hidden input value) before submitting the password-only login, so that a regression in the re-authentication form setup is caught with a clear message.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative-offset slicing in OptimizedCursorPaginator silently returns wrong rows or raises IndexError

When `enable_advanced_features` is true and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code executes `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset` (e.g. `queryset[-5:96]`). Django QuerySets do NOT support negative slicing — this raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported.` at query evaluation time, turning any request with a negative cursor offset into a 500 error. Even if it were supported (e.g. on a list), negative slicing counts from the END of the result set, which would return the wrong rows entirely (the last N rows of the table rather than rows before the cursor), corrupting pagination results. The comment 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is factually wrong. Additionally, the cursor value is attacker-controlled via the `cursor` query parameter, so any client of the audit log endpoint passing `optimized_pagination=true` with a crafted negative-offset cursor triggers this. The negative-offset branch must be removed or replaced with a correct reverse-pagination implementation.

true_positives.golden_comment: When requests are authenticated with API keys or org auth tokens (which have user_id=None), organization_context.member is None. Line 71 attempts to access organization_context.member.has_global_access without checking if member is None, causing an AttributeError crash when optimized_pagination=true is used, even though the request passed all permission checks with valid org:write scope.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
AttributeError risk: organization_context.member may be None, and has_global_access is not a documented field

`enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` dereferences `organization_context.member` without a None check. `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is an optional RPC field (it is None when the request is not authenticated as an organization member, e.g. certain internal/service or staff flows that still reach this endpoint), which would raise `AttributeError` and return a 500 instead of a paginated response. Additionally, `has_global_access` is not a standard field on the member RPC model used elsewhere in this codebase (global access is typically determined via `OrganizationMember` flags / `has_global_access` on the ORM model or via `organization_context.flags`), so this check may silently never grant access or may not exist on the RPC type at all — it needs verification against the actual RPC schema.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the audit log endpoint orders by '-datetime'

`OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` does `int(math.floor(value) ...)` on `getattr(item, self.key)`. The endpoint wires it with `order_by="-datetime"`, so `self.key == "datetime"` and `value` is a `datetime` object — `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError`, so every paginated request through this paginator crashes with a 500. The class is a copy of `Paginator` (integer keys) and was never adapted to datetime keys; it should subclass/reuse `DateTimePaginator`'s key handling (millisecond conversion via `strftime("%s.%f")` and `value_from_cursor` converting back with `datetime.fromtimestamp`), otherwise the 'optimized' path is entirely broken for the only endpoint that uses it.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Importing non-existent OptimizedCursorPaginator

false_positives.candidate:
BasePaginator.get_result clamps negative offsets to 0, breaking prev-cursor pagination and enabling duplicate rows

The change `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` alters existing behavior for ALL paginators using BasePaginator (Paginator, DateTimePaginator, etc.), not just the new one. Previously `queryset[offset:stop]` with a negative offset would raise Django's 'Negative indexing is not supported' error; now a negative offset is silently clamped to 0, so the query restarts from the beginning of the dataset. Cursor offsets are derived from client-supplied cursor strings (`Cursor.from_string` parses `int(bits[1])` with no validation), so a client can send a cursor with a negative offset and receive the first page of results while the returned next/prev cursors are computed from those wrong results — producing duplicated rows across pages and inconsistent pagination state. This is a data-integrity regression in a shared, core pagination path used by many endpoints. Negative offsets should be rejected with BadPaginationError (as OffsetPaginator and ChainPaginator already do), not clamped.

Comment claims negative offsets are allowed, but Cursor.from_string and all paginators reject or mishandle them

The added comment states 'Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios', but nothing in `Cursor` validates or specially handles negative offsets: `from_string` happily parses them, `OffsetPaginator.get_result` raises `BadPaginationError("Pagination offset cannot be negative")` for them, `ChainPaginator` and `CombinedQuerysetPaginator` do the same, and `BasePaginator` now silently clamps them to 0 (see other finding). The comment documents behavior that does not exist and contradicts the rest of the codebase; it should be removed or replaced with an explicit statement that negative offsets are invalid.

No tests cover the new optimized-pagination branch, the negative-offset path, or the paginator changes

The PR adds a new paginator class, a new endpoint branch keyed on `optimized_pagination=true` and user privilege, and modifies the shared `BasePaginator.get_result` slicing logic — but includes no tests. Existing paginator tests (tests/sentry/api/test_paginator.py) and audit log endpoint tests (tests/sentry/api/endpoints/test_organization_auditlogs.py) are untouched, so the regressions described in the other findings (negative-offset clamping in BasePaginator, TypeError on datetime keys, AssertionError on negative slicing) would all pass CI. At minimum, tests are needed for: BasePaginator with a negative-offset cursor (must raise, not clamp), OptimizedCursorPaginator with a datetime-ordered queryset, and the audit log endpoint with `optimized_pagination=true` for superuser vs regular member.

OptimizedCursorPaginator is a near-verbatim duplicate of BasePaginator.get_result with no actual optimization

The new `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` (lines 845-911) duplicates `BasePaginator.get_result` almost line-for-line, including the same `count_hits` subquery, the same `extra` row fetch, and the same slicing strategy. The only behavioral differences are the broken negative-offset branch and the broken datetime key handling. There is no performance optimization present — no keyset/seek pagination (the `build_queryset` range filter is identical to the base class), no deferred `count_hits`, no `only()`/`values()` projection. Shipping a duplicate ~70-line method that claims 'optimized query path for large datasets' in its docstring is misleading and adds maintenance surface for zero benefit; either implement a real optimization (e.g. seek/keyset pagination on (datetime, id)) or delete the class and use DateTimePaginator.

OptimizedCursorPaginator prev-page trimming uses unclamped negative offset in length comparison

In the `cursor.is_prev and cursor.value` branch, the code checks `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra:` where `offset = cursor.offset` can be negative (the new code path explicitly allows negative offsets). With a negative offset this comparison can never be true when it should be, or can be true when it should not, so the extra fetched row is not trimmed correctly — resulting in an off-by-one row appearing (or disappearing) at the boundary of reverse pagination. The comparison should use the actual `start_offset` used for the slice, not the raw (possibly negative) `offset`.

Pre-existing typo `queryset.query.order_b` introduced/preserved in ordering-reversal path

Line 105 assigns `queryset.query.order_b = tuple(new_order_by)` — the attribute is `order_by`, not `order_b`. This is in the `elif ("-%s" % self.key) in queryset.query.order_by:` branch of `build_queryset`, which executes when a queryset already ordered by `-key` is paginated with an ascending (prev-page) cursor. The assignment silently sets a nonexistent attribute, so the intended ordering reversal never happens and the queryset keeps its original `-key` ordering — producing incorrectly ordered results for prev-cursor pagination on pre-ordered querysets. This path is reachable from the audit log endpoint (queryset ordered by `-datetime` via `order_by="-datetime"` combined with a prev cursor).

Undocumented, unvalidated query parameter gates a different paginator based on superuser/global-access status

`use_optimized = request.GET.get("optimized_pagination") == "true"` introduces a hidden, undocumented API parameter that switches the response's pagination behavior (different paginator class, different cursor semantics) for superusers and members with global access. Because the two paginators produce different cursor formats and edge-case behavior (and the optimized one is broken — see other findings), clients that cache or persist cursors across requests can get inconsistent results. More importantly, the parameter is not declared in any serializer or API documentation, so it is invisible to API consumers and to schema generation, and the `enable_advanced_features=True` flag is passed unconditionally whenever the user is privileged — there is no way to opt out per-request. Feature-gating pagination internals on a raw query-string flag is a contract hazard; the paginator choice should be deterministic per endpoint, not client-controlled.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch in get_result() passes cursor.offset directly as start_offset to queryset slicing when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator negative-offset branch crashes on Django negative slicing and mis-trims results

In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, the branch `if self.enable_advanced_features and cursor.offset < 0:` sets `start_offset = cursor.offset` (a negative number) and executes `list(queryset[start_offset:stop])`. Django ORM raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported.` for negative slice starts, so any request that reaches this paginator with a negative cursor offset (which the endpoint enables via `optimized_pagination=true` for superusers/global-access members) will 500. Additionally, the following block `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra: results = results[:-1]` (line 891) compares against the raw negative `offset`, so even if the slice did not crash, the extra-row trimming for prev cursors would be computed against the wrong value, potentially dropping a legitimate row or keeping the sentinel row. The claim in the comment that 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is incorrect.

true_positives.golden_comment: In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
BasePaginator.get_result allows negative offsets for is_prev cursors, breaking pagination invariants

The change replaces `stop = offset + limit + extra; results = list(queryset[offset:stop])` with `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`. For `is_prev` cursors, `start_offset` is now the raw (possibly negative) `cursor.offset`. Django QuerySets raise `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported` when sliced with a negative start, so any client-supplied prev cursor with a negative offset (e.g. `cursor=1700000000.0:-1:1`) will crash the request with a 500 instead of returning an empty page or a BadPaginationError. Even before that, the subsequent logic `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra: results = results[:-1]` (line 192) uses the raw negative `offset`, so the row-trimming arithmetic is wrong for negative offsets. Other paginators in this same file (OffsetPaginator line 287, MergingOffsetPaginator line 351, CombinedQuerysetPaginator line 701, ChainPaginator line 748, CallbackPaginator line 804) all explicitly reject negative offsets with `raise BadPaginationError("Pagination offset cannot be negative")`; this change silently removes that guard for the BasePaginator path used by DateTimePaginator and Paginator, which paginate most list endpoints. The comment claiming 'the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions' is factually wrong — Django does not handle negative slice starts.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key assumes a numeric sort key, but is used with order_by="-datetime"

`OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` does `value = getattr(item, self.key); return int(math.floor(value) ...)`, which requires the sort key to be a number. However the only caller, `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint.get` in src/sentry/api/endpoints/organization_auditlogs.py line 80, instantiates it with `order_by="-datetime"`, so `self.key == "datetime"` and `getattr(item, "datetime")` returns a `datetime` object. `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime` inside `build_cursor` (sentry/utils/cursors.py line 122/137/197), so the optimized path will crash on the first page whenever it returns any results. The class should either subclass DateTimePaginator's key handling (multiplier=1000, strftime-based) or the endpoint should not use it with a datetime ordering. As written, `optimized_pagination=true` from an admin on the audit log endpoint is a guaranteed 500.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.

false_positives.candidate:
Comment claims Cursor offsets may be negative, but no validation or handling exists and other paginators reject them

The added comment 'Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios' on `self.offset = int(offset)` implies the Cursor class now supports or handles negative offsets. In reality the class does nothing special — it just stores the int — and every paginator that consumes cursors either crashes on negative offsets (Django negative slicing, per the paginator.py findings) or explicitly rejects them with BadPaginationError. The comment documents an intention that the code does not implement and that the rest of the pagination stack contradicts; it will mislead maintainers into thinking negative offsets are a supported, safe feature.

Endpoint passes enable_advanced_features=True to self.paginate, which does not forward it to the paginator constructor

The endpoint calls `self.paginate(..., paginator_cls=OptimizedCursorPaginator, ..., enable_advanced_features=True)`. `paginate` (in sentry/api/base.py) constructs the paginator as `paginator_cls(queryset, order_by=..., max_limit=..., on_results=...)` and only forwards a fixed set of kwargs; `enable_advanced_features` is not among them, so it is either swallowed or raises a TypeError depending on the paginate implementation. Consequently `OptimizedCursorPaginator.enable_advanced_features` stays at its default `False`, and the 'advanced' negative-offset path is never actually enabled — the flag is dead configuration that misleads readers into thinking a special mode is active. Either thread the kwarg through `paginate` or remove it from the call.

Eviction via zpopmin during insert can drop spans that were just added, silently losing trace data

The new block `if span_count > 1000 then redis.call("zpopmin", set_key, span_count - 1000) end` evicts the lowest-scored members of the sorted set whenever a segment exceeds 1000 spans. Because members are scored by `end_timestamp_precise` (set in src/sentry/spans/buffer.py line 198), `zpopmin` removes the spans with the *earliest* end timestamps — which are exactly the spans that arrived first and are most likely to be the root/oldest spans of the segment. Dropping them means the flushed segment is missing spans, and if the evicted span was the segment root, the `span-buf:hrs:` flag logic (lines 66-70) may still claim a root span exists (or vice versa), producing a corrupted segment that is emitted to the `buffered-spans` topic and ingested as an incomplete trace. This is silent data loss in the tracing pipeline. Additionally, `span_count` is only assigned from `zunionstore` return values; when neither union branch runs (e.g. root span arriving into an empty set), `span_count` falls back to `zcard` (line 59), which is correct, but when a union runs the count reflects post-union cardinality — however if both unions run, the second `zunionstore` overwrites `span_count` with the cardinality after the second union only, which is still the full set size, so the eviction bound itself is consistent; the core issue is that eviction during insert destroys segment completeness. The previous code enforced the span-count limit at flush time (buffer.py `_load_segment_data` skipped oversized segments with an error metric), which preserved data integrity by refusing to emit rather than truncating. Note also that the flush-time `max_segment_spans` check was removed in this PR (see buffer.py diff), so oversized segments are no longer detected or logged at flush time either — the only enforcement is now this destructive in-place eviction.

No test covers the new 1000-span eviction path in add-buffer.lua

The PR adds eviction logic (`if span_count > 1000 then zpopmin ...`) to the Lua script and removes the flush-time `max_segment_spans` guard, but tests/sentry/spans/test_buffer.py contains no test that ingests more than 1000 spans into a single segment and asserts which spans survive eviction or that the segment remains complete/consistent. All existing tests use 4-5 spans per trace. Given that eviction drops the lowest-scored (earliest end_timestamp) members — potentially including the segment root — the behavior of the eviction path (which spans are dropped, whether the hrs flag stays consistent, whether flushed output is a truncated segment) is completely unverified. A test should ingest >1000 spans with distinct end_timestamp_precise values and assert the surviving set and the emitted segment contents.

OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates ~70 lines of BasePaginator.get_result instead of overriding a hook

The new class copies the entire `get_result` body from `BasePaginator` (lines 136-215) and adds one conditional branch for negative offsets. Any future fix to the shared logic (e.g. the `order_b` typo, cursor trimming edge cases, hits handling) must be applied in two places or the paginators diverge. The negative-offset behavior could be a small override or a parameter on BasePaginator. As a standalone duplication it is a maintenance hazard rather than an immediate bug, but it already diverges: the copy retains the `max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` line from the modified base, so the two implementations will drift as the base evolves.

Pre-existing typo queryset.query.order_b (missing _by) in BasePaginator.build_queryset

Line 105 reads `queryset.query.order_b = tuple(new_order_by)` — the attribute is `order_by`, so this silently sets a new, meaningless attribute and leaves the ordering unchanged. This is a pre-existing bug (not introduced by this PR), but it sits directly in the code path that the new OptimizedCursorPaginator inherits and that the modified `get_result` exercises for prev-cursors on already-ordered querysets, so the PR's changes interact with it: when a prev cursor is used on a queryset already ordered by `-key`, the intended order reversal never happens. Worth fixing while touching this file, since the PR's stated goal is correct bidirectional pagination.

Redirect-chain depth limit reduced from 10000 to 1000 without handling the overflow case

The loop `for i = 0, 1000 do ... end` previously ran to 10000. If a redirect chain exceeds the loop bound, the loop exits with `set_span_id` still pointing at an intermediate span ID rather than the chain root, and the script proceeds to `hset`/`zunionstore` against a non-root key. The original comment acknowledged this ('theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly'); reducing the limit to 1000 makes the failure 10x more likely for deep span trees (long-lived traces with thousands of nested spans), and the resulting split segments would be flushed as separate segments, breaking trace assembly. There is no detection or metric when the loop exhausts. Either keep the higher bound, or detect exhaustion and fall back to using the last resolved ID consistently (and log/metric it).

Removal of the max_segment_spans flush-time guard leaves only destructive in-insert eviction to bound segment size

The diff removes the block in `_load_segment_data` that checked `if len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans:` and skipped the segment with `metrics.incr("spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded")` and an error log. The constructor still accepts `max_segment_spans: int = 1001` (line 150) and stores it (line 158), but it is now completely unused — dead configuration. Previously, an oversized segment was detected at flush time and *skipped* (with a metric), preserving the invariant that emitted segments never exceed the span limit. Now the only enforcement is the Lua script's `zpopmin` eviction during insert, which silently truncates the segment (see the add-buffer.lua finding). The safety net that turned a data-integrity problem into a visible, measurable error has been removed while its configuration knob remains, which is misleading. Either restore the flush-time check (as a defense in depth) or remove the now-unused `max_segment_spans` parameter and document that eviction is the sole mechanism.

Undocumented query parameter switches audit log endpoint to a different paginator based on client input

`use_optimized = request.GET.get("optimized_pagination") == "true"` lets any client toggle which paginator implementation serves the audit log endpoint. The two paginators have different cursor semantics (OptimizedCursorPaginator treats the cursor value as a raw integer key rather than a millisecond timestamp like DateTimePaginator), so a client can craft a cursor string that is valid for one paginator and silently misinterpreted by the other, producing wrong pages, skipped or duplicated audit rows, or (combined with the negative-offset bug) errors. The endpoint is marked `ApiPublishStatus.EXPERIMENTAL` and the parameter is undocumented; an unversioned, undocumented behavior switch on an audit/compliance endpoint is an API-contract hazard. The paginator choice should be a server-side configuration, not a per-request query parameter.

__reduce__ drops segment_page_size, max_segment_bytes, and max_segment_spans when pickling SpansBuffer

`__reduce__` returns `(SpansBuffer, (self.assigned_shards, self.span_buffer_timeout_secs, self.span_buffer_root_timeout_secs, self.redis_ttl))` — it omits `segment_page_size`, `max_segment_bytes`, and `max_segment_spans`. The factory (src/sentry/spans/consumers/process/factory.py) uses `run_task_with_multiprocessing(partial(process_batch, buffer), ...)`, which pickles the buffer to worker processes. Any non-default values for those three parameters are silently reset to defaults (100, 10 MiB, 1001) in workers. This was already the case for the first two before this PR, but the PR makes `max_segment_spans` newly dead (see related finding), compounding the confusion. The pickle round-trip should include all constructor parameters that affect behavior.

process_batch assumes end_timestamp_precise is always present in the span payload

`end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"]` uses direct key access on the parsed SpanEvent. The schema type `SpanEvent` (sentry_kafka_schemas.schema_types.ingest_spans_v1) may mark this field optional, and Relay/older producers may omit it; a missing key raises `KeyError`, which would fail the entire batch in `process_batch` and, because offsets are only committed after successful processing (CommitOffsets is downstream of the flusher), cause the consumer to retry the batch indefinitely — a poison-pill that stalls the spans consumer partition. The neighboring fields use `.get()` with defaults (`val.get("parent_span_id")`, `val.get("is_remote")`), showing the codebase's convention for optional fields. Use `val.get("end_timestamp_precise") or <fallback>` (e.g. the message timestamp already computed as `timestamp`) or validate the schema. The test payloads all include the field, so this path is untested for absence.

zadd with payload as member means duplicate span payloads collapse and scores are overwritten, not summed, on re-ingest

The buffer now stores spans in a sorted set keyed by payload: `p.zadd(set_key, {span.payload: span.end_timestamp_precise for span in subsegment})`. With ZADD's default behavior (no XX/GT/LT flags), re-adding an existing member *updates* its score rather than creating a duplicate. For at-least-once Kafka delivery, the same span payload redelivered after a consumer restart will simply update its score — which is benign — but the Lua script's ZUNIONSTORE (add-buffer.lua lines 47/53) *sums* scores for members present in both source sets, so a payload that exists in both `set_key` and `span_key`/`parent_key` gets a doubled `end_timestamp_precise` score. That corrupted score then drives `zpopmin` eviction ordering (evicting the wrong spans) and is never corrected. The previous SET-based implementation was idempotent under re-ingest and union. This is a data-integrity regression for the dedup/merge path.

zunionstore overwrites span_count with partial cardinality when both union branches execute

Line 47 `span_count = redis.call("zunionstore", set_key, 2, set_key, span_key)` and line 53 `span_count = redis.call("zunionstore", set_key, 2, set_key, parent_key)` both assign to `span_count`. ZUNIONSTORE returns the cardinality of the *destination* set after the union. When both branches execute (a non-root span whose own span_key exists AND whose resolved parent_key exists and differs), the second assignment overwrites the first; the destination cardinality after the second union is the full set size, so in that specific case the value is still correct. However, when only the first branch executes, `span_count` is the cardinality after merging span_key into set_key — correct. When only the second executes, it is the cardinality after merging parent_key — correct. The real problem is subtler: `zunionstore` with default (non-WEIGHTS) aggregation *sums* scores for duplicate members. Since members are span payloads (unique per span), duplicates across the two source sets would only occur if the same payload was already in set_key, in which case its score becomes the sum of two end_timestamp_precise values — corrupting the score used for eviction ordering and for any score-based reads. The previous code used `sunionstore` (set semantics, no scores), which was immune to this. The migration from SET to ZSET changes the merge semantics: re-adding an already-present payload now doubles its score instead of being a no-op.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache key uses Python's randomized hash(), causing cache misses and cross-process inconsistency

The cache key is built with `hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))`. Python's `hash()` for tuples of ints is deterministic within a process but is NOT stable across processes when PYTHONHASHSEED randomization is enabled (the default for str/bytes, and tuple hashes incorporate element hashes; for ints hash(int) is stable, but relying on `hash()` for cache keys is fragile and the tuple hash combines element hashes — for ints this is actually stable, however the real problem is that `hash()` can return negative values and, more importantly, the same logical key can produce different values across processes if any element type's hash is randomized, and it is simply not a safe serialization). More concretely: the key embeds a process-local hash rather than a stable serialization of the project IDs, so cache entries written by one worker are not reliably found by another, and `invalidate_upsampling_cache` (line 73) recomputes the same unstable hash — invalidation may target a different key than the one stored. The consequence is that the 60-second eligibility cache silently fails to dedupe lookups and invalidation does not work, defeating the stated performance optimization and potentially serving stale eligibility decisions. Use a stable key such as `','.join(map(str, sorted(project_ids)))`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling eligibility is computed against the outer `dataset` but applied to `scoped_dataset`, which can differ in the dashboard discover-split path

In `_get_event_stats`, `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` is called with the closure-captured outer `dataset` (line 220-222), but the query is executed against `scoped_dataset` (lines 236, 253, 279, 298). In the dashboard split path (`get_event_stats_factory`, lines 372-435), `_get_event_stats` is called with `split_dataset = discover` or `scoped_dataset` while `dataset` remains the original (possibly `metrics_enhanced`). The eligibility decision — including `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform(dataset, ...)` and `_is_error_focused_query(request)` — is therefore made for the wrong dataset/query combination. For example, a metrics-enhanced widget split into an errors-only discover query would be evaluated as a metrics dataset (returns False, no upsampling — safe), but the reverse combination (outer dataset = errors/discover, scoped = something else) could apply `upsampled_count()` to a dataset where `sample_weight` is not populated, yielding wrong counts or query errors. The eligibility check must use `scoped_dataset` and the actual `query` string being executed, not the outer `dataset` and the raw request query.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

false_positives.candidate:
A git submodule pointer file 'sentry-repo' was accidentally added at the repository root

The diff adds a new top-level file `sentry-repo` containing `Subproject commit a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a`. This is a git submodule gitlink accidentally committed as a regular file (or a stray `git submodule` artifact) at the repo root of the sentry monorepo. It is unrelated to the error-upsampling feature, pollutes the repository root, and will confuse tooling (and `git status`) — if it is meant to be a submodule it should be registered in `.gitmodules` and added via `git submodule add`, not committed as a plain file. It should be removed from this PR.

Allowlist option value is compared against project IDs without type normalization

`options.get("issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist", [])` returns whatever the operator configured (likely a list of ints, but options are frequently stored/edited as strings, e.g. `["123", "456"]` from a YAML/JSON config or the admin UI), and the check `project_id in allowlist` compares ints against those values. If the option contains strings, `123 in ["123"]` is False, so eligibility silently fails and upsampling is never applied (errors undercounted) with no error or log. The helper should normalize both sides to int (e.g. `{int(p) for p in allowlist}`) and handle malformed entries gracefully.

Caching a boolean eligibility result conflates False (not eligible) with cache miss and caches negative results incorrectly across allowlist changes

`cache.get(cache_key)` returns `None` on miss, and the code treats any non-None value as a hit (line 31: `if cached_result is not None: return cached_result and ...`). This means a cached `False` (projects not allowlisted) is indistinguishable from a miss only by value, which is fine, BUT the deeper issue is that the cached value is the *allowlist eligibility only*, while the final decision also depends on `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform(dataset, request)` — that part is re-evaluated, which is correct. The actual bug: the cache stores `is_eligible` for 60 seconds, but `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is never called anywhere in the codebase (no callers exist in the diff), so when an operator updates `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist`, queries for newly-allowlisted projects will continue to use plain `count()` (undercounting errors) and queries for removed projects will continue to use `upsampled_count()` (potentially querying a non-existent `sample_weight` column or producing wrong results) for up to 60 seconds. Combined with the unstable `hash()` key, invalidation is effectively broken. The docstring claims invalidation 'should be called when the allowlist configuration changes' but no such call site exists, making the cache a correctness hazard rather than a safe optimization.

Factory change sets top-level 'sample_rate' from error_sampling context, which does not populate Snuba's sample_weight column

`_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` copies `contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate` into the event's top-level `sample_rate` field. In Sentry's ingest pipeline, the value written to the events dataset's `sample_weight` column is derived from the event's `sample_rate` (typically `1/sample_rate`) during normalization in the event manager — but this factory path calls `manager.get_data()` and then mutates the normalized dict *after* normalization, and `store_event` in tests typically bypasses the full normalization that computes `sample_weight`. As a result, the Snuba integration tests in `test_organization_events_stats.py` that assert `count == 10` (1 event / 0.1 sample rate) are asserting against a `sample_weight` value that may not actually be written by this code path, making the tests tautological or environment-dependent rather than verifying real ingest behavior. The factory should set the value through the same normalization path production uses (or set `sample_weight` explicitly on the stored event), otherwise the tests do not prove the feature works end-to-end.

Integration tests assert exact upsampled counts (10) without verifying that sample_weight was actually persisted, and never test mixed sampled/unsampled events

The tests assert `data[0][1][0]["count"] == 10` for a single stored event with `client_sample_rate: 0.1`. This only passes if (a) the factory change actually results in `sample_weight = 10` in Snuba (see the factories.py finding — the mutation happens after `get_data()` and may not propagate), and (b) the `upsampled_count` aggregate is correctly resolved. There is no test where an allowlisted project contains a mix of sampled and unsampled events (some with `error_sampling` context, some without), which is exactly the case the `sum(sample_weight)` implementation gets wrong (unsampled events contribute NULL/0). There is also no test for the discover dataset without an explicit `event.type:error` filter, no test for aliased yAxis (`count() as total`), and no test for topEvents queries. These gaps mean the most likely production failure modes (NULL sample_weight, alias collisions, top-events semantic change) are untested.

New 'upsampled_count' aggregate sums sample_weight unconditionally, producing wrong results (or errors) for events without sample_weight

The `upsampled_count` SnQL function is defined as `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))` with no guard for rows where `sample_weight` is NULL/missing (e.g. events ingested before client-side error sampling was enabled, events from SDKs that don't send `error_sampling.client_sample_rate`, or transaction events that slip through the dataset/query checks). In ClickHouse/Snuba, `sum()` over a nullable column ignores NULLs, so groups containing only non-sampled events would return 0 (or NULL → toInt64(NULL)) instead of their actual count — silently underreporting errors. The helper's docstring explicitly states 'We rely on the database schema to ensure sample_weight exists for all events in allowlisted projects, so no additional null checks are needed' — that assumption is not enforced anywhere in this diff (the factory change in testutils only sets `sample_rate` for test events; there is no migration, backfill, or query-time guard). The aggregate should be `sum(coalesce(sample_weight, 1))` (or `countIf(sample_weight IS NULL) + sum(coalesce(sample_weight,0))`) so that unsampled events still count as 1, and the eligibility check must additionally verify the project actually has sampled data.

New integration tests mock the options module globally, bypassing the real allowlist option and the cache, so they don't exercise the actual eligibility path

All four new tests use `@mock.patch("sentry.api.helpers.error_upsampling.options")` and set `mock_options.get.return_value = [...]`. This replaces the entire options module for the duration of the request, which means (a) the real option key `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` is never read, so a typo in the option name in the helper would not be caught; (b) the 60-second cache in `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` is still active across tests within the same process, so test ordering can leak cached eligibility between tests (the cache key includes org id and project ids, which differ per test since projects are recreated, mitigating but not eliminating this); and (c) the tests never verify that `invalidate_upsampling_cache` works or that the cache returns consistent results. At minimum one test should set the real option via `self.options(...)`/`options.set` and assert behavior, and the cache should be cleared in `setUp`/`tearDown` to keep tests hermetic.

New public-ish aggregate 'upsampled_count' is registered only on the discover dataset, but the endpoint can apply it to the errors dataset

`upsampled_count` is added to `DiscoverDataset.function_converter` (discover.py), but `organization_events_stats.py` applies the transformation whenever `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` returns True — which includes `dataset == errors` (error_upsampling.py line 112). If the errors dataset's function resolver does not also register `upsampled_count`, any errors-dataset query with `yAxis=count()` from an allowlisted project will fail at SnQL resolution time with an unknown-function error (a 500), or worse, be silently rejected. The diff shows no corresponding registration in the errors dataset. Either register the function on all datasets where it can be applied, or restrict the endpoint transformation to datasets that support it.

Rewriting 'count()' to 'upsampled_count() as count' hard-codes an alias that can collide with or clobber the user's requested column name

The transformation appends `" as count"` unconditionally. If the caller's `query_columns` already contains a column literally named `count` (e.g. a tag or attribute named `count`), or if the same list contains both `count()` and another expression aliased `as count`, the rewritten SnQL will contain two columns aliased `count`, producing a duplicate-column error from Snuba or silently ambiguous result keys. The response-shaping code downstream (which maps results back by column name) will then read the wrong series. The transform must preserve the caller's original alias (e.g. rewrite `count()` → `upsampled_count() as count` only when no alias was present, and `count() as foo` → `upsampled_count() as foo`), and must detect collisions.

Unit tests never test the public entry point is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects or the cache/invalidation behavior

The test file only tests the private helpers (`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling`, `_is_error_focused_query`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`). The actual public function `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` — which contains the caching logic, the cache-key construction, and the composition of the helpers — has zero coverage. Consequently the `hash()`-based cache key bug, the cached-False handling, and `invalidate_upsampling_cache` (which has no callers and no tests) are completely unverified. Tests should cover: cache hit/miss behavior, that a cached result is returned without calling options.get, that invalidate_upsampling_cache removes the entry, and that the function composes dataset + query checks correctly.

Upsampling is applied to the standard timeseries path even when the query contains transaction events via the discover dataset default

For the discover dataset, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` only applies upsampling when the raw query string contains `event.type:error`. But the discover dataset by default returns both errors and transactions; a query with no `event.type` filter (the common case, e.g. a plain `count()` over an org) will NOT be transformed (safe), however a query like `event.type:error OR message:foo` is transformed even though it can match non-error events depending on search semantics, and a query like `!event.type:transaction` (errors only, but expressed as an exclusion) is NOT transformed, so errors are undercounted. The asymmetry means the same logical 'errors only' query gets different count semantics depending on how it is phrased. This should be resolved by parsing the query to determine the effective event-type set rather than substring matching.

Upsampling transformation is applied to top-events queries, changing top-N semantics from event counts to weighted sums

When `top_events > 0`, the code replaces `query_columns` with `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling(query_columns)` (lines 232-233) and passes them as `timeseries_columns`/`y_axes` to `top_events_timeseries` / `run_top_events_timeseries_query`. Top-events queries rank groups by the aggregate value; replacing `count()` with `sum(sample_weight)` changes both the ranking metric and the returned per-group values. The API contract for `topEvents` is 'top N groups by event count'; silently returning groups ranked by upsampled weight (and reporting `count` as the weighted sum) is a behavioral/API break for any consumer of this endpoint, and the response's `count` field no longer means 'number of events'. Either exclude top-events queries from upsampling or make the semantic change explicit and documented in the response meta.

_are_all_projects_error_upsampled takes an unused organization parameter and performs an O(n*m) allowlist scan per uncached request

The `organization` parameter of `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` is never used (the allowlist is global, not per-org), which is misleading API surface. Additionally, `all(project_id in allowlist for project_id in project_ids)` is O(len(project_ids) * len(allowlist)) with `allowlist` being a list; for queries spanning many projects against a large allowlist this is repeated on every cache miss. Converting the allowlist to a `set` once per call (or caching the parsed set alongside eligibility) would make the check O(n). Minor, but the unused parameter should be removed or the function should actually scope the allowlist per organization if that is the intent.

_is_error_focused_query uses naive substring matching on the raw query string, producing false positives and false negatives

`_is_error_focused_query` checks `"event.type:error" in query.lower()`. This (a) false-positives on negated or unrelated contexts such as `!event.type:error`, `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction` (mixed query — applying sample_weight upsampling to a query that also counts transactions will produce wrong totals because transactions have no `sample_weight`), `message:"event.type:error"`, or a tag value containing that substring; and (b) false-negatives on equivalent queries like `event.type:[error, default]` or `event.type:error event.type:default`. The consequence is that upsampling (which changes `count()` to `sum(sample_weight)`) can be applied to queries that include transaction events — where `sample_weight` does not exist — causing Snuba query failures or, worse, silently wrong counts. The check should parse the search query (e.g. via the existing event_search parser) and determine the resolved event types, and must exclude queries that can match transactions.

_should_apply_sample_weight_transform applies upsampling to the entire errors dataset without checking the query's event types

For `dataset == errors` the function returns `True` unconditionally (line 112-113). The errors dataset can still be queried with filters that exclude error events or with `event.type:transaction`-style exclusions in edge cases, but more importantly the endpoint's `_get_event_stats` is also invoked from the dashboard discover-split path (organization_events_stats.py lines 383-435) where `errors_only_query = f"({query}) AND !event.type:transaction"` is run against the **discover** dataset — that path is guarded by `_is_error_focused_query`, but the errors-dataset branch has no query inspection at all. If a caller uses the errors dataset with a query that matches non-error rows (or with `sampled:true/false` semantics that interact with sample_weight), `count()` will be silently replaced with `sum(sample_weight)`. At minimum the function should verify the query does not explicitly target transactions, consistent with the discover branch.

transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling only matches exact 'count()' and silently drops/mis-handles aliased or parameterized count aggregations

`transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` replaces a column only when `column.lower().strip() == "count()"`. Real queries from the events-stats endpoint commonly use forms like `count() as count`, `count(id)`, `count_unique(...)`, or `count() as my_alias` (the endpoint's yAxis values are user-supplied and may include aliases). Any of these will pass through unchanged, so the query will run a plain `count()` on a sampled dataset and report the *sampled* event count instead of the upsampled count — silently returning wrong (under-)counts with no error. Conversely, if a column is exactly `count()` but the request is a top-events query where the column is used as a group-by/timeseries column rather than an aggregate, the rewrite to `upsampled_count() as count` changes semantics. The function should parse the aggregation properly (or at minimum handle the `count(...)` family and alias suffixes) and should fail loudly rather than silently when it cannot safely transform an expected count aggregation.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes the get_multi result preserves the input order; dict value order is not guaranteed to match error_ids, so event data can be paired with the wrong ID (missing nodes also shift alignment).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
fetch_error_details zips error_ids with events.values() which may not align when some events are missing

`fetch_error_details` builds `node_ids` from `error_ids`, calls `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)`, then constructs `ErrorEvent` objects by `zip(error_ids, events.values())`. `get_multi` returns a dict keyed by node_id; if any event is missing (returns None), the dict will have fewer entries than `error_ids`, and `zip` will silently pair the wrong `event_id` with the wrong `data` (dict ordering is insertion order of the returned dict, not the requested order). The `if data is not None` filter then drops entries, but the id/data pairing is already corrupted — an error event can be attributed to the wrong event_id, producing incorrect error context (wrong title/message/timestamp) in the AI summary.
