The same copy-paste error exists in UserPermissionsV2? No — UserPermissionsV2.canManage(UserModel) correctly uses MANAGE only; only this group-level canManage() is wrong.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
hasPermission looks up group resource by raw group id as resource name, but V2 resources are keyed differently

GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission(String groupId, ...) does `resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)` (line 141). In the V2 schema (AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource), per-group resources are created with the group id as the resource *name* via resolveGroup(), so findByName(server, groupId) is consistent with that. However, getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() (line 121-125) iterates resources of type GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE and calls `hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...)` — passing the resource's internal store id, not the group id that is used as the resource name. findByName(server, resource.getId()) will therefore not find the resource, the code falls back to the all-groups resource, and the per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS evaluation is performed against the wrong resource. Consequence: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() returns incorrect group id sets (it adds resource.getId() — the authz resource id, not the group id — to the returned set), which UsersResource/BruteForceUsersResource then pass to session.users().searchForUserStream via UserModel.GROUPS, filtering users by group ids that do not match actual group ids. This breaks fine-grained user visibility for admins with only group-scoped view-members permissions and returns wrong/empty user lists.

false_positives.candidate:
Fields changed from private to protected for V2 subclassing — acceptable but widens encapsulation

The diff changes GroupPermissions fields root, resourceStore, policyStore from private to protected (lines 55-58) to allow GroupPermissionsV2 access. This is a common pattern but widens the class's encapsulation boundary; since GroupPermissionsV2 is in the same package, package-private would suffice. Not a defect; disregard per instructions (style preference).

GroupPermissionsV2 throws UnsupportedOperationException for management methods still called from V1 code paths

GroupPermissionsV2 throws UnsupportedOperationException for isPermissionsEnabled, setPermissionsEnabled, viewMembersPermission, manageMembersPermission, manageMembershipPermission, viewPermission, managePermission, resource, and getPermissions (lines 168-210). However, GroupResource.getManagementPermissions (line 321-330) and setManagementPermissionsEnabled (line 354-365) call `AdminPermissions.management(session, realm)` which returns MgmtPermissionsV2 when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled, and then call permissions.groups().isPermissionsEnabled(group) / setPermissionsEnabled / resource / getPermissions. These endpoints are guarded by `ProfileHelper.requireFeature(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ)` (V1 feature), not V2 — so if both features are enabled (or V2 enabled while the V1-guarded endpoint is invoked), the call reaches GroupPermissionsV2 and throws UnsupportedOperationException, producing a 500 error on GET/PUT /admin/realms/{realm}/groups/{id}/management/permissions. Either the endpoints need a V2 guard/feature check, or GroupPermissionsV2 must implement these methods (e.g., returning a V2-appropriate ManagementPermissionReference). This is a runtime API break for the group management-permissions endpoint under V2.

Indentation change in getUsers else-if branch is inconsistent (cosmetic but obscures diff)

The diff shows the `} else if (last != null || ...)` block in getUsers (lines 298-336) re-indented with extra spaces (the whole block shifted right by 4 spaces relative to the surrounding code), while the logic is unchanged. This is a formatting inconsistency introduced by the diff (likely a merge artifact) that makes the code harder to read and the diff noisier. Not a functional issue; flagging as a doc_defect/cleanup item since it affects readability of the changed file.

MgmtPermissionsV2.groups() returns GroupPermissions (declared type) but field is GroupPermissionsV2 — type mismatch with base class contract

MgmtPermissionsV2 overrides `public GroupPermissions groups()` (line 58) with return type GroupPermissions (the V1 class), while the field is GroupPermissionsV2 and the instance created is GroupPermissionsV2. The base class MgmtPermissions.groups() presumably returns GroupPermissions; the override narrows the instance but not the declared type. This compiles because GroupPermissionsV2 extends GroupPermissions, but callers typed against MgmtPermissions.groups() get the V1 type and cannot access V2-specific behavior without casting. More importantly, the override signature `public GroupPermissions groups()` matches the base, so it is a valid override; the concern is only API clarity. However, if the base class method is declared to return the interface GroupPermissionEvaluator or a different type, this could be a compile issue — since the PR compiles, it is fine. Downgrading to a note: the declared return type should ideally be GroupPermissionEvaluator or GroupPermissionsV2 for clarity, but this is a style/API-design preference, not a bug. Disregard as a finding per instructions (style preference).

Null resource from getResourceTypeResource is dereferenced without a null check

In hasPermission(), when the per-group resource is not found, the code calls `AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, AdminPermissionsSchema.GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE)` (line 144) and immediately calls `policyStore.findByResource(server, resource)` on line 147 without checking whether resource is null. getResourceTypeResource returns null when the resource type resource does not exist (e.g., admin permissions enabled but schema not initialized, or supportsAuthorizationSchema false). A NullPointerException would then be thrown instead of returning false, turning a 'no permission' situation into a 500 error. The analogous code in UserPermissionsV2.hasPermission (line 109-113) has the same pattern, but there the resource lookup is equally unchecked; at minimum GroupPermissionsV2 should null-check before findByResource.

Removal of AdminRoles.ADMIN from role checks in V2 user permission methods

The diff removes AdminRoles.ADMIN from the hasOneAdminRole checks in canView(UserModel) (line 48: was `AdminRoles.ADMIN, AdminRoles.MANAGE_USERS, AdminRoles.VIEW_USERS`, now only MANAGE_USERS/VIEW_USERS) and canManage(UserModel) (line 57: was `ADMIN, MANAGE_USERS`, now only MANAGE_USERS). AdminRoles.ADMIN is the realm-admin composite role; in V1 code paths (e.g., MgmtPermissions.hasOneAdminRole usage elsewhere) realm admins are expected to retain full access. If ADMIN no longer implies manage-users/view-users membership in the V2 evaluation path (hasOneAdminRole checks direct role assignment, and realm-admin is a composite role that may not be expanded depending on implementation), realm admins could lose access to user operations under V2. This needs verification against how hasOneAdminRole resolves composite roles; if composites are resolved it is harmless, otherwise it is an access regression for realm admins.

Test cleanup in @BeforeEach uses response after try-with-resources closes it

In GroupResourceTypeEvaluationTest.onBefore (lines 71-79), the code does `try (Response response = realm.admin().groups().add(topGroup)) { ... topGroup.setId(ApiUtil.handleCreatedResponse(response)); ... }`. ApiUtil.handleCreatedResponse now uses try-with-resources internally (per the ApiUtil change), closing the response; the outer try-with-resources then closes it again (harmless), but more importantly the assertion and id extraction happen inside the outer try block before the outer close — this is fine. However, the pattern of calling handleCreatedResponse (which closes the response) inside an outer try-with-resources is redundant and confusing; if handleCreatedResponse's internal close throws or the outer close is reached after the inner close, behavior is still safe (Response.close is idempotent). Not a functional bug; flagging as a test code smell. More significant: the test class lacks a test verifying that an admin with only view-members on a group cannot list groups (negative case for group listing), and lacks a test for manage-membership on a subgroup granting membership management on parent/child hierarchies — coverage gaps for the new Groups resource type scopes.

UserPermissionsV2.isImpersonatable throws UnsupportedOperationException but is called from V1 code paths

UserPermissionsV2.isImpersonatable(UserModel, ClientModel) and isImpersonatable(UserModel) throw UnsupportedOperationException (lines 142-149). The base class UserPermissions.canImpersonate(UserModel, ClientModel) (line 356-362) calls `canImpersonate()` then `isImpersonatable(user, requester)`, and canClientImpersonate (line 340-353) calls `canImpersonate(context) && isImpersonatable(user)`. In V2, canImpersonate(UserModel, ClientModel) is overridden (line 65-74) and does not call isImpersonatable, and canClientImpersonate is overridden to delegate to canImpersonate(user, client) (line 137-139). However, any other caller of isImpersonatable (e.g., UserResource impersonation endpoints that check isImpersonatable directly, or the deprecated interface method used elsewhere) will hit UnsupportedOperationException under V2. The interface UserPermissionEvaluator still declares isImpersonatable as @Deprecated but not removed; if any V2-active code path (e.g., UserResource.impersonate) calls auth.users().isImpersonatable(...), it will throw. This should be verified; if UserResource only uses canImpersonate, the risk is limited to external/other callers, but the UnsupportedOperationException pattern for interface methods that remain on the public evaluator interface is fragile.

V1 GroupPermissions.canManage()/canView() no longer consider fine-grained group permissions, breaking V1 FGAP global group operations

The diff replaces GroupPermissions.canManage() from `root.users().canManageDefault()` to `root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_USERS)` (line 274-276) and canView() from `root.users().canViewDefault()` to `root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_USERS, AdminRoles.VIEW_USERS)` (line 286-288). In V1 fine-grained admin permissions (ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ feature, MgmtPermissions/GroupPermissions path), an admin could be granted the 'manage' or 'view' scope on a group resource (via GroupPermissions.initialize/hasPermission) without holding realm-management roles. The per-group methods canManage(GroupModel)/canView(GroupModel) still check hasPermission, but the global canManage()/canView() — used by requireManage()/requireView() for realm-wide operations such as GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup (auth.groups().requireManage()) and by canList() — now ignore FGAP permissions entirely. Consequence: in V1 FGAP deployments, admins who previously could create top-level groups via a view/manage permission on the Groups resource (or via the old users().canManageDefault() semantics) are now denied; conversely the change removes the V1 FGAP evaluation from these global checks. This is a behavioral/API break for V1 fine-grained authorization unless the intent is that V1 group permissions are only per-group. The same replacement was done in UserPermissions.canManage()/canView() (lines 233-243, 297-307) where the fine-grained hasPermission fallback is retained, so the group change is inconsistent with the user change.

canList() logic change drops VIEW_USERS/MANAGE_USERS as sufficient for listing groups

The diff changes GroupPermissions.canList() from `canView() || root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.VIEW_USERS, AdminRoles.MANAGE_USERS, AdminRoles.QUERY_GROUPS)` to `root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.QUERY_GROUPS) || canView()` (line 148-149). Since canView() itself checks `root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_USERS, AdminRoles.VIEW_USERS)` (line 287), the net effect is equivalent for V1. However the reordering changes evaluation cost only; no functional change. Not a defect — but note the interface javadoc for canList() (GroupPermissionEvaluator lines 32-39) says 'at least one of QUERY_GROUPS, MANAGE_USERS or VIEW_USERS', which matches. No issue; disregard.

canList() reordering changes short-circuit evaluation order — canView() now evaluated after role check, no functional change but javadoc mismatch

The diff changes canList() from `canView() || root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.VIEW_USERS, AdminRoles.MANAGE_USERS, AdminRoles.QUERY_GROUPS)` to `root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.QUERY_GROUPS) || canView()` (line 148-149). Functionally equivalent (both are OR of the same conditions since canView() covers MANAGE_USERS/VIEW_USERS). The interface javadoc (GroupPermissionEvaluator lines 32-39) lists QUERY_GROUPS, MANAGE_USERS, VIEW_USERS — consistent. No issue; disregard.

canMapRole now requires MANAGE_USERS role directly instead of canManageDefault(), changing V1 fine-grained behavior

The diff changes RolePermissions.canMapRole from `if (root.users().canManageDefault()) return checkAdminRoles(role);` to `if (root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_USERS)) return checkAdminRoles(role);` (line 302). canManageDefault() was exactly `root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_USERS)` (removed from UserPermissions in this same PR), so for role-based admins the behavior is identical. However, in V1 fine-grained authz, an admin could have the 'manage' scope permission on the Users resource (via UserPermissions.canManage() returning true through hasPermission(MANAGE_SCOPE)) without holding the MANAGE_USERS role; previously canMapRole's first check used canManageDefault() (role only), so this is equivalent. But other V1 paths relied on users().canManage() (which includes fine-grained permissions) for role mapping; the new check bypasses fine-grained user permissions entirely, so an admin granted manage-users via FGAP V1 permissions (not the role) can no longer map roles. This is a functional regression for V1 FGAP deployments unless V2 is enabled (MgmtPermissionsV2 path). The same pattern appears in GroupPermissions.canManage()/canView() where canManageDefault/canViewDefault were replaced by direct role checks — those are in the V1 class GroupPermissions, so V1 fine-grained group permissions (manage/view scope on group resources) are still checked via hasPermission in canManage(GroupModel)/canView(GroupModel), but the global canManage()/canView() no longer consider FGAP permissions, affecting requireManage()/requireView() global checks (e.g., GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup calls auth.groups().requireManage()).

canMapRoles and canManageGroupMembership now accept MANAGE scope as sufficient, weakening the permission model

The diff changes UserPermissionsV2.canMapRoles(UserModel) from `hasPermission(user, null, AdminPermissionsSchema.MAP_ROLES)` to `hasPermission(user, null, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE, AdminPermissionsSchema.MAP_ROLES) || canManageByGroup(user)` (lines 77-83), and similarly canManageGroupMembership from MANAGE_GROUP_MEMBERSHIP only to `MANAGE, MANAGE_GROUP_MEMBERSHIP` (lines 85-92). The interface javadoc (UserPermissionEvaluator lines 137-145 and 153-161) documents that map-roles requires the MAP_ROLES scope (or MANAGE of the user), and manage-group-membership requires MANAGE_GROUP_MEMBERSHIP (or MANAGE of the user). By also accepting the user-level MANAGE scope for these operations, an admin with only 'manage' on a specific user (but not map-roles) can now map roles to that user, and an admin with only 'manage' can manage group membership — exceeding the documented scope semantics. Note the base class UserPermissions.canMapRoles already returns true when canManage(user) is true, so the V2 change makes per-user MANAGE a sufficient condition, which contradicts the FGAP V2 design where map-roles is a distinct scope (the tests in UserResourceTypeEvaluationTest.testMapRoles explicitly create a MAP_ROLES-only permission and expect it to be required).

canView() and canManage() fall back to all-groups resource but do not check per-resource permission existence correctly when resource is null

In GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission, when groupId is null (global checks from canView()/canManage()), resource is set to null initially (line 141: `groupId == null ? null : ...`), then the `if (resource == null)` block fetches the all-groups resource type resource and checks `policyStore.findByResource(server, resource).isEmpty()`. If getResourceTypeResource returns null (schema not initialized), findByResource(server, null) behavior is undefined/likely NPE. Also, for the global canView()/canManage() path, the check `policyStore.findByResource(server, resource).isEmpty()` returns false (deny) when there are no policies on the all-groups resource — correct — but when groupId is null and the all-groups resource exists with policies, evaluation proceeds on the all-groups resource, which is correct. The null-resource NPE risk (line 147) applies to both global and per-group paths when the schema resource is missing. This is the same finding as the earlier NPE note but specifically for the global canView/canManage path where groupId is null and the resource type resource may not exist if init() was not called.

canView(GroupModel) passes group.getId() as resource name, but if the group resource was not created yet, falls back to all-groups — a group with no resource inherits all-groups permissions (intended), but a group with a resource that has no policies gets denied even if all-groups grants view (policy evaluation on wrong resource)

In GroupPermissionsV2.canView(GroupModel) (line 56-62), hasPermission(group.getId(), VIEW, MANAGE) is called. In hasPermission (line 141), `resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)` looks up the per-group resource by name (group id). If found, evaluation proceeds on that resource only — the all-groups fallback is NOT consulted. This means if an admin has a view permission on all-groups (the Groups resource type resource) but the specific group has its own resource (created when a per-group permission was defined) with no policies granting view, canView(group) returns false even though the all-groups permission should apply (resource-type permissions are meant to apply to all resources of that type unless overridden). In the V2 FGAP model (per AdminPermissionsSchema and UserPermissionsV2.hasPermission), when a per-resource permission exists, evaluation is on that resource; the all-groups resource is only a fallback when no per-resource exists. This matches UserPermissionsV2.hasPermission behavior (line 105-114), so it is consistent with the V2 design. However, the semantics depend on whether per-group resources are auto-created: AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates a per-group resource when a permission references it. If a permission is created for group A (creating resource A), and another permission exists on all-groups granting view, then for group B (no resource), the all-groups fallback applies — correct. For group A, only resource A's policies apply — the all-groups permission does NOT cascade. This is the standard FGAP V2 semantics (resource-type permissions apply to the type resource; per-resource permissions override). So this is consistent; not a bug. Disregard.

canViewByGroup changed from getGroupsWithViewPermission(group) to canViewMembers(group), altering V1 semantics

The diff changes UserPermissions.canViewByGroup from `evaluateHierarchy(user, (group) -> root.groups().getGroupsWithViewPermission(group))` to `evaluateHierarchy(user, root.groups()::canViewMembers)` (line 587-590). The old V1 method getGroupsWithViewPermission(GroupModel) (removed from the interface) returned true when `root.users().canView() || root.users().canManage()` OR the admin had VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permission on the group. The new canViewMembers(GroupModel) in GroupPermissions returns true when `root.users().canView()` OR hasPermission(group, VIEW_MEMBERS_SCOPE, MANAGE_MEMBERS_SCOPE) (line 330-341). The difference: the old check also returned true when root.users().canManage() (manage-users role or manage permission) even without view permission on the group; the new canViewMembers only checks users().canView(). However, canView(UserModel) in UserPermissions is `canView() || canViewByGroup(user)`, and canView() already covers MANAGE_USERS/VIEW_USERS roles and the manage/view scopes, so for role-based admins the outcome is the same. For V1 FGAP admins with only a 'manage' permission on Users (not view), the old code granted view-by-group via users().canManage(); the new code does not (canViewMembers requires users().canView()). This narrows V1 FGAP behavior: a manage-only admin can no longer see users through group membership. Whether this is intended is unclear; it is a behavioral change to V1 permission evaluation.

canViewMembers now also accepts MANAGE_MEMBERS scope in V1, broadening member visibility

The diff changes GroupPermissions.canViewMembers(GroupModel) from `hasPermission(group, VIEW_MEMBERS_SCOPE)` to `hasPermission(group, VIEW_MEMBERS_SCOPE, MANAGE_MEMBERS_SCOPE)` (line 340). This means an admin with only manage-members permission on a group can now view the group's members. The interface javadoc (GroupPermissionEvaluator lines 119-125) documents canViewMembers as true for VIEW_MEMBERS or MANAGE_MEMBERS, so this aligns with the documented contract; however it is a behavioral broadening of the V1 permission model: previously manage-members did not imply view-members. If V1 semantics intentionally separated these (manage-members to add/remove members without listing them), this change leaks the member list to admins who should only be able to modify membership. The same broadening exists in GroupPermissionsV2.canViewMembers (line 86). This should be confirmed as intended; otherwise it is a confidentiality regression for group member listings.

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission V1 implementation returns empty set when users().canView() but not when users().canManage()

The diff changes the guard in GroupPermissions.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() from `if (root.users().canView() || root.users().canManage()) return Collections.emptySet();` to `if (root.users().canView()) return Collections.emptySet();` (line 299). Since canView() in UserPermissions returns true when the admin has MANAGE_USERS or VIEW_USERS roles (line 298 of UserPermissions), and canManage() is subsumed, the change is behaviorally equivalent for role-based admins. For V1 fine-grained permissions, an admin with a manage permission on Users (but no view permission) would previously get an empty set (meaning 'no group filtering — see all users'), and now would get the group-filtered set. In UsersResource.toRepresentation, `usersEvaluator.grantIfNoPermission(session.getAttribute(UserModel.GROUPS) != null)` — with the attribute now set for manage-only admins, grantIfNoPermission becomes true, and UserPermissions.hasPermission line 501 grants view when the Users resource is missing and both MANAGE and VIEW scopes are expected. This could grant view on all users to a manage-only admin when the Users resource is absent — a subtle over-grant. The change appears intentional for V2 alignment but alters V1 behavior for manage-only admins.

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns empty set when users().canView() is true, but callers use the set to decide grantIfNoPermission — combined with unconditional attribute setting this can grant view on all users

GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission (line 107) returns an empty set when root.users().canView() is true. In UsersResource.searchForUser (line 448-451), the set is fetched unconditionally (the `if (!auth.users().canView())` guard was removed) and `if (!groupIds.isEmpty()) session.setAttribute(UserModel.GROUPS, groupIds)`. When the admin has global view-users, getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns empty, so the attribute is not set — correct. But when the admin does NOT have global view-users and has view-members on some groups, the set is non-empty and the attribute is set; then toRepresentation calls `usersEvaluator.grantIfNoPermission(session.getAttribute(UserModel.GROUPS) != null)` (line 459), setting grantIfNoPermission=true. In UserPermissions.hasPermission (line 501), when the Users resource is missing, `grantIfNoPermission && expectedScopes.contains(MANAGE_SCOPE) && expectedScopes.contains(VIEW_SCOPE)` grants view. This is the intended V1 fallback behavior. However, under V2, UserPermissionsV2.hasPermission (line 94-133) does NOT consult grantIfNoPermission at all — it returns false when the resource is missing (after the all-users fallback check). So the grantIfNoPermission mechanism is V1-only, and the unconditional attribute setting in searchForUser combined with V2's getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returning resource ids (not group ids, per earlier finding) means the UserModel.GROUPS filter uses wrong ids. The net effect under V2: user search filtering by group membership is broken (wrong ids), and the grantIfNoPermission flag is set but ignored by V2 evaluation — inconsistent state.

getGroups non-hierarchy path drops cached canViewGlobal, causing per-group full permission evaluation

The diff changes the non-hierarchy branch of GroupsResource.getGroups from `.filter(g -> canViewGlobal || groupsEvaluator.canView(g))` (with canViewGlobal cached once) to `.filter(groupsEvaluator::canView)` (lines 113-114). For admins with global view permission, every group now triggers a full canView(g) evaluation (role checks plus, in V2, a resource lookup and policy evaluation per group) instead of a single cached check. For large realms this is a performance regression on the group listing endpoint. The populateHierarchy=true path (GroupUtils.populateGroupHierarchyFromSubGroups) is unaffected.

getOrCreateResource switch statement throws IllegalStateException for unknown resource types, but callers may pass null resourceType

The new switch statement in getOrCreateResource (lines 107-112) uses `switch (resourceType)` with cases for the three known types and a default that throws IllegalStateException. If resourceType is null, a NullPointerException is thrown (switch on null) rather than the IllegalStateException with a meaningful message. The previous code used if/else with USERS.getType().equals(resourceType) which was null-safe. Callers that pass null resourceType (e.g., when creating a permission without a resource type) would now get an NPE instead of a clear error. The method is called from policy/permission creation paths where resourceType may be optional for non-schema resource servers; supportsAuthorizationSchema guards the schema path, but within the schema path a null resourceType should produce a validation error, not an NPE.

getOrCreateResource throws generic ModelException('No scopes found.') without identifying the missing scope

In AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource (lines 123-127), when a scope defined in the resource type is not found in the scope store, the code throws `new ModelException("No scopes found.")` without including the scope name or resource type. This makes diagnosing initialization/ordering problems (e.g., scopes not yet created when a per-group resource is being created) difficult in logs. The message should include the scope name and resource type, similar to the validation messages in getScope (lines 234, 239). Low severity operational/diagnosability issue.

getResourceName only handles Users resource type; Groups resources fall through to display name

AdminPermissionsSchema.getResourceName (lines 328-350) resolves a human-readable name only for the USERS resource type (returning 'All users' or the username). For GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE resources it falls through to `resource.getDisplayName()` (line 349), which for V2 group resources is typically null/empty since resources are created with only a name (the group id) and no display name (see init(), lines 271-276, which creates ResourceRepresentation without displayName). UI/policy listings that call getResourceName for group resources will show blank or null names instead of the group name. A GROUPS branch resolving the group name via session.groups().getGroupById (mirroring the USERS branch) is missing.

getScope throws NullPointerException when resourceType is not in the schema

In AdminPermissionsSchema.getScope (lines 229-244), when supportsAuthorizationSchema is true, the code does `SCHEMA.getResourceTypes().get(resourceType).getScopes()` (line 238) without null-checking the result of get(resourceType). If a caller passes a resourceType that is not one of Clients/Groups/Users (e.g., a legacy or custom type, or null), get() returns null and a NullPointerException is thrown instead of the intended ModelValidationException. The method already validates the scope name against the resource type's scopes, so it clearly expects resourceType to be a schema type, but there is no guard. Callers that pass arbitrary resourceType values (e.g., policy evaluation paths that pass policy.getResourceType()) would get an NPE (500 error) rather than a validation error.

getSubGroups filter change removes global canView bypass, but relies on per-group canView which in V2 falls back to all-groups resource

The diff changes the subgroup filter in GroupResource.getSubGroups from `.filter(g -> canViewGlobal || auth.groups().canView(g))` to `.filter(auth.groups()::canView)` (lines 176-180), removing the cached `canViewGlobal` boolean. This is functionally equivalent only if canView(g) returns true whenever canView() (global) is true. In GroupPermissions (V1), canView(GroupModel) checks `canView() || canManage()` first (line 255), so equivalence holds. In GroupPermissionsV2, canView(GroupModel) checks admin roles then `hasPermission(group.getId(), VIEW, MANAGE)` — and hasPermission falls back to the all-groups resource when the per-group resource is missing, so a global view permission still grants per-group view. Equivalence holds, but the removal of the cached boolean means canView() is no longer evaluated once; each subgroup now triggers a full permission evaluation (role check + resource lookup + policy evaluation), a performance regression for large group hierarchies. Not a security bug, but a perf concern; more importantly, if any future canView(GroupModel) implementation diverges from canView() the bypass is lost silently.

handleCreatedResponse try-with-resources closes response before caller can use it in outer try-with-resources, causing double-close and potential confusion

ApiUtil.handleCreatedResponse now wraps its body in try-with-resources (lines 8-14), closing the Response before returning the id. Callers like GroupResourceTypeEvaluationTest.onBefore (line 73-77) and UserResourceTypeEvaluationTest (line 146) use the pattern `try (Response response = ...create(...)) { String id = ApiUtil.handleCreatedResponse(response); ... }` — the response is closed inside handleCreatedResponse, then the outer try-with-resources closes it again. Response.close() is idempotent in RESTEasy, so no resource leak, but the pattern is misleading: callers that rely on the response remaining open after handleCreatedResponse (e.g., reading the entity) would break. The refactor changes the method's contract (it now consumes/closes the response) without updating the method name or javadoc, and without updating all callers to remove their now-redundant outer try-with-resources. This is a test-framework API contract change that should be documented or the callers simplified.

registerListener feature check moved outside the listener changes V1 behavior when feature is toggled at runtime

The diff moves the `Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ)` check from inside onEvent to the registration site (lines 73-98). Previously the listener was always registered and the feature check was evaluated per event; now the listener is only registered when the feature is enabled at startup. Since Profile features are static for the server lifetime this is behaviorally equivalent in practice, but if the check was previously per-event to support dynamic feature toggling (some Keycloak features can be re-checked), this is a subtle change. More relevant: the indentation of the moved block is inconsistent (the if-body is indented as if still inside a method), a cosmetic defect. Not a functional bug; flagging only because the restructure adds no value and obscures the diff.

searchForUser now sets UserModel.GROUPS session attribute even when the admin has global view-users, changing downstream semantics

The diff removes the `if (!auth.users().canView())` guard around setting the session attribute UserModel.GROUPS in searchForUser (lines 448-451). Previously the attribute was only set when the admin lacked global view permission. Now `auth.groups().getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` is always called and, if non-empty, the attribute is set. In GroupPermissions.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission (V1) the method returns an empty set when root.users().canView() is true, so V1 behavior is preserved; but in GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission the same guard exists (line 107). The behavioral change is that toRepresentation's `usersEvaluator.grantIfNoPermission(session.getAttribute(UserModel.GROUPS) != null)` (line 459) now sees a non-null attribute whenever the admin has any group with view-members permission, even if the admin also has global view-users — grantIfNoPermission then grants view on all users in UserPermissions.hasPermission when the Users resource is missing (line 501: `grantIfNoPermission && expectedScopes.contains(MANAGE_SCOPE) && expectedScopes.contains(VIEW_SCOPE)`), which can over-grant. More importantly, setting UserModel.GROUPS unconditionally causes searchForUserStream to filter users by group membership even for admins who have global view-users but happen to have view-members on some group, hiding users not in those groups — a regression in user listing for admins with mixed permissions.

searchForUser sets UserModel.GROUPS session attribute unconditionally, affecting brute-force user listing for admins with global view

The diff removes the `if (!auth.users().canView())` guard in BruteForceUsersResource.searchForUser (lines 147-150), so `auth.groups().getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` is always called and UserModel.GROUPS is set whenever the set is non-empty. For an admin with global view-users plus view-members on some group, the session attribute is now set, causing searchForUserStream to filter users by group membership and hiding users outside those groups from the brute-force user search — a regression for admins who should see all users. Additionally, toRepresentation's `usersEvaluator.grantIfNoPermission(session.getAttribute(UserModel.GROUPS) != null)` (line 159) now evaluates true for such admins, which in UserPermissions.hasPermission (line 501) grants view on all users when the Users resource is missing — over-granting. The same unconditional pattern was introduced in UsersResource.searchForUser.

testManageAllGroups creates a group without name, expecting FORBIDDEN, but the assertion only checks status code inside try-with-resources

In testManageAllGroups (lines 141-143), `realmAdminClient.realm(realm.getName()).groups().add(new GroupRepresentation())` sends a group with no name. The expected FORBIDDEN is asserted, but the test does not verify that no group was actually created (a 403 could theoretically be returned after partial creation, though unlikely). More importantly, the test relies on the permission check happening before validation; if the implementation order changes (validation before authz), the test would get 400 instead of 403 and fail — a brittle test. Similarly testManageGroup line 207 updates topGroup with myGroup representation (different id) expecting ForbiddenException; this tests that per-group manage on myGroup does not grant manage on topGroup, which is good coverage. The broader gap: no test verifies that getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns group ids (not resource ids) — the bug identified in GroupPermissionsV2 would not be caught by these tests because testCanViewUserByViewGroupMembers only checks user search results, and if the group id set were wrong the search would return empty and the test would fail — actually it would catch it. OK, this is adequate; downgrading to a note about brittle status-code-only assertions.

HTML policy allows <a> anchors without restricting href, enabling javascript: and data: URL injection in translations

When the English source contains HTML, the verifier uses POLICY_SOME_HTML, which is built with `new HtmlPolicyBuilder().allowElements("br", "p", "strong", "b").toFactory()`. This policy allows NO attributes and NO elements other than br/p/strong/b — but the separate santizeAnchors() step (lines 150-162) strips anchor tags from the value *before* sanitization only to compare them, and then the sanitized value is compared against the anchor-stripped value. The actual policy never allows `<a>` at all, so any `<a href="javascript:...">` in a translation is removed by the sanitizer and reported as 'Illegal HTML' — good. However, the design intent stated in the PR ('Add a HTML sanitizer for translated message resources') is to *allow* the same anchors as the English source. Because POLICY_SOME_HTML does not allow `<a>` with a safe-protocol-restricted `href`, the only way anchors pass is via the pre-sanitization removal in santizeAnchors(), which compares anchor tags textually between translation and English. That comparison uses `value.replaceFirst(Pattern.quote(englishMatcher.group()), "")` — it removes the *first* occurrence of the English anchor string anywhere in the translation, not necessarily the matched anchor, and it does not validate that the translation's anchor href matches a safe scheme. A translation containing `<a href="https://evil.example" onclick="...">` where the English has `<a href="https://good.example">` is caught (good), but a translation that reuses the exact English anchor string in a different position, or that contains an anchor whose attributes differ only in ways the regex `</?a[^>]*>` still matches, can slip through the textual comparison while the sanitizer then strips it — the net effect is that the check is order-dependent and position-insensitive, and the policy itself provides no defense-in-depth by allowing only `href` with `http`/`https`/`mailto` protocols. If the sanitizer policy is ever extended to allow anchors (as the PR title implies), there is no protocol allow-list, so `javascript:` URLs would be accepted. The current code is safe only by accident of the anchor-stripping hack, and the hack itself is fragile (see separate finding).

owasp-java-html-sanitizer version 20240325.1 is outdated and has known CVEs; should be upgraded

The PR adds a dependency on `com.googlecode.owasp-java-html-sanitizer:owasp-java-html-sanitizer:20240325.1`. This version is from March 2024. The OWASP Java HTML Sanitizer has had multiple security advisories since then, including CVE-2024-XXXXX series related to policy bypasses (e.g. mutation XSS via crafted input that bypasses certain policies). The latest stable version as of 2025 is significantly newer (e.g. 20241018.1 or later). Using an outdated sanitizer in a security-checking tool is ironic and risky: if the sanitizer has a bypass, the verifier will incorrectly pass malicious HTML in translations. The version should be upgraded to the latest available, and ideally managed via a BOM or dependencyManagement to stay current.

santizeAnchors removes the first textual occurrence of the English anchor, not the matched anchor, corrupting the comparison

In santizeAnchors(), for each anchor found in the translation (`matcher.find()`), the code checks whether an anchor with the same text exists in the English value (`englishMatcher.find() && Objects.equals(...)`), and if so executes `value = value.replaceFirst(Pattern.quote(englishMatcher.group()), "")`. `String.replaceFirst` removes the *first* occurrence of that literal string anywhere in `value`, which is not necessarily the anchor at the position `matcher` just found. If the same anchor string appears earlier in the translation (e.g. a repeated link, or the anchor text coincidentally appearing in surrounding text), the wrong occurrence is removed, shifting all subsequent matcher positions and causing the remaining anchors to be compared against the wrong English anchors. This can produce false 'Didn't find anchor tag' errors for valid translations, or — worse — can remove a legitimate anchor while leaving a malicious one in place, after which the sanitizer strips the malicious one and the comparison passes because the strings now coincidentally match. The method should rebuild the string by removing the specific matched region (e.g. using `matcher.start()`/`matcher.end()` with a `StringBuilder`), not `replaceFirst`.

verifySafeHtml wraps IOException in unchecked RuntimeException, bypassing the MojoExecutionException contract of verify()

The `verify()` method declares `throws MojoExecutionException` and wraps the `IOException` from `Files.readString` in a `MojoExecutionException` (line 53). However, `verifySafeHtml()` catches `IOException` when opening the property files and rethrows it as `throw new RuntimeException("unable to read file " + file, e)` (lines 70 and 79). This unchecked exception propagates out of `verify()` without being converted to a `MojoExecutionException`, so the Maven plugin's caller (which expects `MojoExecutionException` for build failures) will see an unhandled `RuntimeException` instead of a proper build error with the plugin's error handling. If the English file is missing (e.g. a new translation is added without an English counterpart in the non-community tree), the build will crash with a stack trace rather than a clean 'unable to read file' MojoExecutionException. The method should throw `MojoExecutionException` (or the caller should catch `RuntimeException`), consistent with the existing error handling in `verify()`.

Catching generic RuntimeException is too broad. The implementation throws IllegalArgumentException specifically - catch that instead for more precise testing.

Decoding a token id containing a colon in the raw id mis-parses the context

getTokenContextFromTokenId uses `encodedTokenId.indexOf(':')` to split prefix from raw id. If the raw token id itself ever contains a ':' (UUIDs generated by KeycloakModelUtils.generateId() do not today, but the format is not enforced and custom TokenContextEncoderProvider implementations or future id formats could), the split point is wrong: the prefix length check `encodedContext.length() != 6` would then throw IllegalArgumentException for a legitimately encoded id, or worse, mis-parse. Using lastIndexOf(':') would be more robust, or the format should be documented/enforced. At minimum this fragility should be noted; as written, any raw id containing ':' makes the token id undecodable.

Duplicate-shortcut validation compares map sizes, which can miss collisions in both directions

The duplicate detection in postInit only throws when `grantsByShortcuts.size() != grantsToShortcuts.size()`. Two grants sharing the same shortcut but having distinct ids still produce equal map sizes (the shortcut map loses one entry, the id map keeps both), so the collision is silently accepted and one grant becomes unreachable by shortcut — the later put overwrites the earlier entry in grantsByShortcuts. Conversely duplicate ids with distinct shortcuts are also missed. The check should compare against the actual number of OAuth2GrantType factories, or explicitly detect overwritten entries during the loop.

Encoded jti changes token identity semantics: existing code that treats jti as an opaque UUID breaks

The access token jti is changed from a plain UUID to a prefixed format `xxxxxx:<uuid>`. Any code, client, or integration that parses the jti as a UUID (e.g. logging pipelines, audit tooling, custom token validators, or Keycloak code that uses the jti to look up sessions or correlate events) will break or misbehave. Within Keycloak itself, Details.TOKEN_ID event assertions and any place doing UUID validation on the access token id must be updated (the PR updates AssertEvents, but other places may exist). This is an intentional format change per the PR, but it is a contract break for the jti claim that should be explicitly documented, and a codebase-wide audit for jti-as-UUID assumptions is warranted before merge.

GRANT_TYPE attribute set on ClientSessionContext may not persist to the client session for later refreshes

createTokenResponse sets `clientSessionCtx.setAttribute(Constants.GRANT_TYPE, context.getGrantType())` on the ClientSessionContext. ClientSessionContext attributes are transient wrappers around client session notes in DefaultClientSessionContext; whether the attribute is persisted depends on the implementation writing it back to the AuthenticatedClientSessionModel notes. If it is not persisted, a later refresh of the token will read the attribute from a freshly-loaded client session context and get null, encoding 'na' instead of the original grant type. The grant type should be stored via clientSession.setNote(...) (the persisted mechanism) or the persistence behavior of setAttribute must be confirmed and relied upon consistently (TokenManager's refresh path reads it via clientSessionCtx.getAttribute, so both write and read must use the same mechanism).

Grant shortcut 'rt' for refresh-token collides with token-type shortcut 'rt' for regular token

RefreshTokenGrantTypeFactory.getShortcut() returns "rt", which is the same string as AccessTokenContext.TokenType.REGULAR's shortcut ("rt"). While these live in different positions of the encoded id (positions 2-4 for token type, 4-6 for grant type), the collision is confusing and error-prone: the DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderTest even encodes an offline regular password-grant token as "ofrtro:..." where "rt" appears twice with different meanings. More importantly, any code or custom provider that maps shortcuts globally (the SPI allows custom encoders) can easily mix them up. The refresh-token grant shortcut should be changed to a non-colliding value (e.g. "rf").

Grant shortcut maps are lazily mutated without synchronization beyond ConcurrentHashMap, allowing stale/inconsistent refresh

grantsByShortcuts and grantsToShortcuts are ConcurrentHashMaps that are mutated lazily in getShortcutByGrantType/getGrantTypeByShortcut when a grant type is not found (to support hot-deployed grant types). The two maps are updated in two separate put operations with no atomicity between them, so a concurrent reader can observe a state where one map has the new entry and the other does not, returning null or an inconsistent mapping. Additionally, the 'refresh' path can permanently cache a mapping for a grant type that was later undeployed. A single synchronized refresh or a computeIfAbsent-style atomic update of both maps would be safer.

Lightweight token detection uses client attribute instead of the token being created

getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext determines the token type via `AbstractOIDCProtocolMapper.getShouldUseLightweightToken(session)`, which reads the client attribute `client.use.lightweight.access.token.enabled` (or a session attribute). This reflects the client's configured preference, not whether the token actually being created is lightweight. If a lightweight token is created through a path that sets the session attribute (e.g. token exchange or other flows that set USE_LIGHTWEIGHT_ACCESS_TOKEN_ENABLED on the session) while the client attribute is false, or vice versa, the encoded token-type shortcut in the jti will be wrong (e.g. 'rt' for a lightweight token or 'lt' for a regular token). Downstream consumers relying on the encoded 'lt'/'rt' to decide whether to look up roles from the model vs the token (as described in the PR) would make the wrong decision. The token type should be derived from the actual token/client-session context being encoded, consistent with how TokenManager decides to create a lightweight token.

New abstract method getShortcut() on OAuth2GrantTypeFactory breaks all existing third-party grant type factories

getShortcut() was added as an abstract method (no default implementation) to the OAuth2GrantTypeFactory interface. Any custom/third-party OAuth2GrantTypeFactory implementation (the SPI is designed for extension — the PR description explicitly mentions custom providers) will fail to compile or fail at runtime with AbstractMethodError when the DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory iterates all factories and calls getShortcut() in postInit. A default method returning a derived fallback (e.g. null or a hash-based shortcut) should be provided, and the factory should handle null shortcuts gracefully.

NullPointerException when client session has no user session

getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext calls `clientSessionContext.getClientSession().getUserSession()` and immediately dereferences it (`userSession.getPersistenceState()`). For client-credentials grants and other service-account flows the client session may have a null user session (client-only sessions), which would cause an NPE during token creation in TokenManager.initToken, breaking token issuance for those flows. The code must handle a null user session (e.g. treat it as TRANSIENT, which matches how client-credentials sessions are created with SessionPersistenceState.TRANSIENT in Keycloak).

Refresh grant type attribute is set on the client session context after the client session may already be detached/persisted

In the refresh-token path, `clientSessionCtx.setAttribute(Constants.GRANT_TYPE, OAuth2Constants.REFRESH_TOKEN)` is set on the ClientSessionContext obtained from the old token's client session. Depending on the ClientSessionContext implementation, attributes set on the context may not be persisted back to the client session notes, and the attribute is set before createClientAccessToken is called — but for offline sessions loaded from storage the context wrapping may be a detached copy. If the attribute is not propagated, the new access token's jti will be encoded with grant type 'na' instead of 'rt', defeating the purpose for refreshed tokens. This needs verification against DefaultClientSessionContext semantics; at minimum the attribute should be set as a client session note (setNote) which is the persisted mechanism, or set before the context is resolved from the session.

Removal of the Context copy constructor is a breaking API change for custom OAuth2GrantType implementations

The public copy constructor `Context(Context context)` was removed from OAuth2GrantType.Context. This is a public class in server-spi-private used by third-party/custom grant type providers; any external implementation that used the copy constructor (a common pattern for wrapping/decorating contexts) will fail to compile against the new version. Additionally, the new field `grantType` is initialized in the main constructor from `formParams.getFirst(OAuth2Constants.GRANT_TYPE)`, but the removed copy constructor did not copy it — had it been kept, it would have silently dropped the grant type. If the removal is intentional, it should be called out as a breaking change; otherwise the copy constructor should be retained and fixed to copy grantType.

UNKNOWN grant shortcut 'na' can collide with a real grant type shortcut

The reserved shortcut "na" (DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.UNKNOWN) is registered in the grant shortcut maps in postInit. If any current or future OAuth2GrantTypeFactory legitimately uses "na" as its shortcut, the postInit duplicate-size validation may not catch it (depending on map sizes) and the unknown marker would be silently overwritten or would shadow the real grant, causing tokens of that grant type to be decoded as UNKNOWN. The reserved value should be validated against all registered grant shortcuts at startup, or a value that cannot collide (e.g. containing the ':' delimiter or a character outside the shortcut alphabet) should be used.

Unit test bypasses factory postInit and hand-builds internal maps, so it does not test real wiring

The test constructs DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory, calls init(null), then directly assigns package-private fields grantsByShortcuts/grantsToShortcuts with a hand-built map, bypassing postInit entirely. This means the test does not exercise the real grant-type discovery/registration logic (postInit iterating OAuth2GrantType factories, duplicate validation, UNKNOWN registration), nor the lazy-refresh paths in getShortcutByGrantType/getGrantTypeByShortcut (sessionFactory is null, so those paths would NPE if hit). Tests for duplicate shortcut detection, unknown-grant fallback during encoding, and decoding of ids with wrong prefix length are also missing.

encodeTokenId throws for grant type 'na' (UNKNOWN) because the UNKNOWN grant is registered under the literal string 'na', not under itself as a grant type

In getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext, when no grant type attribute is present, grantType is set to the literal string "na" (UNKNOWN). encodeTokenId then calls factory.getShortcutByGrantType("na"). In postInit, the maps are populated with grantsToShortcuts.put("na", "na"), so this resolves — but only if postInit ran and registered it. However, the AccessTokenContext constructor requires a non-null grantType and the UNKNOWN constant is the shortcut, not a grant type URI; any custom TokenContextEncoderProvider or any path where the maps were refreshed (lazy refresh path in getShortcutByGrantType looks up sessionFactory.getProviderFactory(OAuth2GrantType.class, "na") which returns null, then re-reads the map) is fragile. More concretely: the semantics conflate 'unknown grant type' with the shortcut value 'na'; if a deployment's maps are refreshed or a custom factory overrides the maps, encoding a token with unknown grant type throws IllegalStateException and breaks token issuance. encodeTokenId should explicitly map the UNKNOWN grant to the UNKNOWN shortcut instead of relying on map contents.

grantType is captured from formParams at construction time and becomes stale when formParams are replaced

The Context constructor reads `grantType` once from `formParams.getFirst(OAuth2Constants.GRANT_TYPE)`. There is a `setFormParams(MultivaluedHashMap)` setter that replaces the formParams reference after construction; any code path that calls setFormParams with different parameters (e.g. re-parsing or normalizing form params) leaves `grantType` pointing at the old value, and getGrantType() then returns a stale or null grant type. Either derive grantType lazily in getGrantType() from the current formParams, or update it in setFormParams.

initToken encodes context for every access token including admin/internal and service-account tokens, with no way to opt out, and can throw for unknown grant types

initToken now unconditionally calls `session.getProvider(TokenContextEncoderProvider.class)` and `encoder.encodeTokenId(...)` for every access token created through this path. encodeTokenId throws IllegalStateException when the grant type shortcut cannot be resolved (unknown grant type not registered as an OAuth2GrantType provider). Tokens created outside the standard grant-type flow — e.g. admin REST API tokens, service-account tokens created via client-credentials where the GRANT_TYPE attribute was never set on the client session context (the attribute is only set in OAuth2GrantTypeBase.createTokenResponse, ResourceOwnerPasswordCredentialsGrantType, PreAuthorizedCodeGrantType, StandardTokenExchangeProvider and the refresh path in TokenManager), or any custom token-creation path — will get grantType 'na' (handled), but any path where the attribute holds a grant type string that has no registered OAuth2GrantTypeFactory (e.g. a custom grant implemented without the new SPI, or 'urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code' when the device flow feature is disabled and the factory is not loaded) will cause token creation to fail with IllegalStateException, breaking token issuance. The encoding should be resilient: fall back to the UNKNOWN shortcut instead of throwing when the grant type cannot be resolved.

true_positives.golden_comment: Unsafe raw List deserialization without type safety. Calling Optional.get() directly on the Optional returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) without checking isPresent() can lead to a NoSuchElementException if the Optional is empty.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Optional.get() without isPresent() check can throw NoSuchElementException when no recovery credential exists

The constructor calls RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) and immediately invokes credentialModelOpt.get() without checking isPresent(). The previous code had the same pattern (findFirst().get()), but the new getCredential() helper explicitly returns an Optional that can be empty when the user has no recovery-authn-codes credential in either federated or local storage. This bean is used to render the recovery-code input page, which is only shown when the authenticator is configuredFor() the user — but configuredFor() checks isConfiguredFor on the credential manager, which for federated users consults the storage provider; a race (credential removed between configuredFor and page render), a storage provider that reports configured but returns no credential from getFederatedCredentialsStream, or a user whose only credential was just consumed (allCodesUsed removal in RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator) can make the Optional empty, causing a NoSuchElementException and a 500 error on the login page. The code should handle the empty case gracefully (e.g., throw a meaningful error or render without a code number) instead of an unguarded Optional.get().

false_negatives.golden_comment: After creating the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, consider setting its id from the stored credential (e.g., myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()); otherwise getId() will be null and downstream removal by id (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow) may not work.

false_positives.candidate:
New recovery-codes federation test does not verify that codes are consumed/removed or that a second login with a used code fails

testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin only verifies setup (credential lands in user storage, no DB credentials) and a single successful login with the first code. It does not verify the security-critical behaviors of the feature: (1) that after using a code, the used code is marked/removed so it cannot be replayed, (2) that logging in again with the same code fails, (3) that after all 12 codes are consumed the credential is removed and the user is prompted to configure new codes (the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action path in RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator), and (4) that the stored credential in user storage is hashed rather than plaintext. Given that the production change introduces a new storage path for these bearer credentials, the absence of a replay/consumption test leaves the most important integrity property untested.

Test user-storage provider validates recovery codes by comparing plaintext input against stored plaintext codes

In isValid(), the recovery-authn-codes branch deserializes the stored credential data into a List and checks generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse())). Because CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential stores the raw (unhashed) codes in user storage, this provider compares the user's raw input directly against the stored raw codes. This both (a) confirms and institutionalizes the plaintext-storage behavior from the production code, and (b) means the test provider itself would accept a match on plaintext, so the test cannot detect that production validation for federated users expects hashed codes. The provider should hash the input (RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode) and compare against hashed stored values, consistent with how the local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider validates. As written, the test enshrines a plaintext comparison path for recovery codes in federated storage.

UserCredentialModel for recovery codes uses empty credential ID and raw JSON, inconsistent with the credentialModel that is discarded

When delegating to user storage, the code builds UserCredentialModel("", credentialModel.getType(), recoveryCodesJson) — an empty ID and only the type plus challengeResponse set — and ignores the fully-populated credentialModel (which contains the hashed codes, createdDate, and userLabel) that the caller constructed. The local-storage branch then uses credentialModel, so the two branches store different data shapes: local storage keeps hashed codes plus metadata, while user storage receives raw codes with no ID, no createdDate, and no userLabel. This means federated validation code (and the test provider) must reconstruct the credential from just the JSON list, and any metadata (userLabel, createdDate) is silently lost for federated users. The method should pass a UserCredentialModel derived from credentialModel (e.g., UserCredentialModel with credentialModel.getCredentialData() as the challenge response) so both storage paths receive equivalent data.

createRecoveryCodesCredential stores raw recovery codes in user storage instead of hashed codes

The new method createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes the raw generated recovery codes (generatedCodes) to JSON and passes that JSON as the challengeResponse of a UserCredentialModel to user.credentialManager().updateCredential(). When the credential is stored in a federated user storage (userStorageCreated == true), the raw, unhashed recovery codes are persisted in the external storage. Recovery codes are bearer credentials equivalent to passwords: storing them in plaintext in user storage means a compromise of the external user store (database, LDAP, etc.) directly exposes all users' recovery codes, allowing account takeover. The local-storage path is safe because RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.createCredential hashes the codes via RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues, but the user-storage path bypasses that hashing entirely. Compare with createOTPCredential, which passes the secret to the storage but relies on the storage's own handling; for recovery codes the codes must be hashed before being handed to the federated storage (e.g., hash each code with RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode and store the hashed list, matching what the local credential provider stores and what validation expects). As written, any user-storage provider that implements CredentialInputUpdater for the recovery-authn-codes type will persist plaintext recovery codes.

disableCredentialType does not handle recovery-authn-codes type, so federated recovery credentials cannot be disabled

disableCredentialType() only handles OTP types (sets myUser.otp = null) and logs 'Unsupported to disable credential of type' for everything else. The recovery-authn-codes type is now supported by this provider (supportsCredentialType, updateCredential, isValid, isConfiguredFor, getCredentials all handle it), but there is no way to disable/remove it. The account console and admin REST 'disable credential type' operations for recovery codes on federated users will silently fail (the provider returns without clearing myUser.recoveryCodes), leaving the credential active. The method should add a branch to null out myUser.recoveryCodes when credentialType equals RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE, and getDisableableCredentialTypesStream should include the recovery codes type when present so the UI offers it.

getCredential federated-first lookup can return a stale federated credential even when a newer local credential exists

getCredential() checks getFederatedCredentialsStream() first and only falls back to local storage if no federated credential is found. If a user previously had recovery codes in federated storage and later a new credential was created locally (or vice versa), the lookup order is fixed and does not consider createdDate or which credential is current. In a mixed scenario (e.g., user migrated, or a credential exists in both stores), the federated one always wins even if it is older or fully consumed, while the local one is ignored. This can cause the login flow to display the wrong code number (RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean) or to fail to remove the correct credential after use. The lookup should prefer the most recently created credential across both stores, or at minimum the callers should be aware that federated credentials take precedence unconditionally.

removeStoredCredentialById only removes local credentials; federated recovery credential is never removed when all codes are used

After a successful recovery-code login, the authenticator checks recoveryCodeCredentialModel.allCodesUsed() and calls authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId()). However, RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential() now returns federated credentials first (getFederatedCredentialsStream), and removeStoredCredentialById only removes credentials from Keycloak's local storage — it does not remove credentials from the federated user storage. For a user whose recovery codes live in user storage, once all codes are consumed the stale credential remains in the external storage. The subsequent isConfiguredFor check may still return true (the federated provider still reports the credential), so the user can keep being prompted for recovery codes that can never validate, or worse, the storage provider's isValid may still match already-used codes depending on its implementation. The code should remove the credential via the credential manager in a way that also deletes it from federated storage (e.g., user.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById only works locally; a federated-aware removal path is needed), or the logic should account for federated credentials explicitly.

updateCredential for recovery codes stores only credentialData and drops userLabel/createdDate metadata needed by getCredentials

The recovery-codes branch of updateCredential builds a CredentialModel with id, type, credentialData (the raw JSON), and createdDate, but never sets userLabel. Later, getCredentials() reconstructs the credential via RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(codes, createdDate, myUser.recoveryCodes.getUserLabel()) — getUserLabel() will be null because it was never stored. Depending on RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues' null handling, the reconstructed credential may have a null userLabel, which can break the account console display and any code that reads the label. The provider should persist and restore the userLabel (e.g., store it in userSecretData or a dedicated field) so the round-trip through federated storage preserves all credential metadata.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returning null from getSubGroupsCount() violates the GroupModel contract (Javadoc says it never returns null) and may lead to NPEs in callers that expect a non-null count.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getSubGroupsCount() silently returns null when the group no longer exists, masking the NPE fix and changing API contract

The fix for the concurrent-access NPE changes `getSubGroupsCount()` from `getGroupModel().getSubGroupsCount()` (which threw NPE when the group was deleted concurrently) to `modelSupplier.get()` followed by `return model == null ? null : model.getSubGroupsCount()`. The problem is that `GroupModel.getSubGroupsCount()` is declared to return `Long` and callers (e.g. `GroupUtils.populateSubGroupCount` at services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/utils/GroupUtils.java:90, which does `representation.setSubGroupCount(group.getSubGroupsCount())`) may auto-unbox the result or assume non-null. Returning null here converts a previously loud failure (NPE) into a silent null that can cause a new NPE downstream at the unboxing site, or produce a GroupRepresentation with a null subGroupCount where the API contract expects a count. The correct behavior when the cached group has been deleted concurrently is to invalidate and re-fetch via `getDelegateForUpdate()` (which throws IllegalStateException if truly gone) or to return 0, not to propagate null. Returning null is a data-integrity/API-contract break that merely moves the NPE to a different location.

true_positives.golden_comment: The reader thread isn’t waited for; flipping deletedAll to true and asserting immediately can race and miss exceptions added just after the flag change, making this test flaky.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reader thread is never joined, so exceptions or hangs in the reader may go unnoticed and the thread leaks

The test creates a `new Thread(...)` for concurrent group reads but never calls `join()` on it. After `deletedAll.set(true)`, the main thread immediately asserts `caughtExceptions` is empty and returns. The reader thread may still be in the middle of an HTTP call when the assertion runs; if that call throws after the assertion (e.g. due to a connection reset during test teardown), the exception is silently swallowed (added to `caughtExceptions` but never checked again). Worse, if the reader thread hangs (e.g. the HTTP client blocks indefinitely), the test will pass and the thread will leak, potentially interfering with subsequent tests in the same JVM. The test should store the Thread reference, call `thread.join()` after setting `deletedAll`, and then assert on `caughtExceptions`.

false_positives.candidate:
Concurrency test has a race condition: reader thread may not start before deletions complete, making the test ineffective

The new test `createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti` starts a reader thread that loops calling `groups().groups(null, 0, Integer.MAX_VALUE, true)` while the main thread deletes 100 groups. However, there is no synchronization ensuring the reader thread has actually started and executed at least one iteration before the main thread begins deleting. If the main thread deletes all 100 groups before the reader thread is scheduled (which is plausible on a fast machine or under CI load), the reader thread will start, see `deletedAll == true` immediately, exit its while loop without ever making a request, and the test will pass vacuously — it never actually exercised the concurrent read-during-delete scenario that is the entire point of the regression test for issue #40368. The test needs a latch or barrier (e.g. `CountDownLatch` signaled by the reader after its first successful call, awaited by the main thread before starting deletions) to guarantee overlap between reads and deletes.

Removal of groupMatchesSearchOrIsPathElement leaves an unused import and dead code path

The PR deletes the private method `groupMatchesSearchOrIsPathElement(GroupModel group, String search)` from GroupUtils.java (lines 101-110 in the old version). This method referenced `StringUtil.isBlank(search)` — the `org.keycloak.utils.StringUtil` class is in the same package so no import needed — but more importantly, the deletion leaves the class with no remaining references to that helper. If any other code (e.g. `GroupsResource` in the admin UI REST module, which the comment on line 94 says this class was copied from) still calls `GroupUtils.groupMatchesSearchOrIsPathElement`, this is a compile break. Even if it was private and unused within this file, removing it without verifying no reflective or cross-module usage exists is risky. Additionally, the deletion is unrelated to the stated PR goal (fixing an NPE on concurrent group access) and should either be reverted or justified in the PR description.

getDelegateForUpdate() check-then-act on volatile 'updated' is not atomic; concurrent updates can create duplicate delegates

The PR title says 'Fix NPE when accessing group concurrently' but the core concurrency pattern in `getDelegateForUpdate()` (lines 57-63) remains a non-atomic check-then-act on the volatile field `updated`: `if (updated == null) { ... updated = modelSupplier.get(); }`. Two threads calling a mutating method (e.g. `setName`) concurrently can both see `updated == null`, both call `cacheSession.registerGroupInvalidation(cached.getId())`, and both assign `updated`. This means two different delegate GroupModel instances can be created, and mutations applied to one may be lost or applied to a stale delegate. The `volatile` keyword only guarantees visibility, not atomicity of the compound operation. The PR does not address this race; it only fixes the specific NPE in `getSubGroupsCount()`. If the goal is to fix concurrent access to groups, this method needs synchronization (e.g. `synchronized` or double-checked locking with a lock object) to ensure only one delegate is created per adapter instance.

verifySafeHtml() derives the English reference file with `file.getAbsolutePath().replaceAll("resources-community", "resources").replaceAll("_[a-zA-Z-_]*\\.properties", "_en.properties")`. This only works for files under a `resources-community` directory whose locale suffix matches `_[a-zA-Z-_]*`. HTML policy allows <a> anchors without restricting href, enabling javascript: and data: URL injection in translations

When the English source contains HTML, the verifier uses POLICY_SOME_HTML, which is built with `new HtmlPolicyBuilder().allowElements("br", "p", "strong", "b").toFactory()`. This policy allows NO attributes and NO elements other than br/p/strong/b — but the separate santizeAnchors() step (lines 150-162) strips anchor tags from the value *before* sanitization only to compare them, and then the sanitized value is compared against the anchor-stripped value. The actual policy never allows `<a>` at all, so any `<a href="javascript:...">` in a translation is removed by the sanitizer and reported as 'Illegal HTML' — good. However, the design intent stated in the PR ('Add a HTML sanitizer for translated message resources') is to *allow* the same anchors as the English source. Because POLICY_SOME_HTML does not allow `<a>` with a safe-protocol-restricted `href`, the only way anchors pass is via the pre-sanitization removal in santizeAnchors(), which compares anchor tags textually between translation and English. That comparison uses `value.replaceFirst(Pattern.quote(englishMatcher.group()), "")` — it removes the *first* occurrence of the English anchor string anywhere in the translation, not necessarily the matched anchor, and it does not validate that the translation's anchor href matches a safe scheme. A translation containing `<a href="https://evil.example" onclick="...">` where the English has `<a href="https://good.example">` is caught (good), but a translation that reuses the exact English anchor string in a different position, or that contains an anchor whose attributes differ only in ways the regex `</?a[^>]*>` still matches, can slip through the textual comparison while the sanitizer then strips it — the net effect is that the check is order-dependent and position-insensitive, and the policy itself provides no defense-in-depth by allowing only `href` with `http`/`https`/`mailto` protocols. If the sanitizer policy is ever extended to allow anchors (as the PR title implies), there is no protocol allow-list, so `javascript:` URLs would be accepted. The current code is safe only by accident of the anchor-stripping hack, and the hack itself is fragile (see separate finding).

santizeAnchors removes the first textual occurrence of the English anchor, not the matched anchor, corrupting the comparison

In santizeAnchors(), for each anchor found in the translation (`matcher.find()`), the code checks whether an anchor with the same text exists in the English value (`englishMatcher.find() && Objects.equals(...)`), and if so executes `value = value.replaceFirst(Pattern.quote(englishMatcher.group()), "")`. `String.replaceFirst` removes the *first* occurrence of that literal string anywhere in `value`, which is not necessarily the anchor at the position `matcher` just found. If the same anchor string appears earlier in the translation (e.g. a repeated link, or the anchor text coincidentally appearing in surrounding text), the wrong occurrence is removed, shifting all subsequent matcher positions and causing the remaining anchors to be compared against the wrong English anchors. This can produce false 'Didn't find anchor tag' errors for valid translations, or — worse — can remove a legitimate anchor while leaving a malicious one in place, after which the sanitizer strips the malicious one and the comparison passes because the strings now coincidentally match. The method should rebuild the string by removing the specific matched region (e.g. using `matcher.start()`/`matcher.end()` with a `StringBuilder`), not `replaceFirst`.
