The state change should be a POST/PUT (with the GET page rendering the confirmation UI), or at minimum the mutation should require an explicit confirmation.

check_xhr is skipped for unsubscribe, allowing non-XHR state changes `skip_before_filter :check_xhr, only: [:show, :unsubscribe, :feed]` disables the CSRF/XHR check for the unsubscribe action. Combined with the GET route, this means the notification-level mutation can be triggered by any cross-site GET request (e.g., an tag on a third-party page pointing at the unsubscribe URL) while the victim is logged in, since no CSRF token is required for GET. This is a CSRF risk on a state-changing endpoint.

Route creates a new topic record with only an id, producing an invalid/partial model

The model hook does `this.store.createRecord("topic", { id: params.id })` and then `topic.updateFromJson(json)`. createRecord pushes a brand-new (unsaved, empty) record into the Ember Data store; updateFromJson then mutates it. This leaves a phantom 'new' topic record in the store (isNew remains true, and it is not properly materialized as a loaded record), which can confuse other code that queries the store for topic id, and the record lacks the slug needed by the template/controller (stopNotificiationsText uses model.fancyTitle, which will be undefined). The correct pattern is `this.store.find('topic', params.id)` or pushing the JSON via store.pushPayload, not createRecord.

PostStream.loadTopicView is not a known API and the route ignores slug/access errors

`PostStream.loadTopicView(params.id)` is called without any evidence this static method exists on the PostStream model in this codebase (the model exposes instance methods like refresh; topic loading normally goes through the store or Discourse.Topic). If it does not exist, the route's model hook throws and the unsubscribe page fails to load. Additionally, the promise rejection is unhandled, so a 404/403 for a topic the user cannot see results in an unhandled error rather than a proper error page.

Triple-stache rendering of stopNotificiationsText injects the topic title as raw HTML

The template renders `{{{stopNotificiationsText}}}` (unescaped). The string is built from `I18n.t("topic.unsubscribe.stop_notifications", { title: this.get("model.fancyTitle") })`. `fancyTitle` is HTML-escaped server-side (ERB::Util.html_escape in Topic#fancy_title), but I18n interpolation does not re-escape interpolated values, and the locale string itself wraps {{title}} in <strong> tags. If fancyTitle ever contains markup that survives escaping (e.g., via SmartyPants entities or a title containing encoded entities that get double-unescaped), or if the translation is overridden, this becomes an HTML injection vector in the unsubscribe page. The title should be passed through Ember's escaping (double-stache with a separate escaped binding) rather than triple-stache of a pre-interpolated string.

dropdown-button renderString interpolates unescaped values into HTML (XSS) renderString builds HTML by string concatenation: `buffer.push("
  • ")` and `buffer.push("" + row.title + "")` etc. None of `id`, `row.title`, `row.description`, `row.styleClasses`, `this.get('text')`, `title`, or `longDescription` are HTML-escaped. Any caller that passes user-controlled data (topic titles, category names, usernames) into these fields gets HTML/XSS injection in the dropdown. The change in this PR (adding the `title` field) expands the attack surface. All interpolated values should be escaped (e.g., with a Handlebars escape or _.escape) before being pushed into the buffer.

unsubscribe_url passed to email template args is never used by the text body path consistently

`send_notification_email` now passes `unsubscribe_url: post.topic.unsubscribe_url` into email_opts, which flows into template_args. The HTML path substitutes it via the `%{unsubscribe_link}` placeholder in the locale string, but the plain-text body path in Email::MessageBuilder#body appends `I18n.t('unsubscribe_link', template_args)` — this works only because template_args includes unsubscribe_url. However, other callers of build_email with `add_unsubscribe_link: true` (e.g., the digest mailer, which sets its own @unsubscribe_key and does not pass unsubscribe_url) will now render the new locale text with a missing `%{unsubscribe_url}` interpolation, producing a broken link ('... [click here]().') or an I18n missing-interpolation error in digest emails. The digest path (UserNotifications#digest) must also supply an unsubscribe_url or the locale must be split.

List-Unsubscribe header still points only to user preferences, not the per-topic unsubscribe URL

header_args sets `result['List-Unsubscribe'] = "<#{template_args[:user_preferences_url]}>"` when add_unsubscribe_link is set. Now that a per-topic `unsubscribe_url` is available in template_args (passed by UserNotifications#send_notification_email), the List-Unsubscribe header — the one-click unsubscribe mechanism used by Gmail and other mail clients — still directs users to the generic preferences page instead of the topic-specific unsubscribe URL. For one-click unsubscribe to actually stop notifications for the topic (and to satisfy RFC 8058 List-Unsubscribe semantics for this feature), the header should use `template_args[:unsubscribe_url]` when present, falling back to user_preferences_url.

Unsubscribe link placeholder only substituted in html_override path; plain-text emails rely on body method The template now includes `
%{unsubscribe_link}
`, which is only substituted in MessageBuilder#html_part (via html_override.gsub!). For notification emails that use the template-based text body (no html_override), the `%{unsubscribe_link}` placeholder is appended by MessageBuilder#body, so the HTML template change is consistent for the html_override path. However, the template is also rendered directly in UserNotifications#send_notification_email via UserNotificationRenderer for the non-template-HTML path — in that path the `%{unsubscribe_link}` and `%{respond_instructions}` placeholders are NOT substituted before being passed as html_override... actually they are substituted later by html_part's gsub!, so this is fine; but note the renderer output is passed as html_override and gsub! mutates it in place, which is acceptable. No concrete defect beyond the digest-path gap noted separately; flagging only that the placeholder substitution depends on add_unsubscribe_link being set, and any email using this template without that flag will leak the literal '%{unsubscribe_link}' text into the HTML.

Route ordering change for moderator-liked/summary may shadow or alter existing URL matching

The diff reorders routes: `t/:slug/:topic_id/moderator-liked` was moved after `t/:topic_id/wordpress`, and the `summary` routes had their constraints changed from `{topic_id: /\d+/, post_number: /\d+/}` to `{topic_id: /\d+/}`. The constraint change for `t/:slug/:topic_id/summary` and `t/:topic_id/summary` removes the post_number constraint that was previously (incorrectly) present, which is fine, but the reordering means `t/:topic_id/wordpress` is now matched before `t/:slug/:topic_id/moderator-liked`; since the wordpress route only matches a two-segment path (`t/:topic_id/wordpress`), a URL like `/t/some-slug/123/moderator-liked` has three segments and will not be captured by it, so behavior is preserved. However, the new `t/:topic_id/unsubscribe` route placed before `t/:topic_id/summary` is fine, but `t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe` placed before `put "t/:slug/:topic_id"` is fine for GET. The main risk: `get "t/:topic_id/unsubscribe"` (line 441) will also match `/t/123/unsubscribe` where 123 could be a slug-less id — intended. No concrete breakage found, but the reordering was unnecessary churn that increases review risk; the summary constraint change should be verified against existing tests.

unsubscribe_url uses absolute url (includes base_url) while other URL helpers use relative or base_uri

`unsubscribe_url` is defined as `"#{url}/unsubscribe"` where `url` is `self.class.url id, slug, post_number` = `"#{Discourse.base_url}/t/#{slug}/#{id}"` — an absolute URL including the host. This is used in `TopicsController#unsubscribe` for `redirect_to @topic_view.topic.unsubscribe_url` (fine for redirects) and in `UserNotifications#send_notification_email` as `unsubscribe_url: post.topic.unsubscribe_url` for the email link (fine, emails need absolute URLs). However, the Ember route path is `/t/:slug/:id/unsubscribe` and the controller redirects to `unsubscribe_url` when the slug is missing — the absolute URL works. The inconsistency: `relative_url` uses `Discourse.base_uri` while `url` uses `Discourse.base_url`; if base_uri differs from base_url (e.g., behind a proxy with a different path prefix), unsubscribe_url built from `url` may be wrong for redirects. Minor, but the method should be consistent with how it's consumed.

No test verifies the per-topic unsubscribe_url appears in the email body or List-Unsubscribe header

The spec adds `unsubscribe_url: "/t/1234/unsubscribe"` to the message_with_unsubscribe builder, but the existing assertions only check that the List-Unsubscribe header is present and that the body matches the user_preferences_url. There is no assertion that the body contains the per-topic unsubscribe URL (via the updated `unsubscribe_link` locale string with `%{unsubscribe_url}`), and no assertion that the List-Unsubscribe header uses the topic URL. Without these, the core feature of this PR (per-topic unsubscribe link in emails) is untested; a regression that drops unsubscribe_url from template_args or breaks the locale interpolation would pass CI.

Read-modify-write of TopicUser notification_level is not atomic

`tu.notification_level` is read, then conditionally assigned, then `tu.save!` — a classic read-modify-write race. Two concurrent requests (e.g., the user clicking the email link while also changing notification state in the UI via set_notifications) can interleave, and the last writer wins, potentially clobbering a `watching` level set by the other request. `TopicUser.change` exists precisely to do an atomic UPDATE ... WHERE and should be used instead of find_by + save!.

topicUnsubscribe route is registered as a top-level route, not nested under the topic resource

`this.route('topicUnsubscribe', { path: '/t/:slug/:id/unsubscribe' })` is declared outside the `this.resource('topic', ...)` block, so the route is named `topicUnsubscribe` rather than `topic.unsubscribe`, and it will not receive the parent `topic` route's model (the route's own model hook must re-fetch the topic, which it attempts via PostStream.loadTopicView). This means the topic is loaded twice (once by the parent resource if it were nested, once here) and the controller hierarchy differs from other topic sub-pages. It should be nested inside the topic resource as `this.route('unsubscribe', { path: '/unsubscribe' })` so it inherits the topic model and matches the server-side URL structure.

true_positives.golden_comment: Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Authorization failure throws a generic Error instead of a typed TRPC error, producing a 500 rather than a 403

When the credential is not found / not owned, the handler does `throw new Error("Credential not found or access denied")`. In tRPC, a plain `Error` is surfaced to the client as an INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR (HTTP 500) with the message potentially masked in production, whereas an authorization failure should be a `TRPCError` with code `FORBIDDEN` (or `NOT_FOUND`). The client's `onError` currently just toasts a generic "Error deleting cache", so the user cannot distinguish "you don't have access" from a real server fault, and monitoring/alerting will treat an authz failure as a server error. The handler should throw `new TRPCError({ code: "FORBIDDEN", message: "..." })` (imported from `@trpc/server`) for the not-found/not-owned case.

The component already uses `useLocale()` for all surrounding strings, so the timestamp is the only piece of user-facing text that ignores the user's locale and timezone conventions (e.g. a user with locale `de` or `ja` still gets a US-formatted date, and the time is rendered in the browser's timezone rather than the user's configured Cal.com timezone). false_positives.candidate:
deleteCache authorization check misses delegation credentials, allowing cache deletion for credentials the user does not own

The handler verifies ownership with `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { id: credentialId, userId: user.id } })`. In cal.com, delegation credentials are stored with a different `userId` (the organization/service account owner) while the requesting user accesses them via `delegationCredentialId`. A user who can see a delegated Google Calendar credential in the connected-calendars UI (the UI explicitly renders CredentialActionsDropdown for delegated credentials, passing `delegationCredentialId`) will pass a credentialId that fails this `userId` check, so the mutation throws — but more importantly, the check does not consider credentials the user is authorized to act on through delegation, and conversely the subsequent `prisma.calendarCache.deleteMany({ where: { credentialId } })` deletes cache rows purely by credentialId with no scoping to the verified credential beyond the findFirst. If the ownership check is ever broadened (or if a credential row exists where userId matches but the credential is a delegation credential shared across users), any user matching userId could wipe another principal's cache. The authorization must mirror how connectedCalendars resolves credentials (including delegation credentials via `enrichUserWithDelegationCredentialsIncludeServiceAccountKey` / `isDelegationCredential`), and the delete should be scoped to the exact credential record that was verified, not just the raw input id.

getCacheStatusByCredentialIds returns cache status for expired cache rows

`getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` runs `prisma.calendarCache.groupBy({ by: ["credentialId"], where: { credentialId: { in: credentialIds } }, _max: { updatedAt: true } })` with no `expiresAt` filter. Every other read path in this repository (`getCachedAvailability`) filters `expiresAt: { gte: new Date() }`. As a result, a credential whose cache rows have all expired (or whose rows were written long ago and never refreshed) will still report a `cacheUpdatedAt` timestamp, so the UI shows "Cache Status: Last updated ..." and offers "Delete cached data" for a credential that effectively has no usable cache. The groupBy should include `expiresAt: { gte: new Date() }` in the `where` clause (and ideally aggregate `_max` over non-expired rows only) so the status reflects live cache state.

getCacheStatusByCredentialIds includes cache rows belonging to in-memory delegation credentials keyed only by userId

The repository's own `getCachedAvailability` documents that in-memory delegation credentials have no valid DB credentialId and that their cache rows are keyed by `userId` + `key` (see the long comment at lines 101-105: "we use in-memory delegation credentials for this which don't have valid credentialId"). `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` groups strictly by `credentialId`, so for a user whose calendar runs on an in-memory delegation credential, the cache rows exist with `credentialId` unset/null (or a synthetic negative id) and will never be grouped under the real credential id shown in the UI. The connectedCalendars handler then reports `cacheUpdatedAt: null` even though a live cache exists, so the "Delete cached data" action is hidden and the user cannot clear a cache that is actually being served. The status query needs to account for the userId-keyed cache rows used by delegation credentials (or the handler must resolve the effective credential/user pair the same way `getCachedAvailability` does).

connectedCalendars handler always instantiates the real CalendarCacheRepository, bypassing the mock when calendar-cache is disabled

The handler unconditionally does `new CalendarCacheRepository()` and calls `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds`. The codebase provides `CalendarCacheRepositoryMock` specifically for when the calendar-cache feature is disabled (its methods log "Skipping ... due to calendar-cache being disabled"), and `CalendarCache.init(null)` elsewhere selects the mock based on configuration. By hard-constructing the real repository, every `connectedCalendars` query — including for users/teams without the calendar-cache feature — now issues an extra `groupBy` DB query against `CalendarCache`. This adds latency to a hot, frequently-polled endpoint for all users and defeats the purpose of the mock. The handler should resolve the repository via the same factory/feature-flag mechanism used by `CalendarCache.init` (e.g. check the team feature flag or use the existing selection logic) so the query is skipped when the feature is off.

deleteCache mutation does not invalidate connectedCalendars, so cache status UI stays stale after deletion

The `deleteCacheMutation` only shows a toast and calls `onSuccess?.()`. The `disconnectMutation` in the same component explicitly invalidates `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` (and `apps.integrations`) in `onSettled`, but the delete-cache mutation has no invalidation. After a successful cache deletion the server returns `{ success: true }` and the `CalendarCache` rows are gone, yet the `connectedCalendars` query still holds the old `cacheUpdatedAt`, so the dropdown continues to show "Cache Status: Last updated ..." and the "Delete cached data" option remains visible/enabled until some unrelated refetch occurs. The mutation needs `onSettled`/`onSuccess` invalidation of `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` (the same query the wrapper reads `cacheUpdatedAt` from) so the UI reflects the deletion immediately.

Confirmation dialog closes immediately on confirm, before the mutation completes, with no pending/disabled state

In both confirmation dialogs, `onConfirm` fires `mutation.mutate(...)` and then unconditionally calls `setDeleteModalOpen(false)` / `setDisconnectModalOpen(false)` on the same tick. The dialog therefore closes instantly regardless of whether the mutation succeeds or fails, and there is no `isLoading`/pending guard on the confirm button. If the request is slow or fails, the user gets no in-dialog feedback (only a later toast) and can re-open and re-trigger the destructive action while a previous one is still in flight, enabling duplicate deletes/disconnects. The dialog should stay open (with the confirm button disabled/loading) until the mutation settles, then close on success.

The new `updateManyByCredentialId(credentialId, data)` passes `data` straight to `prisma.selectedCalendar.updateMany`. Its only caller (`GoogleCalendarService.fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache`) invokes it as `updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})`, i.e. with an empty payload whose sole purpose is to bump `updatedAt` via the Prisma `@updatedAt` attribute. This is implicit and fragile: it depends entirely on the schema's `@updatedAt` behavior, the method name suggests a general-purpose updater, and any future caller passing real fields would silently mass-update every SelectedCalendar row for the credential (including event-type-scoped rows) with no user scoping. Either make the intent explicit (e.g. a dedicated `touchUpdatedAtByCredentialId(credentialId)` that sets `updatedAt: new Date()`), or at minimum constrain the method so it cannot be used as an unscoped mass-update primitive.

`fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache` writes cache entries per event-type group in a loop (`setAvailabilityInCache`) and only afterwards calls `SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` to bump `updatedAt` on every SelectedCalendar row with that credentialId. Two issues: (1) the `updatedAt` bump is not atomic with the cache upserts, so a crash mid-loop leaves some cache rows written but `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt` stale (or vice versa), giving an inconsistent "last updated" signal; (2) `updateMany({ where: { credentialId } })` matches SelectedCalendar rows regardless of `integration`, so if a credential id were ever shared across integrations it would touch unrelated rows — today it is google-only, but the method itself is unscoped. The PR description itself flags that this `updatedAt` is "not displayed in frontend" and questions whether it should exist at all; if it is kept, it should be scoped to `integration: this.integrationName` and ideally updated in the same flow that writes the cache.

Mock class declares deleteManyByCredential which is not part of ICalendarCacheRepository

`CalendarCacheRepositoryMock` implements `deleteManyByCredential()` (line 23) even though `ICalendarCacheRepository` (the interface it declares to implement) has no such method — the real repository deletes cache via `prisma.calendarCache.deleteMany` directly in `GoogleCalendarService.unwatchCalendar` and the new `deleteCacheHandler`, not through the repository interface. This is dead surface area on the mock that suggests a contract that doesn't exist; if the interface later changes, the mock will silently drift. Either add `deleteManyByCredential` to `ICalendarCacheRepository` (and implement it on the real repository, then use it in `deleteCache.handler.ts` and `unwatchCalendar`) so cache deletion goes through the repository abstraction consistently, or remove the stray mock method.

credentialIds may contain null/undefined for delegation credentials, producing a useless IN query and wrong cache mapping

The handler builds `credentialIds` with `connectedCalendars.map((cal) => cal.credentialId)` and passes them to `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds`, which does `where: { credentialId: { in: credentialIds } }`. For delegation-credential calendars, `credentialId` can be null/absent (the codebase uses `isInMemoryDelegationCredential` / negative ids and `delegationCredentialId` instead — see `getConnectedDestinationCalendars.ts` and the repository's own comments about in-memory delegation credentials having no valid credentialId). Passing nulls into a Prisma `in` filter either throws or silently matches nothing, and the resulting `cacheStatusMap` is keyed by real credential ids, so delegated calendars will always get `cacheUpdatedAt: null` even when a userId-keyed cache exists. The handler should filter out non-positive/null credential ids before the query (mirroring `assertCalendarHasDbCredential`'s `credentialId < 0` guard) and handle the delegation-credential case explicitly.

Migration warning comment contradicts the actual migration (column is added WITH a default)

The migration's header warning states: "Added the required column `updatedAt` to the `CalendarCache` table without a default value. This is not possible if the table is not empty." But the very next statement is `ALTER TABLE "CalendarCache" ADD COLUMN "updatedAt" TIMESTAMP(3) NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW();`, which adds the column WITH a default, so the warning is factually wrong and the migration is safe on non-empty tables. The stale Prisma-generated warning (left over from before the author added `DEFAULT NOW()`) should be removed or corrected, otherwise reviewers and future readers will believe the migration is unsafe and may attempt to rewrite it.

The cache status display (lines 84-97) is wrapped in a `<DropdownMenuItem className="focus:ring-muted">` even though it performs no action — it is purely informational. In Radix dropdowns, a `DropdownMenuItem` is an interactive, focusable, clickable element; rendering a non-interactive status inside one means clicking the status row closes the menu (standard item behavior) and it can steal keyboard focus from the real actions, which is an accessibility and UX defect. The status should be rendered as a non-interactive element (e.g. a plain `<div>` with appropriate padding, or `DropdownMenuLabel`/`DropdownMenuSeparator` semantics) inside `DropdownMenuContent`, not as a `DropdownMenuItem`.

The wrapper computes `shouldDisableConnectionModification = isDisabled || disableConnectionModification` (line 166) and passes it only to `SelectedCalendarsSettingsHeading` (to hide the "Add" selector). However, `ConnectedCalendarList` is rendered with `disableConnectionModification={disableConnectionModification}` (line 182) — the raw prop — not `shouldDisableConnectionModification`. `isDisabled` is true when `disabledScope === scope`, i.e. when the current scope is locked; in that state the heading correctly hides connection modification, but each `CredentialActionsDropdown` still receives `disableConnectionModification=false` and will render the "Remove App" action, letting users disconnect an integration while the scope is supposed to be read-only. The list should receive `shouldDisableConnectionModification` so the per-credential actions respect the disabled scope.

The file declares `type CalendarsRouterHandlerCache = { connectedCalendars?: ...; setDestinationCalendar?: ... }` (lines 8-11) but nothing references it — the handlers are imported dynamically inline in each procedure. It's dead code that will drift out of sync as handlers are added (it already omits `deleteCache`). Remove it or actually use it; as-is it's misleading.

The interface declares `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds(credentialIds: number[]): Promise<{ credentialId: number; updatedAt: Date | null }[]>`. The implementation maps `prisma.calendarCache.groupBy` results, where `_max.updatedAt` is `Date | null` (null only if all grouped rows have null updatedAt — which cannot happen now that the column is `NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()`). More importantly, credentials with no cache rows are simply absent from the result array, so callers must distinguish "absent" from "present with null". The `| null` in the type is misleading given the NOT NULL column, and the contract would be clearer if the method either returned a status for every requested id (with null for missing) or the type documented that only credentials with rows are returned. The current handler works around this with `cacheStatusMap.get(...) || null`, but the interface should make the absence semantics explicit.

This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.

This is a reference equality comparison between two distinct Dayjs instances, which is always false. As a result, an all-day date override (start === end, meaning 'unavailable all day') is not detected as such; the code falls through to the range checks, and since `slotEndTime.isBefore(start) || slotEndTime.isSame(start)` and `slotStartTime.isAfter(end)` can both be false for slots inside that day, `dateOverrides.find(...)` returns undefined while `dateOverrideExist` is true — so the function returns `true` (available) for slots on a day the organizer explicitly marked unavailable. Working-hours check in checkIfIsAvailable uses wrong time units and wrong day, making the new working-hours gate ineffective

The newly added working-hours gate compares `slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute()` (minutes since midnight, e.g. 570 for 09:30) against `workingHour.startTime`/`workingHour.endTime`. The consequence is that after this change, slots can be wrongly filtered out (or wrongly kept) for any organizer whose timezone differs from UTC, breaking availability for round-robin/fixed-host events — the exact scenario this PR is meant to fix. Note the same gate is also applied to non-override days, so this affects normal availability, not just date overrides.

The left side is the override's calendar date expressed in the organizer's timezone (a local date), while the right side is the slot's UTC calendar date. These are different calendars, so for organizers not in UTC the override will be matched against the wrong day (off by the timezone offset), causing slots on the override day to be incorrectly rejected (treated as 'not within the date override') and slots on adjacent days to be incorrectly accepted. The subsequent range checks also mix the organizer-local shifted instants (`date.start + utcOffset`) with UTC slot times, compounding the error. This directly undermines the PR's goal of honoring fixed-host date overrides for round-robin events.

For a non-seated event (`seatsPerTimeSlot === null`) where the user has no reserved (selected) slot, `busy` is empty, so the user is filtered out of `slot.userIds`, and the slot is subsequently dropped by `.filter((slot) => !!slot.userIds?.length)`. That means any slot without a corresponding `selectedSlots` row removes all users and eliminates the slot entirely — the opposite of the intent (a user with no reservation should be considered available). This will incorrectly hide available slots whenever `selectedSlots` exist for the event but not for every user/slot combination.

Comparing a UTC instant against an invitee-local day range means an override that starts on the invitee's local day can be excluded (or one from the adjacent UTC day included) whenever the invitee timezone is not UTC — e.g. an override for 00:30–02:00 local in a UTC+6 invitee timezone starts at 18:30 UTC the previous day and fails the `isBetween` check. The override is then silently ignored and the regular working hours are used, so the timezone fix does not apply consistently.

The override-to-invitee conversion computes a single `offset = inviteeUtcOffset - organizerUtcOffset` using `dayjs(override.start...)` and applies that same offset to both `override.start` and `override.end`. If a DST transition occurs between the override start and end (or the offset differs at the end instant), the end time is shifted by the wrong amount, producing an incorrect override window length. The correct approach is to compute the offset separately for the start and end instants (or convert each instant to the invitee timezone independently). Consequence: date overrides spanning a DST change yield wrong slot boundaries in the invitee's timezone.

The handler does `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { userId, appId } })` and then either `update` or `create` based on the result. Note the sibling `office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts` `isExpired` (line 235-241) compares `expiryDate < Math.round(+new Date() / 1000)` — seconds — but reads `o365AuthCredentials.expires_in` (line 279) which is a relative offset, not the absolute `expiry_date`... the two Office365 adapters are mutually inconsistent about which field holds the absolute expiry and in which unit.

HubSpot isTokenValid logic is inverted: returns true when token is expired

`const isTokenValid = (token: HubspotToken) => token && token.tokenType && token.accessToken && token.expiryDate && (token.expiresIn || token.expiryDate) < Date.now();` — the final condition is `< Date.now()`, meaning the function returns true only when the expiry is in the PAST (i.e., the token IS expired). Then line 210: `getToken: () => !isTokenValid(credentialKey) ? Promise.resolve([]) : refreshAccessToken(...)`. So when the token is expired, `isTokenValid` returns true → `!isTokenValid` is false → `refreshAccessToken` is called (correct by accident). When the token is VALID (expiry in the future), `isTokenValid` returns false → `!isTokenValid` is true → returns `Promise.resolve([])` — an empty array used as the token! This is inverted logic (pre-existing, not introduced by this PR, but the PR's refresh changes interact with it). The condition should be `> Date.now()` for validity. As written, valid tokens are never used and expired tokens trigger refresh — the net effect happens to work for refresh but `getToken` returning `[]` for valid tokens means `hubspotClient.setAccessToken` is never called with the valid token... actually `refreshAccessToken` calls `setAccessToken` at the end. This is fragile pre-existing logic that the PR should have fixed while touching this code.

Zoho CRM isTokenValid is inverted (returns true when expired) — same class of bug as HubSpot

`const isValid = token && token.access_token && token.expiryDate && token.expiryDate < Date.now();` — again `< Date.now()` means 'valid' only when expired. Line 244: `getToken: () => (isTokenValid(credentialKey) ? Promise.resolve() : refreshAccessToken(credentialKey))`. When the token is expired, `isTokenValid` returns true → `getToken` resolves WITHOUT refreshing and WITHOUT setting `this.accessToken` (the `isTokenValid` body sets `this.accessToken = token.access_token` only when `isValid` is true, i.e., when expired — so it sets the EXPIRED token). When the token is valid (future expiry), `isTokenValid` returns false → triggers a refresh unnecessarily. The logic is inverted: it should be `token.expiryDate > Date.now()`. Net effect: Zoho CRM uses expired access tokens and refreshes valid ones — API calls fail with 401 until the credential happens to be refreshed by the inverted path. Pre-existing but directly in the code path this PR modifies.

Zoom isTokenValid mixes expires_in (seconds offset) and expiry_date (ms timestamp) in a single comparison against Date.now()

`const isTokenValid = (token: ZoomToken) => (token.expires_in || token.expiry_date) < Date.now();` — `expires_in` is a relative seconds offset (e.g. 3600) and `expiry_date` is an absolute ms timestamp. The expression prefers `expires_in` when present. The stored credential (from callback line 44-45) has `expiry_date` (ms) and `expires_in` DELETED (`delete responseBody.expires_in`), so `token.expires_in` is undefined and `expiry_date` (ms) is compared to `Date.now()` (ms) — correct. But the schema comment says `expires_in` is 'deprecated, purely for backwards compatibility', and old credentials may still have `expires_in` (a small number like 3600) → `3600 < Date.now()` is always true → token always considered valid → expired tokens are used → 401s. The function name/semantics are also inverted relative to usage at line 137 (`!isTokenValid(credentialKey) ? resolve(access_token) : refresh(...)`) — `isTokenValid` actually returns 'is expired'. Pre-existing confusion, but the PR's refresh changes rely on this check to decide when to call the (broken) sync path.

Webex isTokenValid is inverted (returns true when expired)

`const isTokenValid = (token: WebexToken) => token.expiry_date < Date.now();` — returns true when the token IS expired. Line 119-121: `return !isTokenValid(credentialKey) ? Promise.resolve(credentialKey.access_token) : refreshAccessToken(...)`. When expired: `isTokenValid` true → `!isTokenValid` false → refresh (correct by accident). When valid: `isTokenValid` false → `!isTokenValid` true → returns the access token (correct by accident). So despite the misleading name the net behavior is correct — but this is fragile and confusing; the function should be renamed `isTokenExpired` or the comparison flipped. Flagging as low severity since behavior is accidentally correct, but it's a trap for future edits in code this PR touches.

No tests for the new webhook endpoint or the refresh/sync helpers

The PR adds a new public API endpoint (`apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`) that writes OAuth credentials, plus two new shared helpers (`refreshOAuthTokens`, `parseRefreshTokenResponse`) that are now on the token-refresh path of ~10 integrations. The PR description's checklist explicitly states 'I haven't added tests that prove my fix is effective or that my feature works'. Given the number of shape-mismatch bugs identified in the refresh path (Response vs SDK response), unit tests for `refreshOAuthTokens` (both branches) and `parseRefreshTokenResponse` (including the missing-refresh_token case) and integration tests for the webhook (auth, decryption, upsert race) are essential before merge.

When the sync path is active, the function validates against `minimumTokenResponseSchema` (access_token + numeric props only) and returns that parsed data — dropping provider-specific fields like `token_type`, `scope`, `id`, `instance_url` that the strict schema would have required and that callers persist. For example `googlecalendar` line 97 passes the result to `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })` — wait, it passes `googleCredentials` (the merged object), so Google is ok. But `salesforce` line 90-99 persists `accessTokenParsed.data` directly as the credential key — on the sync path this would be the minimal shape `{ access_token, ...numbers }` plus the fabricated `refresh_token: "refresh_token"`, dropping `id`, `issued_at`, `signature`, `token_type`, `scope` that `salesforceTokenSchema` requires and that jsforce may need. The function should merge the minimal parse back into the original response object (preserving all fields) rather than returning the stripped parse result.

Office365 refresh: handleErrorsJson on the sync-path Response parses the minimal sync JSON, then parseRefreshTokenResponse throws due to broken minimum schema, and the thrown error is unhandled

Line 262: `const responseJson = await handleErrorsJson(response);` — on the sync path `response` is the sync endpoint's Response, so `responseJson` is the minimal `{ access_token, expiry }` object. Line 263 passes it to `parseRefreshTokenResponse(responseJson, refreshTokenResponseSchema)`. Because `minimumTokenResponseSchema` is broken (see separate finding — the computed-key syntax doesn't create an index signature), `safeParse` fails and `parseRefreshTokenResponse` throws `Error("Invalid refreshed tokens were returned")`. This throw is NOT caught in `refreshAccessToken` (no try/catch), so it propagates through `getToken()` → `fetcher` → every Office365 calendar operation fails with an unhandled error when credential sync is enabled. The Office365 sync path is entirely broken.

Lark refresh: sync-path Response from handleLarkError lacks the Lark envelope; data.data is undefined and credential is overwritten with undefined tokens

Even if `handleLarkError` successfully parses the sync endpoint's minimal JSON `{ access_token, <expiry> }` (no Lark `{ code, data: {...} }` envelope), line 84-96 reads `data.data.refresh_expires_in`, `data.data.refresh_token`, `data.data.access_token`, `data.data.expires_in` — all undefined because the sync response has no `data` envelope. Line 91-96 then builds `newLarkAuthCredentials` with `refresh_token: undefined`, `refresh_expires_date: NaN` (Math.round(+new Date()/1000 + undefined)), `access_token: undefined`, `expiry_date: NaN`, and line 98-105 persists this corrupted credential, destroying the user's Lark Calendar integration. The sync path for Lark is broken and destructive.

Zoho Bigin refresh: sync-path minimal response lacks expires_in, producing NaN expiryDate; also refresh_token is overwritten with the old one but access_token shape mismatch

On the sync path, `tokenInfo` is a fetch Response and `tokenInfo.data` is undefined → TypeError (see separate finding). But even if the shape were normalized to the sync JSON `{ access_token, expiry }`, line 98 computes `tokenInfo.data.expiryDate = Math.round(Date.now() + tokenInfo.data.expires_in)` — the sync contract returns an absolute expiry, not a relative `expires_in`, so `expires_in` is undefined → `expiryDate = NaN`. Line 100 sets `refresh_token` to the old one (good), but `api_domain` and `accountServer` come from `credentialKey` (line 99 sets accountServer from credentialKey — ok), while `api_domain` is never set on the sync path → `token.api_domain` is undefined → all subsequent Bigin API URLs become `undefined/bigin/v1/...`. The Bigin sync refresh path produces a broken credential.

refreshOAuthTokens silently falls back to the provider refresh when userId is null, but team/org credentials (teamId set, userId null) then bypass sync entirely with no indication

The condition `if (APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT && userId)` means that when a credential belongs to a team (`credential.userId` is null, `teamId` set), the sync endpoint is NOT called and the provider refresh runs instead. For self-hosters using this feature, team credentials will silently diverge from the app store's source of truth — the app store cannot sync team credentials because the sync endpoint is keyed on `calcomUserId`. This may be intentional (the webhook only supports userId), but it is undocumented in the code and the PR description, and creates an inconsistency where some credentials sync and others don't. At minimum, document this limitation or extend the sync protocol to support teamId.

Credential update overwrites the entire key, discarding fields the app may need (email, expiry_date, type-specific fields)

The update path (lines 72-81) does `prisma.credential.update({ where: { id }, data: { key: keys } })` — replacing the entire `key` JSON with the webhook payload. For apps like Office365/Google whose credential key includes derived fields (`email`, `expiry_date`, `scope`, `token_type`), a sync payload containing only `{ access_token, refresh_token, ... }` will strip those fields. Downstream code that reads `credential.key.email` (e.g., calendar listing uses the stored email) or validates the full schema will break. The update should merge: `key: { ...existingCredential.key, ...keys }`, and ideally validate the merged result against the app's schema. The create path (line 83-90) has the same issue but is less severe.

Salesforce credential update drops the old access_token fields and does not preserve refresh token rotation

Line 96-99: `data: { key: { ...accessTokenParsed.data, refresh_token: credentialKey.refresh_token } }`. Salesforce's refresh response includes a new `access_token`, `signature`, `issued_at`, `id`, `instance_url`, `scope`, `token_type` — but NOT a new `refresh_token` (Salesforce refresh tokens are typically long-lived and not rotated on every refresh). The code correctly preserves the old refresh_token. However, it also means the update runs on EVERY getClient call (see separate finding), rewriting the credential each time. Additionally, if Salesforce ever DOES rotate the refresh token, this code would discard the new one. The update should only happen when the token actually changed, and should preserve any newly-returned refresh_token if present.

MS Teams refresh computes expiry_date from expires_in which the sync endpoint does not return (it returns an absolute expiry), yielding expiry_date = Date.now()

Line 84: `responseBody.expiry_date = Math.round(Date.now() + (responseBody?.expires_in || 0) * 1000);`. On the sync path, the endpoint returns an absolute expiry field (per the PR contract: 'The response should only contain the access token and expiry date') — there is no `expires_in`, so `expiry_date = Date.now() + 0` = now. Combined with the inverted `isExpired` check (always true, see separate finding), the token is refreshed on every call and the stored expiry is always 'now'. Even on the normal path, if Microsoft omits `expires_in` (it doesn't, but defensively), the same corruption occurs. The code should use the absolute expiry returned by the sync endpoint when present, falling back to computing from `expires_in`.

Zoom refresh on sync path: minimal response lacks refresh_token, but key.refresh_token is overwritten with newTokens.refresh_token (undefined)

Line 120: `key.refresh_token = newTokens.refresh_token;`. On the sync path, `parseRefreshTokenResponse` validates against the broken `minimumTokenResponseSchema` (see separate finding) — if it somehow passed, `newTokens` would be the minimal shape without `refresh_token`, so `key.refresh_token = undefined`, destroying the stored refresh token. Even on the normal path, `parseRefreshTokenResponse` fabricates `refresh_token = "refresh_token"` when missing (Zoom DOES return a new refresh_token on refresh, so normal path is ok). But the sync path combined with the fabricated/missing refresh_token corrupts the credential. The update should preserve the existing refresh token when the response doesn't include one: `key.refresh_token = newTokens.refresh_token ?? key.refresh_token`.

Webex refresh overwrites refresh_token unconditionally; sync path (minimal response) would set it to undefined

Line 101: `key.refresh_token = newTokens.refresh_token;`. On the sync path, `webexRefreshedTokenSchema` requires `refresh_token` — so validation fails and the function rejects (see separate finding). But if the schema were relaxed for sync (as it should be), `newTokens.refresh_token` would be undefined and the stored refresh token would be destroyed. Webex rotates refresh tokens on use, so the normal path is fine, but the sync path must preserve the existing refresh token when the response omits it. Use `newTokens.refresh_token ?? key.refresh_token`.

Google refresh on sync path never calls the provider, so googleCredentials.refresh_token is preserved but the sync endpoint's response is not merged into googleCredentials beyond access_token/expiry_date

Lines 94-96: on the sync path, only `access_token` and `expiry_date` are copied from the (broken, see finding) token object into `googleCredentials`. The sync endpoint contract returns only those two fields, which is fine for Google. But because `res?.data` is undefined on the sync path (Response has no `.data`), the code throws before reaching this point (see the high-severity finding). Once that's fixed, this merge is correct for Google. No additional issue beyond the shape mismatch already reported.

APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is read at module scope in constants.ts but refreshOAuthTokens also checks process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT at call time — inconsistent gating between webhook and refresh paths

`refreshOAuthTokens` gates on `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT && userId`, while the webhook gates only on `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED`. This means a deployment can have the webhook enabled (secret + encryption key set) but no sync endpoint — in which case credentials can be pushed IN via webhook but token refreshes go direct to the provider. That's a valid configuration. Conversely, if `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` is set but the webhook secret is not, refreshes go to the sync endpoint but no credentials can be pushed — the sync endpoint becomes the only source of tokens, which may be intended. The asymmetry is worth documenting but is not a bug per se. Flagging as low/speculative — the main issue is that `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` doesn't include `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`, so the name is misleading.

Webhook header name is configurable via env var, allowing an operator to accidentally weaken verification (e.g., set to a header an attacker controls like 'user-agent')

`req.headers[process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME || "calcom-webhook-secret"]` — the header name is read from an environment variable with no validation. If an operator sets `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME=user-agent` (or any commonly-sent header), the 'secret' check compares the User-Agent header value to `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` — an attacker who knows the secret (or if it's weak) could pass verification by setting User-Agent. More realistically, a misconfiguration could make the check compare against a header that proxies set. The header name should be a hardcoded constant (or at least validated against a whitelist / not a standard header). The env var configurability adds risk without benefit.

refreshTokenResponseSchema transforms expires_in into an absolute timestamp, but the same schema is used to validate the STORED credential in getToken where expires_in is absent and expiry_date holds the absolute value

The schema at lines 51-57 requires `expires_in` (a relative offset) and transforms it to an absolute timestamp. It is used in two places with different data shapes: (1) line 263 to parse the refresh RESPONSE (which has `expires_in` — correct usage), and (2) line 278 to validate the STORED credential (`o365AuthCredentials`), which has `expiry_date` (absolute, seconds) and NO `expires_in` (deleted in the callback). The second usage always fails safeParse, making the validity check at line 278-281 always take the refresh path (see separate finding). The stored-credential validation should use a separate schema with `expiry_date: z.number()` and optional `expires_in`.

HubSpot getToken returns Promise.resolve([]) (empty array) when token is 'valid' per inverted logic — downstream code receives an array instead of a token

Line 210: `getToken: () => !isTokenValid(credentialKey) ? Promise.resolve([]) : refreshAccessToken(credentialKey.refreshToken)`. Due to the inverted `isTokenValid` (see separate finding), when the token is actually valid (future expiry), `isTokenValid` returns false, `!isTokenValid` is true, and `getToken` resolves to `[]` — an empty array, not a token. Callers (`createEvent` line 239: `await auth.getToken();`) ignore the return value and rely on `hubspotClient.setAccessToken` being called inside `refreshAccessToken`. So when the token is valid, `setAccessToken` is NEVER called and the hubspotClient uses whatever token was last set (possibly none) — API calls fail with 401. The inverted logic means valid tokens are never applied to the client. This is a pre-existing bug in the gating logic that the PR's changes interact with.

Unrelated change: redirectUri hardcoded to 'zoho-bigin' instead of appConfig.slug

The diff changes `const redirectUri = WEBAPP_URL + `/api/integrations/${appConfig.slug}/callback`;` to `const redirectUri = WEBAPP_URL + `/api/integrations/zoho-bigin/callback`;`. If `appConfig.slug` is `zoho-bigin` this is a no-op refactor, but if the config slug ever differs (e.g., for a white-label variant), the hardcoded path breaks the OAuth redirect URI registration. This change is unrelated to the credential-sync feature and should be reverted to use `appConfig.slug` for consistency with the callback (which uses `appConfig.slug` at line 36).

Three sequential DB queries (user, app, credential) could be reduced, and app metadata lookup duplicates the DB app check

The handler performs `prisma.user.findUnique`, `prisma.app.findUnique`, then `prisma.credential.findFirst` sequentially. The user and app lookups are independent and could be parallelized with `Promise.all`. More importantly, the `prisma.app.findUnique` check is redundant with the `appStoreMetadata` lookup — if the slug exists in `appStoreMetadata`, the app is valid for credential purposes; the DB check only confirms the app is installed/enabled in this instance. If the intent is to ensure the app is enabled, the check should also verify the app is not disabled. As written, the three sequential round-trips add latency to a webhook that should be fast. Low severity (webhook volume is low) but worth noting.

Pre-existing: getAvailability catch block logs and returns Promise.reject([]) — rejecting with an empty array instead of resolving

Line 183-186: `catch (err) { console.log(err); return Promise.reject([]); }`. Rejecting with an empty array (not an Error) is an anti-pattern — callers awaiting this get a rejection whose reason is `[]`, which is truthy-checkable but not an Error instance, breaking error logging/handling upstream. This is pre-existing code not touched by the PR diff, but it's in a file heavily modified by the PR. Flagging as low since it's out of scope but a maintainer reviewing this file should note it.

Salesforce parseRefreshTokenResponse throws on failure, making the `if (!accessTokenParsed.success)` check at line 92 unreachable dead code

Line 90: `const accessTokenParsed = parseRefreshTokenResponse(accessTokenJson, salesforceTokenSchema);` — but `parseRefreshTokenResponse` throws `new Error("Invalid refreshed tokens were returned")` when `safeParse` fails (it never returns a `{success: false}` object). Line 92-94 `if (!accessTokenParsed.success) { return Promise.reject(...) }` is therefore unreachable — a parse failure surfaces as a thrown Error from `parseRefreshTokenResponse`, not as the intended Promise.reject. The thrown error propagates out of `getClient` (which is called in the constructor via `this.getClient(credential).then(...)`) resulting in an unhandled promise rejection in the constructor. The dead code indicates the contract mismatch between `parseRefreshTokenResponse` (throws) and its callers (expect SafeParseResult).
