Without a negative control (e.g., removing the USERS permission and showing the user-role mapping fails), the test cannot distinguish which permission is being exercised, weakening its value as a regression test for the new Clients resource type.

getClientsWithPermission evaluates permissions per resource with no caching, causing N policy evaluations

getClientsWithPermission(String scope) iterates all resources of type 'Clients' via resourceStore.findByType and, for each resource, calls hasGrantedPermission(), which performs a full root.evaluatePermission(...) policy evaluation (loading policies, evaluating the policy chain) for every single client resource. For a realm with many clients this is O(N) full authorization evaluations in a single admin request (e.g., when listing clients the admin can manage), which can be very slow and does not scale. The Users V2 equivalent has the same shape, but for Clients the resource count is typically much larger. At minimum this should be noted; ideally evaluation should be batched or the method should evaluate the type-level resource once and only fall back to per-resource checks when needed.

hasPermission(ClientModel, scope) silently returns false for cross-realm admins, but canView(ClientModel) composes checks that can mask missing per-client authorization

hasPermission(ClientModel, String) returns false when !root.isAdminSameRealm(). That is correct as a deny. However, canView(ClientModel client) first returns true if canView() (realm-wide view) OR canConfigure(client) is true. canConfigure(client) returns true if canManage(client) is true. This composition is fine, but note that canManage(ClientModel) checks root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_CLIENTS) — a realm-management role check that ignores whether the admin is from the same realm as the target client in a cross-realm admin setup. In V2 the FGAP permissions are realm-scoped to the admin permissions client of the admin's realm; if MgmtPermissionsV2 is constructed with a different target realm (the (session, realm, adminsRealm, admin) constructor), hasOneAdminRole may still return true based on the adminsRealm roles while the resource server used for evaluation (root.realmResourceServer()) belongs to a different realm, mixing realms. The class should consistently use the target realm's resource server and reject cross-realm role checks, as the Users V2 implementation does via isAdminSameRealm() guards in every method.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
canManage() checks VIEW scope instead of MANAGE scope

In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() (line 70), the fallback permission check is `hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)`, which grants manage rights to any admin holding only the VIEW scope on the Groups resource type. The per-group variant canManage(GroupModel) on line 79 correctly checks only MANAGE, and the interface javadoc for canManage() states it should return true for a permission to MANAGE groups. Consequence: an admin granted only 'view' on all groups (or on the Groups resource type) can create, update, and delete groups, a privilege escalation. The same copy-paste error exists in UserPermissionsV2? No — UserPermissionsV2.canManage(UserModel) correctly uses MANAGE only; only this group-level canManage() is wrong.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments point to the same bug. GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() falls back to hasPermission with both VIEW and MANAGE, so an admin holding only VIEW gets manage access.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission passes resource id instead of group id (resource name) to hasPermission

In GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() (lines 121-125), for each group resource found by type, it calls `hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), VIEW_MEMBERS, MANAGE_MEMBERS)`. But hasPermission(String groupId, ...) resolves the resource with `resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)`, i.e., it expects the resource *name*, which for V2 group resources is the group id (see AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource / resolveGroup). Passing the internal resource id means findByName fails, the code falls back to the all-groups resource, and the per-resource permission check is evaluated against the wrong resource — so the set of group ids collected does not reflect per-group view-members permissions. Additionally the collected value `granted.add(groupResource.getId())` adds the authz resource id rather than the group id, which downstream consumers (UsersResource.searchForUser sets UserModel.GROUPS to this set; getUsersCount passes it as group ids) interpret as group ids. Both issues together make group-scoped user visibility incorrect under V2.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate describes the same issue as the golden comment. getGroupIdsWithViewPermission passes the resource id to hasPermission, which looks resources up by name, so evaluation falls back to all-groups. It also adds the resource id to granted, while downstream consumers expect group ids.

false_positives.candidate:
Null resource from getResourceTypeResource is dereferenced without a null check

In hasPermission(), when the per-group resource is not found, the code calls `AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, AdminPermissionsSchema.GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE)` (line 144) and immediately calls `policyStore.findByResource(server, resource)` on line 147 without checking whether resource is null. getResourceTypeResource returns null when the resource type resource does not exist (e.g., admin permissions enabled but schema not initialized, or supportsAuthorizationSchema false). A NullPointerException would then be thrown instead of returning false, turning a 'no permission' situation into a 500 error. The analogous code in UserPermissionsV2.hasPermission (line 109-113) has the same pattern, but there the resource lookup is equally unchecked; at minimum GroupPermissionsV2 should null-check before findByResource.

searchForUser now sets UserModel.GROUPS session attribute even when the admin has global view-users, changing downstream semantics

The diff removes the `if (!auth.users().canView())` guard around setting the session attribute UserModel.GROUPS in searchForUser (lines 448-451). Previously the attribute was only set when the admin lacked global view permission. Now `auth.groups().getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` is always called and, if non-empty, the attribute is set. In GroupPermissions.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission (V1) the method returns an empty set when root.users().canView() is true, so V1 behavior is preserved; but in GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission the same guard exists (line 107). The behavioral change is that toRepresentation's `usersEvaluator.grantIfNoPermission(session.getAttribute(UserModel.GROUPS) != null)` (line 459) now sees a non-null attribute whenever the admin has any group with view-members permission, even if the admin also has global view-users — grantIfNoPermission then grants view on all users in UserPermissions.hasPermission when the Users resource is missing (line 501: `grantIfNoPermission && expectedScopes.contains(MANAGE_SCOPE) && expectedScopes.contains(VIEW_SCOPE)`), which can over-grant. More importantly, setting UserModel.GROUPS unconditionally causes searchForUserStream to filter users by group membership even for admins who have global view-users but happen to have view-members on some group, hiding users not in those groups — a regression in user listing for admins with mixed permissions.

canMapRoles and canManageGroupMembership now accept MANAGE scope as sufficient, weakening the permission model

The diff changes UserPermissionsV2.canMapRoles(UserModel) from `hasPermission(user, null, AdminPermissionsSchema.MAP_ROLES)` to `hasPermission(user, null, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE, AdminPermissionsSchema.MAP_ROLES) || canManageByGroup(user)` (lines 77-83), and similarly canManageGroupMembership from MANAGE_GROUP_MEMBERSHIP only to `MANAGE, MANAGE_GROUP_MEMBERSHIP` (lines 85-92). The interface javadoc (UserPermissionEvaluator lines 137-145 and 153-161) documents that map-roles requires the MAP_ROLES scope (or MANAGE of the user), and manage-group-membership requires MANAGE_GROUP_MEMBERSHIP (or MANAGE of the user). By also accepting the user-level MANAGE scope for these operations, an admin with only 'manage' on a specific user (but not map-roles) can now map roles to that user, and an admin with only 'manage' can manage group membership — exceeding the documented scope semantics. Note the base class UserPermissions.canMapRoles already returns true when canManage(user) is true, so the V2 change makes per-user MANAGE a sufficient condition, which contradicts the FGAP V2 design where map-roles is a distinct scope (the tests in UserResourceTypeEvaluationTest.testMapRoles explicitly create a MAP_ROLES-only permission and expect it to be required).

Removal of AdminRoles.ADMIN from role checks in V2 user permission methods

The diff removes AdminRoles.ADMIN from the hasOneAdminRole checks in canView(UserModel) (line 48: was `AdminRoles.ADMIN, AdminRoles.MANAGE_USERS, AdminRoles.VIEW_USERS`, now only MANAGE_USERS/VIEW_USERS) and canManage(UserModel) (line 57: was `ADMIN, MANAGE_USERS`, now only MANAGE_USERS). AdminRoles.ADMIN is the realm-admin composite role; in V1 code paths (e.g., MgmtPermissions.hasOneAdminRole usage elsewhere) realm admins are expected to retain full access. If ADMIN no longer implies manage-users/view-users membership in the V2 evaluation path (hasOneAdminRole checks direct role assignment, and realm-admin is a composite role that may not be expanded depending on implementation), realm admins could lose access to user operations under V2. This needs verification against how hasOneAdminRole resolves composite roles; if composites are resolved it is harmless, otherwise it is an access regression for realm admins.

canList() logic change drops VIEW_USERS/MANAGE_USERS as sufficient for listing groups

The diff changes GroupPermissions.canList() from `canView() || root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.VIEW_USERS, AdminRoles.MANAGE_USERS, AdminRoles.QUERY_GROUPS)` to `root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.QUERY_GROUPS) || canView()` (line 148-149). Since canView() itself checks `root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_USERS, AdminRoles.VIEW_USERS)` (line 287), the net effect is equivalent for V1. However the reordering changes evaluation cost only; no functional change. Not a defect — but note the interface javadoc for canList() (GroupPermissionEvaluator lines 32-39) says 'at least one of QUERY_GROUPS, MANAGE_USERS or VIEW_USERS', which matches. No issue; disregard.

canViewMembers now also accepts MANAGE_MEMBERS scope in V1, broadening member visibility

The diff changes GroupPermissions.canViewMembers(GroupModel) from `hasPermission(group, VIEW_MEMBERS_SCOPE)` to `hasPermission(group, VIEW_MEMBERS_SCOPE, MANAGE_MEMBERS_SCOPE)` (line 340). This means an admin with only manage-members permission on a group can now view the group's members. The interface javadoc (GroupPermissionEvaluator lines 119-125) documents canViewMembers as true for VIEW_MEMBERS or MANAGE_MEMBERS, so this aligns with the documented contract; however it is a behavioral broadening of the V1 permission model: previously manage-members did not imply view-members. If V1 semantics intentionally separated these (manage-members to add/remove members without listing them), this change leaks the member list to admins who should only be able to modify membership. The same broadening exists in GroupPermissionsV2.canViewMembers (line 86). This should be confirmed as intended; otherwise it is a confidentiality regression for group member listings.

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission V1 implementation returns empty set when users().canView() but not when users().canManage()

The diff changes the guard in GroupPermissions.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() from `if (root.users().canView() || root.users().canManage()) return Collections.emptySet();` to `if (root.users().canView()) return Collections.emptySet();` (line 299). Since canView() in UserPermissions returns true when the admin has MANAGE_USERS or VIEW_USERS roles (line 298 of UserPermissions), and canManage() is subsumed, the change is behaviorally equivalent for role-based admins. For V1 fine-grained permissions, an admin with a manage permission on Users (but no view permission) would previously get an empty set (meaning 'no group filtering — see all users'), and now would get the group-filtered set. In UsersResource.toRepresentation, `usersEvaluator.grantIfNoPermission(session.getAttribute(UserModel.GROUPS) != null)` — with the attribute now set for manage-only admins, grantIfNoPermission becomes true, and UserPermissions.hasPermission line 501 grants view when the Users resource is missing and both MANAGE and VIEW scopes are expected. This could grant view on all users to a manage-only admin when the Users resource is absent — a subtle over-grant. The change appears intentional for V2 alignment but alters V1 behavior for manage-only admins.

getSubGroups filter change removes global canView bypass, but relies on per-group canView which in V2 falls back to all-groups resource

The diff changes the subgroup filter in GroupResource.getSubGroups from `.filter(g -> canViewGlobal || auth.groups().canView(g))` to `.filter(auth.groups()::canView)` (lines 176-180), removing the cached `canViewGlobal` boolean. This is functionally equivalent only if canView(g) returns true whenever canView() (global) is true. In GroupPermissions (V1), canView(GroupModel) checks `canView() || canManage()` first (line 255), so equivalence holds. In GroupPermissionsV2, canView(GroupModel) checks admin roles then `hasPermission(group.getId(), VIEW, MANAGE)` — and hasPermission falls back to the all-groups resource when the per-group resource is missing, so a global view permission still grants per-group view. Equivalence holds, but the removal of the cached boolean means canView() is no longer evaluated once; each subgroup now triggers a full permission evaluation (role check + resource lookup + policy evaluation), a performance regression for large group hierarchies. Not a security bug, but a perf concern; more importantly, if any future canView(GroupModel) implementation diverges from canView() the bypass is lost silently.

getGroups non-hierarchy path drops cached canViewGlobal, causing per-group full permission evaluation

The diff changes the non-hierarchy branch of GroupsResource.getGroups from `.filter(g -> canViewGlobal || groupsEvaluator.canView(g))` (with canViewGlobal cached once) to `.filter(groupsEvaluator::canView)` (lines 113-114). For admins with global view permission, every group now triggers a full canView(g) evaluation (role checks plus, in V2, a resource lookup and policy evaluation per group) instead of a single cached check. For large realms this is a performance regression on the group listing endpoint. The populateHierarchy=true path (GroupUtils.populateGroupHierarchyFromSubGroups) is unaffected.

getScope throws NullPointerException when resourceType is not in the schema

In AdminPermissionsSchema.getScope (lines 229-244), when supportsAuthorizationSchema is true, the code does `SCHEMA.getResourceTypes().get(resourceType).getScopes()` (line 238) without null-checking the result of get(resourceType). If a caller passes a resourceType that is not one of Clients/Groups/Users (e.g., a legacy or custom type, or null), get() returns null and a NullPointerException is thrown instead of the intended ModelValidationException. The method already validates the scope name against the resource type's scopes, so it clearly expects resourceType to be a schema type, but there is no guard. Callers that pass arbitrary resourceType values (e.g., policy evaluation paths that pass policy.getResourceType()) would get an NPE (500 error) rather than a validation error.

getResourceName only handles Users resource type; Groups resources fall through to display name

AdminPermissionsSchema.getResourceName (lines 328-350) resolves a human-readable name only for the USERS resource type (returning 'All users' or the username). For GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE resources it falls through to `resource.getDisplayName()` (line 349), which for V2 group resources is typically null/empty since resources are created with only a name (the group id) and no display name (see init(), lines 271-276, which creates ResourceRepresentation without displayName). UI/policy listings that call getResourceName for group resources will show blank or null names instead of the group name. A GROUPS branch resolving the group name via session.groups().getGroupById (mirroring the USERS branch) is missing.

registerListener feature check moved outside the listener changes V1 behavior when feature is toggled at runtime

The diff moves the `Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ)` check from inside onEvent to the registration site (lines 73-98). Previously the listener was always registered and the feature check was evaluated per event; now the listener is only registered when the feature is enabled at startup. Since Profile features are static for the server lifetime this is behaviorally equivalent in practice, but if the check was previously per-event to support dynamic feature toggling (some Keycloak features can be re-checked), this is a subtle change. More relevant: the indentation of the moved block is inconsistent (the if-body is indented as if still inside a method), a cosmetic defect. Not a functional bug; flagging only because the restructure adds no value and obscures the diff.

canMapRole now requires MANAGE_USERS role directly instead of canManageDefault(), changing V1 fine-grained behavior

The diff changes RolePermissions.canMapRole from `if (root.users().canManageDefault()) return checkAdminRoles(role);` to `if (root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_USERS)) return checkAdminRoles(role);` (line 302). canManageDefault() was exactly `root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_USERS)` (removed from UserPermissions in this same PR), so for role-based admins the behavior is identical. However, in V1 fine-grained authz, an admin could have the 'manage' scope permission on the Users resource (via UserPermissions.canManage() returning true through hasPermission(MANAGE_SCOPE)) without holding the MANAGE_USERS role; previously canMapRole's first check used canManageDefault() (role only), so this is equivalent. But other V1 paths relied on users().canManage() (which includes fine-grained permissions) for role mapping; the new check bypasses fine-grained user permissions entirely, so an admin granted manage-users via FGAP V1 permissions (not the role) can no longer map roles. This is a functional regression for V1 FGAP deployments unless V2 is enabled (MgmtPermissionsV2 path). The same pattern appears in GroupPermissions.canManage()/canView() where canManageDefault/canViewDefault were replaced by direct role checks — those are in the V1 class GroupPermissions, so V1 fine-grained group permissions (manage/view scope on group resources) are still checked via hasPermission in canManage(GroupModel)/canView(GroupModel), but the global canManage()/canView() no longer consider FGAP permissions, affecting requireManage()/requireView() global checks (e.g., GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup calls auth.groups().requireManage()).

V1 GroupPermissions.canManage()/canView() no longer consider fine-grained group permissions, breaking V1 FGAP global group operations

The diff replaces GroupPermissions.canManage() from `root.users().canManageDefault()` to `root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_USERS)` (line 274-276) and canView() from `root.users().canViewDefault()` to `root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_USERS, AdminRoles.VIEW_USERS)` (line 286-288). In V1 fine-grained admin permissions (ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ feature, MgmtPermissions/GroupPermissions path), an admin could be granted the 'manage' or 'view' scope on a group resource (via GroupPermissions.initialize/hasPermission) without holding realm-management roles. The per-group methods canManage(GroupModel)/canView(GroupModel) still check hasPermission, but the global canManage()/canView() — used by requireManage()/requireView() for realm-wide operations such as GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup (auth.groups().requireManage()) and by canList() — now ignore FGAP permissions entirely. Consequence: in V1 FGAP deployments, admins who previously could create top-level groups via a view/manage permission on the Groups resource (or via the old users().canManageDefault() semantics) are now denied; conversely the change removes the V1 FGAP evaluation from these global checks. This is a behavioral/API break for V1 fine-grained authorization unless the intent is that V1 group permissions are only per-group. The same replacement was done in UserPermissions.canManage()/canView() (lines 233-243, 297-307) where the fine-grained hasPermission fallback is retained, so the group change is inconsistent with the user change.

canViewByGroup changed from getGroupsWithViewPermission(group) to canViewMembers(group), altering V1 semantics

The diff changes UserPermissions.canViewByGroup from `evaluateHierarchy(user, (group) -> root.groups().getGroupsWithViewPermission(group))` to `evaluateHierarchy(user, root.groups()::canViewMembers)` (line 587-590). The old V1 method getGroupsWithViewPermission(GroupModel) (removed from the interface) returned true when `root.users().canView() || root.users().canManage()` OR the admin had VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permission on the group. The new canViewMembers(GroupModel) in GroupPermissions returns true when `root.users().canView()` OR hasPermission(group, VIEW_MEMBERS_SCOPE, MANAGE_MEMBERS_SCOPE) (line 330-341). The difference: the old check also returned true when root.users().canManage() (manage-users role or manage permission) even without view permission on the group; the new canViewMembers only checks users().canView(). However, canView(UserModel) in UserPermissions is `canView() || canViewByGroup(user)`, and canView() already covers MANAGE_USERS/VIEW_USERS roles and the manage/view scopes, so for role-based admins the outcome is the same. For V1 FGAP admins with only a 'manage' permission on Users (not view), the old code granted view-by-group via users().canManage(); the new code does not (canViewMembers requires users().canView()). This narrows V1 FGAP behavior: a manage-only admin can no longer see users through group membership. Whether this is intended is unclear; it is a behavioral change to V1 permission evaluation.

searchForUser sets UserModel.GROUPS session attribute unconditionally, affecting brute-force user listing for admins with global view

The diff removes the `if (!auth.users().canView())` guard in BruteForceUsersResource.searchForUser (lines 147-150), so `auth.groups().getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` is always called and UserModel.GROUPS is set whenever the set is non-empty. For an admin with global view-users plus view-members on some group, the session attribute is now set, causing searchForUserStream to filter users by group membership and hiding users outside those groups from the brute-force user search — a regression for admins who should see all users. Additionally, toRepresentation's `usersEvaluator.grantIfNoPermission(session.getAttribute(UserModel.GROUPS) != null)` (line 159) now evaluates true for such admins, which in UserPermissions.hasPermission (line 501) grants view on all users when the Users resource is missing — over-granting. The same unconditional pattern was introduced in UsersResource.searchForUser.

Test cleanup in @BeforeEach uses response after try-with-resources closes it

In GroupResourceTypeEvaluationTest.onBefore (lines 71-79), the code does `try (Response response = realm.admin().groups().add(topGroup)) { ... topGroup.setId(ApiUtil.handleCreatedResponse(response)); ... }`. ApiUtil.handleCreatedResponse now uses try-with-resources internally (per the ApiUtil change), closing the response; the outer try-with-resources then closes it again (harmless), but more importantly the assertion and id extraction happen inside the outer try block before the outer close — this is fine. However, the pattern of calling handleCreatedResponse (which closes the response) inside an outer try-with-resources is redundant and confusing; if handleCreatedResponse's internal close throws or the outer close is reached after the inner close, behavior is still safe (Response.close is idempotent). Not a functional bug; flagging as a test code smell. More significant: the test class lacks a test verifying that an admin with only view-members on a group cannot list groups (negative case for group listing), and lacks a test for manage-membership on a subgroup granting membership management on parent/child hierarchies — coverage gaps for the new Groups resource type scopes.

testManageAllGroups creates a group without name, expecting FORBIDDEN, but the assertion only checks status code inside try-with-resources

In testManageAllGroups (lines 141-143), `realmAdminClient.realm(realm.getName()).groups().add(new GroupRepresentation())` sends a group with no name. The expected FORBIDDEN is asserted, but the test does not verify that no group was actually created (a 403 could theoretically be returned after partial creation, though unlikely). More importantly, the test relies on the permission check happening before validation; if the implementation order changes (validation before authz), the test would get 400 instead of 403 and fail — a brittle test. Similarly testManageGroup line 207 updates topGroup with myGroup representation (different id) expecting ForbiddenException; this tests that per-group manage on myGroup does not grant manage on topGroup, which is good coverage. The broader gap: no test verifies that getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns group ids (not resource ids) — the bug identified in GroupPermissionsV2 would not be caught by these tests because testCanViewUserByViewGroupMembers only checks user search results, and if the group id set were wrong the search would return empty and the test would fail — actually it would catch it. OK, this is adequate; downgrading to a note about brittle status-code-only assertions.

GroupPermissionsV2 throws UnsupportedOperationException for management methods still called from V1 code paths

GroupPermissionsV2 throws UnsupportedOperationException for isPermissionsEnabled, setPermissionsEnabled, viewMembersPermission, manageMembersPermission, manageMembershipPermission, viewPermission, managePermission, resource, and getPermissions (lines 168-210). However, GroupResource.getManagementPermissions (line 321-330) and setManagementPermissionsEnabled (line 354-365) call `AdminPermissions.management(session, realm)` which returns MgmtPermissionsV2 when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled, and then call permissions.groups().isPermissionsEnabled(group) / setPermissionsEnabled / resource / getPermissions. These endpoints are guarded by `ProfileHelper.requireFeature(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ)` (V1 feature), not V2 — so if both features are enabled (or V2 enabled while the V1-guarded endpoint is invoked), the call reaches GroupPermissionsV2 and throws UnsupportedOperationException, producing a 500 error on GET/PUT /admin/realms/{realm}/groups/{id}/management/permissions. Either the endpoints need a V2 guard/feature check, or GroupPermissionsV2 must implement these methods (e.g., returning a V2-appropriate ManagementPermissionReference). This is a runtime API break for the group management-permissions endpoint under V2.

UserPermissionsV2.isImpersonatable throws UnsupportedOperationException but is called from V1 code paths

UserPermissionsV2.isImpersonatable(UserModel, ClientModel) and isImpersonatable(UserModel) throw UnsupportedOperationException (lines 142-149). The base class UserPermissions.canImpersonate(UserModel, ClientModel) (line 356-362) calls `canImpersonate()` then `isImpersonatable(user, requester)`, and canClientImpersonate (line 340-353) calls `canImpersonate(context) && isImpersonatable(user)`. In V2, canImpersonate(UserModel, ClientModel) is overridden (line 65-74) and does not call isImpersonatable, and canClientImpersonate is overridden to delegate to canImpersonate(user, client) (line 137-139). However, any other caller of isImpersonatable (e.g., UserResource impersonation endpoints that check isImpersonatable directly, or the deprecated interface method used elsewhere) will hit UnsupportedOperationException under V2. The interface UserPermissionEvaluator still declares isImpersonatable as @Deprecated but not removed; if any V2-active code path (e.g., UserResource.impersonate) calls auth.users().isImpersonatable(...), it will throw. This should be verified; if UserResource only uses canImpersonate, the risk is limited to external/other callers, but the UnsupportedOperationException pattern for interface methods that remain on the public evaluator interface is fragile.

canView() and canManage() fall back to all-groups resource but do not check per-resource permission existence correctly when resource is null

In GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission, when groupId is null (global checks from canView()/canManage()), resource is set to null initially (line 141: `groupId == null ? null : ...`), then the `if (resource == null)` block fetches the all-groups resource type resource and checks `policyStore.findByResource(server, resource).isEmpty()`. If getResourceTypeResource returns null (schema not initialized), findByResource(server, null) behavior is undefined/likely NPE. Also, for the global canView()/canManage() path, the check `policyStore.findByResource(server, resource).isEmpty()` returns false (deny) when there are no policies on the all-groups resource — correct — but when groupId is null and the all-groups resource exists with policies, evaluation proceeds on the all-groups resource, which is correct. The null-resource NPE risk (line 147) applies to both global and per-group paths when the schema resource is missing. This is the same finding as the earlier NPE note but specifically for the global canView/canManage path where groupId is null and the resource type resource may not exist if init() was not called.

getOrCreateResource throws generic ModelException('No scopes found.') without identifying the missing scope

The real issue is the dead code plus the fact that the method does not validate that `signature.length == signLength`; if a caller passes a signature shorter than signLength, `System.arraycopy(signature, len, s, 1, len)` throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, and if longer, trailing bytes are silently ignored. For the DER-encoded ECDSA signatures this provider parses, indefinite length is illegal in DER, so it should be rejected with an IOException rather than treated as an empty sequence. As written, a crafted signature using indefinite-length encoding would be parsed as an empty sequence and then fail later with a confusing 'Invalid sequence with size different to 2' error, or worse, be misinterpreted.

false_positives.candidate:
integerToBytes silently truncates the most significant bytes of R or S when the DER integer is longer than the field length

In `asn1derToConcatenatedRS`, `integerToBytes(BigInteger s, int qLength)` handles the case `qLength < bytes.length` by copying the LAST `qLength` bytes (`System.arraycopy(bytes, bytes.length - tmp.length, tmp, 0, tmp.length)`), i.e. it keeps the least-significant bytes and drops the most-significant ones. For an ECDSA signature this is a signature-malleability/validation hazard: a DER-encoded integer whose value exceeds the curve field size (e.g. R or S >= n, or with extra leading zero/sign bytes making the byte array longer than expected) will be silently truncated instead of rejected. A verifier using this conversion could accept a signature whose R/S components were altered (the high bytes dropped), and the round-trip is not faithful. The correct behavior is to reject values that do not fit in `qLength` bytes (after stripping at most one leading 0x00 sign byte), as done by strict implementations. Note the truncation branch also mis-handles the legitimate DER case of a single leading 0x00 sign byte: for a 32-byte field with a 33-byte array (0x00 || 32 bytes), it would drop the leading zero correctly, but for a 33-byte array where the value genuinely needs 33 bytes it silently corrupts the value.

readLength() bounds check uses total input limit instead of remaining bytes

The check `if (length >= limit)` compares the declared content length against the TOTAL input size (`limit = bytes.length` set in the constructor), not against the number of bytes remaining after the tag and length octets have been consumed. A nested TLV (e.g. the INTEGERs inside the ECDSA SEQUENCE, parsed via `readNext()` on a sub-array) can therefore declare a length that runs past the end of its enclosing element but still be `< limit` of the outer buffer, and `read(length)` will happily read bytes belonging to the following sibling element or throw a misleading EOF. For the top-level sequence this is partially mitigated because `readSequence` re-slices via `readNext`, but for `readInteger()` called directly on a sub-array (as done in `asn1derToConcatenatedRS`: `ASN1Decoder.create(seq.get(0)).readInteger()`), the limit is the sub-array length, which is correct — however the general contract of the class is wrong and any future use on a stream position mid-buffer will over-read. The check should be `length > is.available()` (bytes remaining), not `length >= limit`.

asn1derToConcatenatedRS does not validate that the DER integers fit the expected signature length and does not reject negative/oversized values

The method decodes R and S from the DER sequence and converts them with `integerToBytes(value, len)` where `len = signLength / 2`. It never checks that `rBigInteger` or `sBigInteger` are non-negative or `< n` (the curve order), nor that their minimal byte encoding fits in `len` bytes. Combined with the truncation behavior in `integerToBytes` (see separate finding), a maliciously crafted DER signature with oversized or negative integers (BigInteger can be negative if the high bit of the content is set) will be silently truncated or sign-mangled and produce a fixed-length byte array that a caller may then feed to a raw ECDSA verifier. This is a signature-validation weakness: the conversion layer should reject any R/S that is negative or does not fit in `len` bytes after DER decoding, rather than truncating.

Previously, `detectProvider` threw `IllegalStateException` when more than one CryptoProvider was on the classpath ('Multiple crypto providers loaded...'). Now it sorts by `order()` descending and silently picks the first, only logging the ignored providers at DEBUG level. This is a behavioral/API contract change: any deployment that accidentally had two providers on the classpath (e.g. keycloak-crypto-default and keycloak-crypto-fips1402, or the new authz-client provider alongside the default one) previously failed fast at startup; now it will silently select one based on the arbitrary `order()` values (DefaultCryptoProvider=200, FIPS1402Provider=200, WildFlyElytronProvider=200, AuthzClientCryptoProvider=100). Because the server providers all share order 200 and the authz provider has order 100, the server provider should win — but only if it is visible to that classloader. If the authz-client is loaded by a child classloader that does NOT see the server's crypto provider jars, `AuthzClientCryptoProvider` will be selected and the static `cryptoProvider` will be permanently set to the authz provider for the whole JVM, after which the server's own `CryptoIntegration.init` is a no-op (`if (cryptoProvider == null)`) and the server silently uses the authz provider, whose methods mostly throw `UnsupportedOperationException('Not supported yet.')`. The test constructor generates one key pair with `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()`, which on a standard JVM produces a P-256 (secp256r1) key. `testES384` and `testES512` then sign with `SHA384withECDSA`/`SHA512withECDSA` using that P-256 key and pass `algorithm.getSignatureLength()` (96 and 128 bytes respectively) to the conversion methods. Given the provider's purpose (authz client), either restrict to formats the default JVM supports and document it, or register a BouncyCastle provider and use it explicitly.

UsernameForm skips the username step during re-authentication when conditional passkeys are enabled, breaking the username+password+passkey flow

The intent is to allow passkey re-authentication, but the condition is inverted with respect to the surrounding logic: when conditional passkeys ARE enabled the form is skipped entirely, so a user who must re-authenticate with username+password (e.g. a non-discoverable key, or a user without a passkey) is never asked for their username and the subsequent PasswordForm cannot validate anything. Conversely, when passkeys are disabled the old behavior (skip when user is set) is preserved. The check should be !isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() only for deciding whether passkeys can bypass the form; the skip should still happen when the user has no usable passkey path. As written, the separate UsernameForm + PasswordForm flow cannot complete a password re-authentication when the PASSKEYS feature and realm passkeys are enabled.

Refactor to shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators() changes behavior when the method is overridden to return false but a user is present

fillContextForm() previously branched on user != null to decide whether to build the WebAuthnAuthenticatorsBean (the list of allowed authenticators for a 2FA-style identified user). It now calls shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators(context), whose default implementation is context.getUser() != null, but WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator overrides it to always return false. In WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator.fillContextForm() (which calls super.fillContextForm()), this means that even when a user IS identified in the context (re-authentication with a known user), the ALLOWED_AUTHENTICATORS attribute is never set and isUserIdentified is always false. For the conditional UI this is intentional, but the base-class contract is now misleading: any other subclass overriding shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators() to false while still wanting per-user authenticator lists would silently lose them. More importantly, the new method name and javadoc ('true if the available webauthn authenticators should be shown on the screen') does not match what it actually controls (whether the per-user allowed-authenticators list is populated), which invites future misuse. The override in WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator should instead override a narrower hook or the base method should be documented/renamed to reflect that it gates the allowed-authenticators list.

createErrorResponse() calls setupReauthenticationInUsernamePasswordFormError() unconditionally, hiding the username field even for first-time logins

WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator.createErrorResponse() now calls AuthenticatorUtils.setupReauthenticationInUsernamePasswordFormError(context) on every WebAuthn error rendered through the conditional UI. That helper sets LoginFormsProvider.USERNAME_HIDDEN=true and REGISTRATION_DISABLED=true whenever the auth note USER_SET_BEFORE_USERNAME_PASSWORD_AUTH is 'true'. The note is only set by UsernamePasswordForm when a user is already in the context, so for a normal first-time login the helper is a no-op; however, the helper is invoked before fillContextForm(context) and before errorChallenge.apply(context), and it mutates the shared form provider obtained from context.form(). Because the same LoginFormsProvider instance is reused for the error challenge, any code path that reaches createErrorResponse() with the re-authentication note set (e.g. a passkey error during re-authentication on the username/password form) will hide the username field and disable registration on the error page. That is the desired behavior for re-authentication, but the method is placed in the generic WebAuthn error path rather than in the username/password-specific error challenge, so any future caller of WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator that is not the username/password form (the class is designed to be reusable via the errorChallenge function) would incorrectly get username-hiding/registration-disabling attributes applied to an unrelated form. The call belongs in the errorChallenge lambda supplied by UsernamePasswordForm, not in the generic authenticator.

Static import of USER_SET_BEFORE_USERNAME_PASSWORD_AUTH from AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator creates a package cycle and widens a constant's visibility unnecessarily

AuthenticatorUtils (in org.keycloak.authentication.authenticators.util) now statically imports AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator.USER_SET_BEFORE_USERNAME_PASSWORD_AUTH from org.keycloak.authentication.authenticators.browser. This introduces a dependency from the generic util package back into the browser authenticator package, and it required changing the constant from protected to public in AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator (line 58) solely to make it visible across packages. A public mutable-looking constant on an abstract authenticator class is a wider API surface than needed; the constant is an internal auth-note key. The cleaner approach is to move the constant (or a copy) into AuthenticatorUtils itself or into a shared constants class, and have AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator reference it from there, avoiding both the package cycle and the visibility widening.

reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey asserts absence of the webauthn form with a try/catch that swallows all exceptions, making the assertion ineffective

The test reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey verifies that the webauthn button is absent by calling driver.findElement(By.xpath("//form[@id='webauth']")) inside a try block and catching Exception, with a fail() only if findElement returns normally. Selenium's findElement throws NoSuchElementException when the element is absent, so the catch block is the expected path; however, catching the broad Exception type also swallows any other failure (e.g. StaleElementReferenceException, WebDriverException, or a page not fully loaded) and treats it as success. If the page is in an unexpected state or the driver errors for an unrelated reason, the test will pass even though the webauthn form might actually be present. The assertion should use a proper negative assertion such as assertThrows(NoSuchElementException.class, () -> driver.findElement(...)) or a Hamcrest matcher on findElements(...).isEmpty(), and the same pattern is repeated at line 312 for the re-authentication page.

webauthnLoginWithExternalKey_reauthenticationWithPasswordOrPasskey submits a password without a username during re-authentication and relies on a hidden username field

In webauthnLoginWithExternalKey_reauthenticationWithPasswordOrPasskey, after triggering re-authentication with prompt=login, the test calls loginPage.login(getPassword("test-user@localhost")) (line 377) and later loginPage.login(getPassword(USERNAME)) (line 410) with only a password argument. The single-argument login() overload submits only the password field, assuming the username is pre-filled/hidden. This works only if the form correctly sets USERNAME_HIDDEN and pre-populates the username, which is exactly the behavior changed by this PR (setupReauthenticationInUsernamePasswordFormError). If the re-authentication form regression (username not hidden / not pre-filled) occurs, the test would submit an empty username and fail with a confusing 'Invalid username or password' error rather than clearly asserting the re-authentication form state. The test should explicitly assert that the username field is hidden and contains the expected user (e.g. via loginPage.getAttemptedUsername() or by checking the hidden input value) before submitting the password-only login, so that a regression in the re-authentication form setup is caught with a clear message.

PasskeysUsernameFormTest still asserts that the webauthn form is absent after username entry, contradicting the new behavior where conditional passkeys remain enabled

In passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey, after the user enters a valid username on the UsernameForm, the test asserts Assert.assertThrows(NoSuchElementException.class, () -> driver.findElement(By.xpath("//form[@id='webauth']"))) (line 202), i.e. that the webauthn conditional UI form is NOT present on the subsequent password page. However, the PR's stated goal (and the corresponding change in PasskeysOrganizationAuthenticationTest, which now asserts the form IS present) is that passkeys remain enabled during the username/password flow even after the username is known. The UsernameForm+PasswordForm split flow uses PasswordForm, which does not embed the WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator, so the webauthn form may legitimately be absent here; but the test does not document why this flow differs from the UsernamePasswordForm flow, and the assertion will break if PasswordForm is later changed to support conditional passkeys. At minimum the test should comment why the webauthn form is expected to be absent in this split-form flow, otherwise a future change that enables passkeys on PasswordForm will produce a confusing failure.

false_positives.candidate:
max_processes=0 silently disables all flusher processes

In `SpanFlusher.__init__`, `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` uses `or`, so a caller passing `max_processes=0` (e.g. a misconfigured `--flusher-processes 0` CLI value, which the click option in `src/sentry/consumers/__init__.py` does not validate) silently falls back to one process per shard instead of being rejected. `self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards))` then becomes 0, `process_to_shards_map` is an empty dict, no flusher processes are created, and `submit()` iterates over zero buffers — meaning `record_stored_segments()` and the Redis memory backpressure check are both skipped entirely, so spans accumulate in Redis with no flushing and no backpressure protection. The CLI option should validate `flusher_processes >= 1` (like `convert_max_batch_time` does for batch time), or the constructor should raise on non-positive values.

Division by zero when the consumer is assigned zero shards

`self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards))` followed by `process_index = i % self.num_processes` will raise `ZeroDivisionError` if `buffer.assigned_shards` is empty (i.e. `create_with_partitions` is called with an empty partitions mapping, which can happen transiently during rebalancing in arroyo). Previously the code created a single process unconditionally, so an empty shard list was tolerated. Now the consumer crashes during rebalance instead of running an idle flusher.

Each flusher process creates its own SpansBuffer with only its shards, but the main consumer still writes to the original full-shard buffer — flusher processes never see the spans

In `factory.py`, `create_with_partitions` creates `buffer = SpansBuffer(assigned_shards=[p.index for p in partitions])` and passes it to `process_batch`, which calls `buffer.process_spans(...)` — this buffer writes spans into Redis. However, `SpanFlusher.__init__` no longer stores or uses that buffer; instead `_create_process_for_shards` (flusher.py line 93) creates a *new* `SpansBuffer(shards)` per process containing only that process's shards. `SpansBuffer` instances are independent objects — the new per-process buffers share nothing with the main buffer except the underlying Redis keys. The flusher processes call `buffer.flush_segments(now=now)` on their own buffer instances. Whether this works depends entirely on `SpansBuffer` keeping all mutable state in Redis rather than in instance attributes. If `SpansBuffer` keeps any in-memory state (e.g. cached segment metadata, in-flight segment tracking, `record_stored_segments` bookkeeping, or the `any_shard_at_limit` flag computed from instance state), the flusher processes will flush nothing or corrupt segment state, because the main process's `process_spans`/`record_stored_segments` calls mutate a different object. Additionally, `submit()` calls `buffer.record_stored_segments()` on the per-process buffers (line 269-270), but the spans were written via the *main* buffer — if `record_stored_segments` reconciles in-memory state with Redis, calling it on a buffer that never had `process_spans` called on it is wrong. This needs verification that `SpansBuffer` is fully stateless across instances (all state in Redis), and if so, that should be documented; the old code passed the *same* buffer object to the flusher process, so this is a behavioral change that could silently break flushing.

`any_shard_at_limit` is checked on the per-process buffer but reflects only that process's shards — cross-process backpressure is incomplete

In `SpanFlusher.main`, the backpressure flag is set based on `buffer.any_shard_at_limit` where `buffer` is the per-process `SpansBuffer(shards)` containing only that process's shards. Previously there was a single buffer covering all assigned shards, so `any_shard_at_limit` was a global signal. Now each process only sees its own shards. That part is arguably correct per-process. However, in `submit()` (lines 297-313), the Redis memory check aggregates `get_memory_info()` across all per-process buffers — but if `SpansBuffer.get_memory_info()` only reports memory for its own `assigned_shards`, and the per-process buffers were constructed with `SpansBuffer(shards)` where `shards` is a subset, the aggregation may double-count or miss shards depending on how `get_memory_info` uses `assigned_shards`. More importantly, the per-process buffers in `self.buffers` are *separate instances* from the main consumer's buffer (see related finding) — if `get_memory_info()` reads instance-cached state rather than querying Redis directly, the memory check in `submit()` will report zero/stale memory and the hard backpressure protection (`spans.buffer.max-memory-percentage`) will never trigger, allowing unbounded Redis memory growth.

Dead code: `_create_process_for_shard` is never called

`_create_process_for_shard(self, shard: int)` is defined but never referenced anywhere in the file — `_ensure_processes_alive` calls `_create_process_for_shards` directly with the full shard list for the process. Either this method should be removed, or `_ensure_processes_alive` was intended to use it for per-shard restart granularity. As written it is dead code that will confuse future maintainers.

Restart path leaks the old process object and its buffer without joining or closing it

In `_ensure_processes_alive`, when a process is unhealthy, the code calls `process.kill()` (for `multiprocessing.Process`) and then `self._create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)`, which overwrites `self.processes[process_index]` and `self.buffers[process_index]` with new objects. The old process is killed but never `join()`ed, and the old `SpansBuffer` is dropped without any cleanup. For a `spawn`-context process, `kill()` sends SIGKILL — the process may be in the middle of `buffer.flush_segments()` or `producer.produce()`, potentially leaving Redis segment keys in a partially-flushed state (e.g. segments marked as flushed but not actually produced to Kafka, or vice versa depending on `done_flush_segments` ordering). Since `flush_segments` → `produce` → `done_flush_segments` is not atomic, killing the process between `produce` and `done_flush_segments` means those segments will be re-flushed on restart (duplicate spans in the buffered-segments topic) or, worse, if killed after `done_flush_segments` but before the Kafka produce future resolves, spans are lost. The old code had the same kill-without-join pattern for a single process, but with multiple processes the window and blast radius are larger. At minimum the old process should be `join()`ed after `kill()` before creating the replacement, and the restart logic should be reviewed for segment-loss/duplication semantics.

`join()` terminates processes even if they exited cleanly, and does not join them

In `join()`, after waiting for each process to finish (or the deadline to expire), the code calls `process.terminate()` unconditionally for any `multiprocessing.Process`. If the process already exited on its own (because `stopped.value` was set), `terminate()` on a dead process is a no-op in CPython but the process is never `join()`ed, so its resources (PID, shared memory segments backing the `mp_context.Value` objects) are not reaped until garbage collection. With repeated rebalances (each `create_with_partitions` creates a new `SpanFlusher` with new processes), unreaped zombie processes and leaked shared-memory segments can accumulate. The code should call `process.join(timeout=...)` after the wait loop (or instead of `terminate()` when the process has already exited) to properly reap child processes.

Shared `multiprocessing.Value` objects are never closed, leaking shared memory across rebalances

`SpanFlusher.__init__` creates `self.stopped`, `self.current_drift`, and per-process `process_healthy_since`/`process_backpressure_since` as `mp_context.Value("i", ...)` objects. These allocate shared memory (`/dev/shm` on Linux). Neither `close()` nor `join()` nor `terminate()` closes these `Value` objects (via `.close()` on the underlying `Synchronized` wrapper, available in Python 3.13+ via `multiprocessing.shared_memory` / `Value.close()`). Every rebalance creates a new `SpanFlusher` (via `create_with_partitions`) with a fresh set of `Value` objects and new spawned processes; the old ones are only released when garbage collected, and the spawned child processes hold references to the shared memory segments. Over many rebalances this leaks `/dev/shm` segments and can exhaust shared memory on the host. The flusher should close all `Value` objects in `join()` after the processes have exited.

Drift is applied globally but each flusher process computes `now` independently — clock skew between processes causes inconsistent segment expiry

In `submit()`, `self.current_drift.value = message.payload - int(time.time())` sets a single global drift shared across all processes. In `main()`, each process computes `now = system_now + current_drift.value` using its own `int(time.time())`. Since `system_now` is read at slightly different times in each process and `current_drift` is updated asynchronously, different flusher processes can flush segments at slightly different effective timestamps. More importantly, if one process is slow (e.g. blocked on `future.result()` for Kafka produce), its `system_now` lags, so it flushes with an older `now` than a fast process — segments may be expired by one process but not another in the same cycle, or a segment may be flushed by a process whose clock is behind, causing premature or delayed expiry relative to the consumer's intent. The drift mechanism was designed for a single flusher; with N processes the per-process `time.time()` reads introduce skew. The drift should either be computed from a single authoritative clock read per cycle, or each process should record the `now` it used and the parent should reconcile.

New multiprocess flusher behavior is not actually tested end-to-end; test only checks process count

`test_flusher_processes_limit` only asserts that `len(flusher.processes) == 2` and that shards are distributed — it never submits any spans, never advances the drift, and never asserts that segments are actually flushed to `messages`. It calls `step.join()` immediately after construction, so it would pass even if the flusher processes did nothing at all. The critical behavior of this PR — that multiple flusher processes correctly flush segments from their assigned shards to Kafka — is not covered. There should be a test that submits spans across multiple partitions/shards with `flusher_processes < num_shards`, advances the drift, and asserts that all segments are flushed exactly once (no duplicates, no missing segments), which is the main correctness risk of sharding the flusher.

Kafka produce futures are only awaited when segments were flushed; if `flush_segments` returns empty, pending futures from a previous iteration could be dropped

In `main()`, `producer_futures` is a local list. The loop only reaches `for future in producer_futures: future.result()` (line 200-201) when `flushed_segments` is non-empty (otherwise it `continue`s at line 183 after sleeping). `producer_futures.clear()` at line 203 only runs after the futures are awaited. However, if an exception occurs inside the `produce` timer block (e.g. `orjson.dumps` fails) after some futures were appended but before they are awaited, the exception propagates out of the `while` loop, the process crashes, and those produce futures are never awaited — Kafka messages may or may not have been delivered, and the segments are not marked done (since `done_flush_segments` is after), so they will be re-flushed on restart (duplicates). This is a pre-existing pattern but is more impactful with multiple processes. Consider wrapping the produce+wait in a `try/finally` to always await/clear futures, or at least document the at-least-once semantics on crash.

false_positives.candidate:
delete_matched_rows deletes only the last replay_id instead of all matched replays

In `delete_matched_rows(project_id, rows)`, the loop `for row in rows: delete_replay_recordings(project_id, row)` deletes the recording segments for every row, but the subsequent call `delete_replays(project_id, [row["replay_id"] for row in rows])` is placed AFTER the loop, so `row` refers to the last iterated row. The list comprehension `[row["replay_id"] for row in rows]` is evaluated after the loop completes, which is correct, but the indentation in the shown code places it at function scope after the loop — actually re-reading: the comprehension iterates `rows` again so it does collect all replay_ids. However, the real bug is that `delete_replay_recordings` is called per-row inside the loop (fine), but if `rows` is empty the function returns early (fine). The actual defect: the archive events are published for all rows, but `delete_replay_recordings` is invoked once per row — that is correct. The genuine issue is that `delete_matched_rows` returns `None` always and the caller cannot know how many rows were processed; more importantly, the function name and the loop suggest per-row deletion but the archive publish happens once with all ids — this is fine. The concrete bug: the `for row in rows:` loop variable `row` is reused in the list comprehension after the loop; in Python the comprehension has its own scope so this is safe. The real problem is that `delete_replay_recordings` is called inside the loop but `delete_replays` (which archives) is called after — if `delete_replay_recordings` raises for one row, the archive events for ALL rows are never published, leaving recordings deleted but replays not archived (data integrity: replays remain visible but their segments are gone). This is a data-integrity risk: partial failure leaves inconsistent state.

response[0].get("error_ids", []) assumes the first row contains error_ids without validating the field was requested

`error_ids = response[0].get("error_ids", []) if response else []` — `process_raw_response` is called with `fields=request.query_params.getlist("field")`. If the client does not request the `error_ids` field, the Snuba response rows will not contain `error_ids`, and `.get("error_ids", [])` silently returns `[]`, so error context is silently omitted even when `enable_error_context` is not "false". The endpoint should either always request `error_ids` from Snuba or document that error context requires the field. Consequence: error context is silently dropped depending on client `field` params, making the `enable_error_context` query param unreliable.

Unauthenticated endpoint logs full request body at info level, risking PII/secret leakage into logs

The endpoint has `permission_classes = ()` and is CSRF-exempt, and `logger.info("browser_report_received", extra={"request_body": request.data})` logs the entire raw request body (which includes `body` dicts that can contain arbitrary page content, URLs, user agents, and potentially user-entered data from the page) at INFO level. Browser reports can contain sensitive page content (e.g., CSP violation reports include the blocked URI and sometimes form data; deprecation/intervention reports include source file URLs and messages). Logging full request bodies from an unauthenticated, internet-facing endpoint at INFO level creates a log-injection/PII-exposure risk and unbounded log volume (DoS via log flooding). Consequence: sensitive data leakage into logs and potential log-based DoS.

Non-list request body is logged with full data before validation, and 422 returned without size limits

Combined with the unauthenticated nature of the endpoint, this is a log-flooding vector. Additionally, the serializer validation loop returns on the FIRST invalid report, discarding all subsequent reports in the batch — a single malformed report causes the entire batch to be rejected (fail-closed), which may be intended but should be documented; more importantly, the full `raw_report` is logged on validation failure (`extra={"validation_errors": serializer.errors, "raw_report": report}`), again logging unvalidated user-controlled data.

This is a minor design issue.

Regex for validating attribute keys rejects valid EAP span attribute keys containing hyphens in tag names

The validation regex `/^[a-zA-Z0-9_.:-]+$/` allows hyphens, but the comment says "EAP spans contain tags with illegal characters / SnQL forbids `-` but is allowed in RPC. So add it back later". The second regex `/^tags\[[a-zA-Z0-9_.:-]+,number\]$/` also allows hyphens inside the tag name. However, the first regex is applied to ALL attribute keys, including `tags[...]` keys. A key like `tags[http.status_code,number]` would fail the first regex (because of `[`, `]`, `,`) but pass the second. But a key like `tags[my-tag,number]` passes the second regex (hyphen allowed). The issue: the first regex does NOT match `tags[...]` format at all (square brackets and comma not in the character class), so `tags[...]` keys are only accepted via the second regex. But the second regex only matches `tags[...,number]` — string tags in `tags[name]` format (without `,number`) would fail BOTH regexes and be silently dropped. This means string-valued tag attributes in `tags[attr]` format are incorrectly filtered out. Consequence: valid string tag attributes are missing from the search bar suggestions.

request.user.id will raise AttributeError for unauthenticated requests (org auth token auth)

processing_deadline_duration=30 for schedule_webhook_delivery may be too short for batch webhook scheduling

run_top_events_timeseries_query now accepts equations parameter but passes it through — verify rpc_dataset_common supports it for ourlogs

findAllFieldRefs filters writablePageParams.aggregateFields with isBaseVisualize but readablePageParams with isVisualize — inconsistent filtering may miss field refs

ChartInfo.yAxes is now always a single-element array [visualize.yAxis], but downstream code may expect multiple yAxes per chart

Analytics visualizes field changed from raw Visualize[] to visualizes.map(v => v.toJSON()), but the analytics event schema may expect a different shape

yAxes useMemo pushes DEFAULT_VISUALIZATION then dedupes and sorts — but the sort order may not match visualize order

queryOptions useMemo dependency on `selection` object causes unnecessary recomputation when selection reference changes

`const queryOptions = useMemo(() => {...}, [selection, traceItemType, type, projectIds])` — `selection` is an object from `usePageFilters()`. If `usePageFilters` returns a new object reference on every render (even if the contents are the same), the `useMemo` will recompute every render, and the `queryKey` will change, causing `useQuery` to refetch. This is a common React pitfall. The `selection` object should be destructured to its primitive dependencies (e.g., `selection.datetime`, `selection.projects`) to avoid unnecessary refetches.

determineDefaultChartType reduce starts with ChartType.AREA as initial accumulator, which biases toward AREA on ties

`return [ChartType.AREA, ChartType.BAR, ChartType.LINE].reduce((acc, ct) => (counts[ct] >= counts[acc] ? ct : acc), ChartType.AREA)` — the initial accumulator is `ChartType.AREA`. On a tie (e.g., all counts are 0, or AREA and BAR have equal counts), the `>=` comparison means the later element wins only if strictly greater or equal. Since AREA is first in the array and the initial acc, if all counts are 0, AREA wins (0 >= 0). If BAR and LINE tie at 1 each and AREA is 0, BAR wins (1 >= 0), then LINE (1 >= 1) wins — so LINE wins ties against BAR. The initial AREA means AREA wins when all are 0. This is arbitrary but not a bug per se. The function is only called with a single yAxis now, so the counts will always be 0 or 1 for one chart type.

parseBaseVisualize uses Number(parsed.chartType) which coerces string chart types to NaN, silently dropping valid string enum values

`const chartType = Number(parsed.chartType); if (Object.values(ChartType).includes(chartType))` — `ChartType` is a TypeScript enum. If it's a numeric enum, `Number(parsed.chartType)` works. But if `ChartType` is a string enum (e.g., `LINE = 'line'`), `Number('line')` is `NaN`, and `Object.values(ChartType).includes(NaN)` is false, so the chartType is silently dropped. The test `converts from JSON with chart type` passes `chartType: ChartType.AREA` which is already the enum value (number or string). If the URL contains the string representation (e.g., `"line"`), `Number("line")` is NaN and the chart type is lost. This depends on whether ChartType is a numeric or string enum. If it's a string enum, this is a bug — the chartType from URL params would always be dropped.

Label generation String.fromCharCode(65 + i) breaks for more than 26 visualizes (produces non-letter characters)

`label: String.fromCharCode(65 + i)` — this generates labels 'A', 'B', ..., 'Z' for i=0..25. For i >= 26, it produces '[', '\', ']', etc. — non-letter characters. The `MAX_VISUALIZES = 4` constant limits visualizes to 4, so i will never exceed 3 in practice. But the code in `getAggregateFieldsFromLocation` doesn't enforce MAX_VISUALIZES — it processes all parsed visualizes from the URL. A crafted URL with 30 visualizes would produce labels like '^', '_', '`'. This is a minor robustness issue.

updateLocationWithAggregateFields flatMap return type is string[] but location.query.aggregateField expects string[] — the flatMap produces one string per yAxis for BaseVisualize, which is correct, but the type of aggregateFields parameter is Array<GroupBy | BaseVisualize> which doesn't include Visualize

The function signature is `updateLocationWithAggregateFields(location, aggregateFields: Array<GroupBy | BaseVisualize> | null | undefined)`. But callers may pass `AggregateField[]` which is `GroupBy | Visualize`. `Visualize` is not assignable to `BaseVisualize` (Visualize has `yAxis`, BaseVisualize has `yAxes`). The `isBaseVisualize` check would return false for a `Visualize` instance (since it checks for `yAxes` array), so a `Visualize` would fall through to the `else` branch and be JSON.stringified directly — producing `{"yAxis": "...", "label": "...", ...}` instead of the expected `{"yAxes": ["..."]}` format. This would create malformed URL params. The caller in `aggregateColumnEditorModal.tsx` converts Visualize to BaseVisualize via `toJSON()` before calling, so it's fine there. But the type signature suggests Visualize should be accepted, which would break.

else branch assumes aggregateField is a Visualize (has yAxis) but the type is AggregateField = GroupBy | Visualize — TypeScript should catch this but the isGroupBy check narrows correctly

The code does `if (isGroupBy(aggregateField)) { ... } else { ... aggregateField.yAxis ... }`. TypeScript's type narrowing with `isGroupBy` (a type guard `value is GroupBy`) should narrow the else branch to `Visualize`, which has `yAxis`. This is correct. No bug.

dedupeArray import is still used but could be replaced with a Set for clarity since yAxes are now unique per Visualize

`dedupeArray` is still imported and used on `allYAxes` which is `visualizes.map(v => v.yAxis)` plus `DEFAULT_VISUALIZATION`. Since each Visualize has a unique yAxis (they're separate charts), the only possible duplicate is `DEFAULT_VISUALIZATION` appearing both as a visualize's yAxis and as the injected default. `dedupeArray` handles this correctly. Not a bug, just noting the import is still needed.

Removed check for visualizes with multiple yAxes — but Visualize no longer supports multiple yAxes, so the check was dead code

The removed check `if (visualizes.some(visualize => visualize.yAxes.length > 1)) { return undefined; }` was checking for multi-yAxis visualizes. Since `Visualize` now only has a single `yAxis`, this check would always be false (dead code). Removing it is correct. However, the comment above the hook says "There's a limitation with this hook when a top n query < 5 series. This hook always returns 5" — this limitation still exists and is now more pronounced since each visualize is a single series. The hook returns `TOP_EVENTS_LIMIT` (5) whenever there's at least one group by in aggregate mode, regardless of how many visualizes (series) exist. In BaseDetectorTypeValidator.update(), the validator incorrectly updates instance.type using validated_data.get('detector_type') instead of validated_data.get('type').

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative-offset slicing in OptimizedCursorPaginator silently returns wrong rows or raises IndexError

When `enable_advanced_features` is true and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code executes `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset` (e.g. `queryset[-5:96]`). Django QuerySets do NOT support negative slicing — this raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported.` at query evaluation time, turning any request with a negative cursor offset into a 500 error. Even if it were supported (e.g. on a list), negative slicing counts from the END of the result set, which would return the wrong rows entirely (the last N rows of the table rather than rows before the cursor), corrupting pagination results. The comment 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is factually wrong. Additionally, the cursor value is attacker-controlled via the `cursor` query parameter, so any client of the audit log endpoint passing `optimized_pagination=true` with a crafted negative-offset cursor triggers this. The negative-offset branch must be removed or replaced with a correct reverse-pagination implementation.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same issue as the golden comment. It names negative slicing on Django querysets in OptimizedCursorPaginator and explicitly says this raises an AssertionError.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the audit log endpoint orders by '-datetime'

`OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` does `int(math.floor(value) ...)` on `getattr(item, self.key)`. The endpoint wires it with `order_by="-datetime"`, so `self.key == "datetime"` and `value` is a `datetime` object — `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError`, so every paginated request through this paginator crashes with a 500. The class is a copy of `Paginator` (integer keys) and was never adapted to datetime keys; it should subclass/reuse `DateTimePaginator`'s key handling (millisecond conversion via `strftime("%s.%f")` and `value_from_cursor` converting back with `datetime.fromtimestamp`), otherwise the 'optimized' path is entirely broken for the only endpoint that uses it.
